pages.transcription:
Taft Hotel
Newhaven, Conn

15.2.41

Dear Hanna,
Don't be surprised if Eva writes you that she had
to change school in Groton after a few days. The head-mistress
of the private, 'progressive' school (I wrote you all about it before)
was very eager to have Eva and as good as promised me a scholar-
ship for her which, as she said, would almost certainly be granted
if she wanted to accept a child. The board of trustees (by the trustees
however, only met after an unforeseen delay of a few days)
and she told Mrs Schaeffer to send Eva to her school in the meantime.
Now unfortunately the trustees decided that their resources did not
allow for another scholarship, even though the head of the school had
recommended it and so Eva had to change. I am sorry for Eva to
whom this change probably is not too welcome, although she knew that
all depended on the decision about the scholarship. But we explained
her before, and Mrs. Sch. told me she explained her again that it had
nothing to do with her personal qualities but depended on the school's
funds, and so I hope she will soon settle down in the public school
which is also supposed to be good. I have no reports yet how she
likes it, it is too soon, but some other children of Mrs Sch's also
go there and are very happy there. And as Mrs. Sch. told me that all
her children took part in all of the private school's festivals and
other functions, it will be no complete break and she will continue
to meet the friends she may have made in those few days. - I wrote you
in my last letter that I had visited Eva and found her happy
in her new surroundings and quite her old self as she was at
home, and Mrs Sch wrote me that she continues that way and is quite
"zugänglich" and satisfied. The children I met there I liked extremely
well and she certainly does not lack nice company, and Mrs. Sch of
whom both Stefan and I have a very good impression, thinks and
speaks and treats children like ourselves. Eva may go away over
the weekend once a month (have visitors or go out for the day every
Sat. and Sunday) and we will have her here as soon as we can. -
We have nearly given up hope for finding a furnished apartment,
it is extremely difficult here, and we will probably remain at this hotel.
It is not ideal, but Stefan got a nice room to work in, I do my best
not to lose myself in all the papers in the bedroom, and so we are
quite satisfied and work quite hard. There is the library very near at hand,
a long wanted pleasure, Stefan may take books home and there is no
question of being lonely. He had lunch with the head librarian and
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief auf Hotelpapier. Sehr gut lesbar.
Rückseite der ersten Seite, leer.

pages.transcription:
his wife - a sculptor - today, both extremely nice, Thornton Wilder
and Hindemith live in Newhaven, Shalom Asch who has a house about
an hour away, dropped in two days ago, Maass is with us to day,
and several other friends live not too far away. The trains to
Newyork are a real pleasure and I can't tell you how much I
enjoy it after all that flying which is boring and makes you
tired without any special reason. - I address this letter to Bath
as we hope that you have gone there with Manfred to have a good
rest after his exam. You should not spend the spring in London, it
is so much quieter in Bath, and how lovely is spring there! I wish we
could be with you!
Tell Lotte Smollett again how sorry I was not to be
able to see her children. But it takes nearly an hour by train
to go out there, and I had lots of things to do in that short
time, I unfortunately could not manage it. My hope is that
someone will take me out in a car one day, and I certainly keep
it in mind. - About Carmel's children I wrote you some time ago.
I saw Robin and had the impression that he felt quite at home
and was on the best terms with Berner's and Rose. John who is now
with a friend of Carmel's, Tony --? seems to be really very diffi-
cult. He apparently has made up his mind to dislike everything
and is only satisfied when he goes to the movies. I have the im-
pression that Berner's and Rose really tried their best to understand
him, to please him and by discussing things with him. But he
seems to want not to like America.
I must go out now, so only kindest regards
and best love,
Lotte

pages.transcription:
Taft Hotel
Newhaven, Conn.                                     17.2.41

Dear Hanna u Manfred, I have written you two days ago about Eva's
schools. In the meantime I phoned her and Mrs. Sch. and heard
that everything is alright. This week I expect information about
her music lessons - that is to say, new teacher - and also, whether and
when she has holidays and in March, and I suppose we will then take
her here although besides us there are no attractions in Newhaven.
There is not much to report from here. The weather is rather bad at the
moment, storm or snow or cold alternatively, so we work quietly
without any desire to go out. We had Maass here for two days this
afternoon comes Thornton Wilder, Wednesday Landshof who just phoned
that he has seen Manfred before leaving and we are naturally
impatient to meet him. Saturday we may go up to Newyork to see
the publisher as well as a "Fidelio" performance conducted by Bruno
Walter. - We had no letter from you last week, but as the clipper
arrived yesterday, I hope to get one to-morrow.
                                     Best love and kisses Lotte
Please give the attached letter to Rauman's.

Dear Mr. and Mrs. Rauman,
                                     Newhaven, 17.2.41
I am glad to hear that you have become faithful Bethonians
and it is a good feeling to know you at "Rosemount", keeping Mama
company and I hope, enjoying Bath as we always did. Hanna wrote me
that the children were acting Mr. Rauman's play, and this information
combined with the fact that you also like coffee, gives me complete
assurance that our tradition is being maintained. I hope that your
pets are on good terms with the children and suppose that they enjoy
being in the country. Stefan has just written a short story - the main
character a bulldog, the setting the Kenneth-Avon canal (is the name
right, I have half forgotten it already) in a house on the hill to Bethampton,
I am sure you would like this combination of families landscape
and dog psychology. It gave Stefan pleasure to write it and kept me
busy in Newyork besides my other activities of resettling Eva and
flat-hunting in Newhaven. I have been successful with Eva, I
believe, but unsuccessful in finding a flat, and so we are continuing
our hotel life which gets more complicated in the degree as papers,
necessary books and manuscripts accumulate. But we are enjoying
being again in a smaller town, seeing snow and having cold fresh air,
and the greatest pleasure are the books. - Once more: we are very happy to
know you in our house and hope that you will continue to enjoy it in relative
peacefulness and quiet. 
                                     Kindest regards from us both, Lotte Zweig
pages.notes: Brief auf rosa Papier. Am linken Rand vertikal geschriebene Notizen: 'We enclose a letter of Eva's which just arrived' (oben) und 'Kindest regards Stefan Zweig' (unten).
Rückseite des Dokuments, leer.

pages.transcription:
New Haven, Hotel Taft
Dear Hannah and Manfred, Lotte phoned yesterday with your daughter
and we heard with pleasure that she feels happy and also the new school
- the public school in which she is now going as the progressive school was
no more scholarship available - seems to please her. She is there the youn-
gest of all, the nearest to her a boy which will be 13 soon. Perhaps she
will have to work harder there as in New-Rochelle, but she will manage it,
I am quite sure. Mr. Salmon has invited her for the week end and I hope
she will enjoy it very much, meeting her schoolfellows. She will have
her school holidays in March and we will do our possible to see her then
or to have her with us.
We are living here in a little, not very artistic town, but I have all
facilities at the Yale University. I can take as many books at home
as I like and you may imagine, how helpful this is; the head librarian is
a charming man and we have been invited in his house; today Thornton
Wilder is coming, yesterday and last week Shalom Asch and Joachim
Maas - you see, we live not in a wilderness, but I have time to read and
to write.
As you are managing all my things I would ask you to send
through my bank eighteen Pounds to Max H. Bresch consultant
on International Law Ibex-House, Minories London EC 3 which
amount I am due for a consultation of his American office. Con-
cerning all other things I shall write directly to my chartered
accountant Mr. Wilmot. As to the house I know that all is there
in best order; please give my best regards to Mr. Miller and all
the good helpers. Sometimes we are weary of this Hotel life but
there are such difficulties with apartments - service etc - that we
must continue. Perhaps in Rio, where everything is cheaper and easier
than here. But who can make plans? We live and wait and wait
and live, so dont let us wait to long for good news that you have
a well merited rest at Bath. Love to all. Yours Stefan Zweig
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief auf rosa Papier. Sehr gut lesbar.
Rückseite des Dokuments, leer.

pages.transcription:
Taft Hotel
Newhaven, Conn.                                          March 7th, 41

Dear Hanna & Manfred, Finally, after 4 weeks without news (except
that cable last week) your letter N° 4, Hanna, of Febr. 16th. Letter N° 3
has not yet arrived, but I hope we will still get it. There has
been such a muddle with the clippers lately, which were delayed,
damaged, flown another route, all owing to storms, that I am not
surprised about a mix-up in mail, bad as it is for us who wait
just as impatiently for your letters as you for ours and Eva's.
First of all, congratulations to Manfred for his exam! Actually we had
expected a telegram about it as it is after all a superior degree
and as far as I know, rather difficult. We hope that you follow
our advise and take Manfred to Bath for a good long rest after
this strain, Hanna. Why should he spend spring in London if he can
take his holiday in the country? I fully understand that you miss
Eva and that you sometimes wish she were still with you. It is an
unreasonable mood, yet I often feel the same about our being
here and think that in spite of all and everything I would prefer
to be in Rosemount with you and in our old surroundings. But
as you say yourself those are moods and one can reason them
away. - Now about Eva. At last I feel sure that you get regular
news as Sunday is writing-day whatever happens, and I asked
Mrs. Sch to add a few words to you now and then. I am in
constant touch, phoned Eva several times, and we had letters
- those sunday letters - from her and Mrs. Sch. She seems very
happy there, has come to like the new school - I wrote you
that she is after all in the Public School, a big modern
school and that we are not at all sorry that the Private
school was not possible in the end - has a piano teacher,
"a very ambitious one" - she writes, plays two Mozart sonatas, one
for practice and one for reading, has spent a weekend with
Salmon's, has been to a concert and feels altogether fine.
There are more children about her age now at Sch's, and
so far as I saw the children, I liked them very much.
Just when I was there last time, two Alstein-children, a boy
and a girl of 12 and 14 (third generation of the publishing firm)
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief auf Taft Hotel Briefpapier. Seite 1.
Rückseite der ersten Seite, leer.

pages.transcription:
2)
just arrived, both extremely nice. One thing Eva is not too keen
about yet, is being outdoors, and as it was a nasty cold winter
I do not blame her for it. She is well equipped for it though,
for I bought her, what all the others wear there a snow suit, jacket
and trousers, wind- and waterproof, with a hood, and high snow boots.
Besides this she did not need anything to keep her warm as the
house and school are well-heated. (Not to have central-heating
and a huge refrigerator means extreme poverty in USA). Eva has holi-
days in the beginning of March and April and I think we will
take her here although it will not be very exciting for her, but we
would like to have her with us. On the whole I am very glad that
we have finally settled her with Mrs. Sch. and I feel that it
is the right thing for her. In all the deliberations and consi-
derations what would be best for Eva I have tried to do always
as I think you would have acted, and I feel quite sure that
you would have come to the same conclusions as I did and
chose Mrs. Sch. as a home with the advantage that there are
more children, more supervision and entertainment and a woman
which you would like very much, as the head of the whole who
spends all her time on it and runs it as much as possible on
family lines. As to schools, the one in Groton is good and you
would find the same story everywhere, all the English children
I hear about are about a year ahead of the American children. -
Now about us: we lead a quiet life with plenty of work and books,
enjoy the neighborhood of the library and are not at all lonely.
I have been in Newyork once and Stefan twice since we are here,
and we have had several visitors; one of them was Landshof who
told us that he had seen Manfred just before leaving and who
brought for Eva a little parcel which I hope he has sent her in
the meantime. He had the same idea like I with the Smollett
children, he said he would pass at Eva's place one day, and I
had to explain that it was 40 minutes by train. - I am glad
to hear that in Bath all is going well and that instead of Love
(where has she gone to?) you have another member of the Miller
family. I don't know how well Hilda cooks and I hope she likes
work better than her sister, but in any case it is good that you
have people on whom you can rely that they will not leave you.

It is strange to think that there are people living now even in
the garden house and I imagine it pretty drafty now, although it
must be lovely in summer time. You were right in taking more
civil servants in the house; it will give you more work and no
profit, but on the other hand it is better to have them than
friends, and in this way you have more privacy to yourself.
Has Lizzy left Bath for good? Give Mr. Rauman once more
my thanks for advising you if business matters come up, I
wrote them a few weeks ago. I hope we will still get your last
letter in which it seems you wrote about business matters.
And please, give us occasionally when you have time, a list
of all that has happened with respect to Stefan's works and
publishers, who has paid royalties etc. etc. - just that we have an
idea what is going on. - About Hans: I quite agree with
what you say and I certainly did not mean to offer
him a rent. I must think the letter over carefully and
shall send it in a few days, and you will get a copy.
In the meantime don't give him anything. I am sorry
you have all this bother and wish he were not in London.
Mother has asked me now to get him an affidavit to USA.
But how can you guarantee such a man? With your brother
things are different and I was able to ask a stranger for it
with the best conscience. I do hope Mr. Landan's affidavit
is accepted as valid, it seems that he has given quite a
number already. - Now I have written a lot and made up
for the fact that last week I did not write, waiting from
day to day for a letter from you.
Kindest regards to all and best love
and kisses to you
Lotte

pages.transcription:
Newhaven Hotel Taft 12 March. Dear Hannah and Manfred, we had
today your letter from the 27. February - very quick, but mail is not
regularly at all. On the other hand your letter N° 3, which you answered
in your letter N° 4 as commercial[?] never arrived and it seems that you did not get our first
letters from Newyork about your daughter. There are now delays - The weather
is terrific, snowstorms and blizzards and furthermore we are in war.
Lotte behaves very badly against me. She knows that I have retired to New-
haven for work and instead of helping me she gets asthma-attacks and now
a thick influenza so that I, poor chap, have to care for her. I hope she will
be able to leave the bed tomorrow. In any case she must be careful as the
weather is disgusting, sharp winds blowing with ice and rain, the streets so
muddy that I who hate this since my early childhood has to buy rubbers.
Newhaven is a little place, not nice and one is lost in an American
little town without a car. If we are invited one has to bring us back as
there are not many busses - it is understood, that even a poor man has
his car in America (except in New York where it is paradoxically imprac-
ticable). The advantages are 1/ the library of the University, I can take
as many books at home as I want and go to the shelves myself, and that
is for me a delight as I have been without books for nearly a year
2/ I am not bothered by all this people which is now crowded in Newyork
- the whole Vienna, Berlin, Paris, Frankfurt and all horrible towns. So
I have time to work and even to think. 3/ We have opportunity to see
those who are real good friends quietly. There was Shalom Asch here,
Joachim Maass, Jules Romains, Bertolt Viertel, Friday comes Van Loon,
you see a very good choice 4/ it is altogether cheaper: not the Hotel,
which I do not like very much but all the daily expenses and the
Schnorrers. I do here some little work and prepare for the greater one
which I will write in Rio if we should return there. Nothing is sure
and we make no plans. America has its advantages - libraries,
possibilities of income and - and Brazil - beauty, quiet life. Our de-
cision depends from so many things, especially the developments in the
world. Everyones life is but a microbe in this monsters body which we
call: the War, shall we ever see a more sensible mankind?
Now to your pet! I have sincerely the conviction that Eva could not have
been better placed than at Mrs Schaeffer. It is just what I liked for her,
a modest surrounding without luxury, a careful and intelligent person who
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief auf zwei Seiten (hier Seite 1). Violette Tinte. Sehr gut lesbar.
Rückseite des ersten Blattes, leer.

pages.transcription:
understands children and is nearer to our own conceptions of education
good company and - if this terrific winter ends - a beautiful surrounding.
You may understand that we have been ourselves anxious the first days
if she would like it and we enjoy it very much that she seems to be
happy as possible. We all together have pressed her very hard to write
more substantially to you because I understand that you like just to
hear the little trifles of her daily life. I do not want to make a pro-
fessional writer out of her but she is now in the age where she could
learn to talk also with the pen to her mother. And she must under-
stand that you are waiting miles and miles away for every word from
her and that she should therefore give a little push to her brain to write more
than a few quick words - I can imagine so well how you open her letters
and in midst of your joy (and your tears) wishing they should contain
somewhat more of her.
From England I had except of Friedentals letter not a single one
for months and months. I know nothing what happens. As to material
things I shall have to make a tax report very soon, but I do not know
what came in from literary sources all this year. I will write about all this to my accountant
and give you a copy of it, so that you make it with him together, as
far as we can - I carry no files and no accounts here. But I will pre-
pare everything. Here I hope to come through - I could have some
wellpaid articles but I prefer to continue my own work and let these
possibilities always open. Would it not be for the exterior things we
would continue here our quiet and modest life - I want no publicity,
no more big towns and noisy pleasures. The only thing everybody of us
would like most of all - security! - seems to be gone for our genera-
tion and we must learn to ride on the waves. Now nothing more
then kindest regards to all! Yours ever

Stefan

Dear Mr Miller I heard with great pleasure that you
feel allright again. How often are we remembering the
garden and how beautiful it will be in spring. Unfortunately
there is now no possibility to return as we hoped - no passages
for months! But let us hope the best! Kindest regards
Stefan Zweig

pages.transcription:
Taft Hotel                                Newhaven, March 13th, 1941.

Dear Hanna,

Finally your letter Nr. 3 from Febr. 8th has arrived,
delayed because you had written 18th Street 48 East instead of
18 East 48th Street. You were of course right not to give Hans
any more money after the first 35£ which after all is a considerable
sum. I am terribly sorry that through the vague expressions in my
letter to him he got the impression that you could dispose of Stefan's
money quite freely and that you had the disagreeable task of refusing
him any more. I have written him again to-day telling him quite
clearly that another £20 is the utmost we can give him until August.
This is Stefan's instruction to you which I transmit that you may
give Hans once more £20 and that then - with these 55£ - he has nothing
to expect from us until at least August. By that time, I hope, he will
have found a good job.

Otherwise there is nothing to report. We had a nice
letter from Eva, a special effort on her part for style, and the
funny part about it is that it sounded curiously like one of Manfred's
letters in style. - I got up to-day for the first time after my 'flu
and hope that poor Stefan soon gets his secretary back.

Best love, kisses,
Lotte

Dear Hannah, this is the first letter to be able
to write since 10 days. After her heavy astma-attack
she has a very bad flu and is still in bed; I hope she can go up tomorrow.
Of cause it is not nice to have this in an American Hotel which has a
resemblance of {resemblance} with a railway-station, no personal touch and interest. We
has only a doctor from an other century and no else in this little town.
And we are both so tired of this nomadic life as you cannot imagine. But
the first thing is that she gets fit again and later we shall see what to do
next - all is uncertain in those times. I am only glad that we can rely
on Mr. Klaeffer for Eva, as it will not be possible to see her next week and
perhaps before April. It Lotte feels better we have still to go for two days
to Baltimore, for one day at least to Newyork. But time flies! - I wrote
you about the birth-certificates and forgot to tell you, that it will be
perhaps better to tear them through Ingram as this proves that I want them
for a legal matter, but if you have already done it, there is no harm.
Kindest regards to you all
Stefan Zweig

pages.transcription:
Taft Hotel                                      Newhaven, 13th March 1941.

Dear Jan,

I am sorry that you seem to have misunderstood my letter
to mean that we would be able to help you indefinitely until you had
found a suitable position for yourself. Unfortunately this is not
the case. You must realise that besides all the other obligations
(house, support of former wife, relatives and friends, enormous taxes)
Stefan is now maintaining our mother completely since months. I am
happy that this has been possible and that in these difficult times
I have been able to take over temporarily from you, Manfred and Richard
the care for mother, and I sincerely hope that for the next future I
will be able to continue that. - But that we are now temporarily in
America means in no way a pleasure trip, and Stefan is working hard to
meet both ends, although I purposely have avoided to mention this in my
letters to Mama. Hardly anyone has been so severely hit in his pro-
fessional activity that a Jewish writer whose books are forbidden in
all Europe except England (where nearly the whole stock was burned ~~at~~
the ~~bookbinder~~. And the sales in America have always been but the smallest
part of his former income.

I am sorry that this misunderstanding has arisen, sorry for
you and for Hanna who of course could not dispose of Stefan's money
without instruction from us, after she had given you those £ 35. With
Stefan's consent I am now asking her to-day to let you have once more
£ 20 (twenty pounds) which is all which we can do for you until August.

As to an affidavit for USA I have also no good news for you
much as I had liked to help[?] you. We are unfortunately experts in
this matter as since months Stefan gets letters from relatives and
friends nearly every day. Unfortunately the situation has now become
very difficult. The affidavit-giver, besides many other things has to
show his bank account and income and to undertake a guarantee. And we
have had in the last weeks nothing but refusals, as all our friends have
already given too many or have no money themselves. Should I hear of
anybody, however, I shall of course let you know it at once.

Hoping that you have good news from your wife and that your
own situation will quickly improve,
                                                Lotte

As I do not know whether your address is still the same, I have to
send you this letter through Hanna.

Taft Hotel
Newhaven, 19.3.41
Dear Hanna u Manfred,
I wrote twice last week, once with a letter to Jan enclosed, I hope you got the letter. In the meantime nothing much has
happened. I am up again and already cleared up a great amount of my
so long neglected work. The main part of the manuscript for the Brasil
book has been sent away at last and Stefan feels better since the piles
of paper have somewhat diminished. The weather has been dreadful all
the time, storms, snow and extreme cold, and in the 2 months of our stay in
USA we got already thoroughly tired of the winter. Nevertheless time
seems to fly away and in another few weeks I suppose we will go back
to New York and try to make up our minds what to do that is to say where
to go next. Do you realise that it is already a year almost since we se-
parated? Your letter about Bath brought everything back so clearly and made
me feel rather homesick for a while. I am glad at least that you can be
there and enjoy the products and the beauty of the garden. What a pity
that Manfred's X-Ray course is not yet finished! But I hope he will take
long weekends, we are very much concerned about it that he does. - From
Eva we hear regularly and also Mrs Sch. reports frequently, I asked
her to join a few words to Eva's letters to you now and then. We both
feel that Eva is well looked after and happy there. She has again
started her music lessons and from what she and Mrs Sch write the teachers
seem to succeed in making her enjoy it again. She has holidays in April
and I plan to take her here for a few days at least. We look forward
to having her and she loves to come, but there is nothing for her to
do in Newhaven and I am afraid she will not know what to do with
herself all day long. If it is possible with regard to time, I shall one
day take her to visit Harriet's sister Elizabeth who has a boy and a
girl in about Eva's age and who lives halfway between New York and
Groton. I have seen Elizabeth and her children but once, but in any
case it can do no harm if Eva knows someone of the family, Leo and
the other two, Marcus and Samson, who are in New York live far away
and are without interest for Eva - and myself. - Tell Lotte please how
sorry I am that I could not yet visit her children. I hope that when
we are back in Newyork again, someone will take me out there in
car, otherwise it is very long and a little complicated to get there.
Hoping to have good news from you soon,
with best love and kindest regards
to all
Lotte

pages.transcription:
March 31, Hotel Wyndham 42 West 58 Street
Dear Hannah and Manfred, we got your letter about Eva and I was very
ashamed. I should have foreseen that our first news about Salmon would
have frightened you as you have perhaps supposed that we did hide you dread-
ful things - we had written in whole sincerity with the feeling that it was
a trifling misunderstanding between Mr. Salmon's goodhearted vanity and her
Manfredish incapability of showing her feelings. But imagine our situation -
should we have invented some story or told you the whole truth as it was and
a simple and innocent ~~true~~ truth? Altogether we are satisfied it came as
it came. We have an excellent impression of Mrs. Schaeffer, her reports are so
clear and human and we have the best feeling that the surroundings are excellent
for Eva. She will come to New York now in her schoolholidays and we shall have
her with us for a few days and she will do all to multiply her acquaintances
that you may be still more sure. Dont believe that I am severe; I know that
this incapacity of showing her feelings is a heritage and who has more ex-
perience in dealing with it than we both, you with Manfred and I with Lotte.
But on the other hand I think it is useful if a certain carelessness in
exterior details is corrected just in these decisive years of formation and
I believe that the example of Schaeffers will be an excellent one. My
dear Hannah, you cannot imagine how we are disqusted of the impoliteness
the rudeness, the arrogant way of the American children and it is an enor-
mous advantage that she will brought up in our conceptions; on the other
hand it will {in the coming world} be necessary to be effective, reliable and
independent, it will not be a world for dreamers and the earlier she
learns that one has to think for oneself, the better for her. That's why I insist
that in the small matters like letter-writing she has not always to be remin-
ded and that her feeling for responsability must get independent as soon
as possible. More and more I see, that one has to do all one self and that
not as in our own youth one had a large and influential family around
to smoothe the ways; life also after the war will ask much more energy
than was asked from our generation. Please rely upon us and dont be
frightened that your poor lamb has to suffer here; I know it is a hard strain
for you both to miss her and I understand that in certain hours you will
even regret having sent her away. But we have all to overcome this ordeal
- also our life is disturbed here by the constant uncertainty. I am dis-
gusted to go from one place to the other and to decide always and without

Rückseite des ersten Blattes, leer.

pages.transcription:
to come to an definite decision. I suppose we will go back to Rio for the
summer as we could not stay here in New York in the summer; the great diffi-
culty is how to assure the in advance how to come back when the summer
begins as visitors-visa will be not available (especially in case of declaration
of open war) on the other hand if we would take an immigrants visa it could
easely be misunderstood as if I would like to change my citizenship. You cannot
imagine how many of such questions assail me every day and in the same time
the dirty letters and cables for affidavits and visas. But I continue working,
my book on Brasil (which will be perhaps useful to tighten the cultural rela-
tions between the English-speaking and Latin world) will appear here in English
in autumn (the translator is frightfully slow) and I have some new work
on hand; so we have no material worries, but the moral ones are big enough.
The United States will give England all possible help, the whole country
is transformed in an enormous factory. What we are afraid of personally is
to become cut off during the duration of war and also for Eva we would
not like that, as nobody can foresee how long this will take.
I shall see today or tomorrow Edemanns brother. We have a few good
friends here and have to avoid the big crowd of the refugees. I have made
no public appearance and do not write for newspapers, because the most
important is for me to continue my work quietly and to keep fit. Lotte feels
much better since we left Petropolis; the winter was hard and endless, in
more of six weeks we had not a single walk there. About my other more
material things I shall write to Mr. Wilmot in the next days and send
you a copy of the letter so that you may be informed. I hope you enjoy
Bath at Easter and when Manfred has passed his examinations he will
stay there for good. Yours ever
Dear Hannah & Manfred, I cannot tell you how
sorry I am that you misunderstood our desire to
let you participate in all our actions by giving you a complete
description of all our impressions of Eva and Salmon's, of all our
deliberations, enquiries and decisions. We did not criticize Eva for
not being a "loving daughter" to Mr. Salmon. We tried to describe you the
whole situation in greatest detail and to explain their and Eva's feelings
in order to explain why their relationship was not perfect, although they
were very nice and pleasant together. There was nothing else behind it
as you seem to imagine and Eva did not behave badly at all.
Stefan Zweig

pages.transcription:
Dear Hanna u Manfred
To-day your letter of Feb. 27 last week your letter Nr 4, - there is still one (Nr. 3)
missing, where you apparently wrote about mother and business as I gather
from the other letters. Lots of our letters must be lost or delayed, for I
wrote almost daily in the period where I was settling Eva. Resumé: Eva
had a lovely home at Salmon's, a nicely-furnished modern country house
in beautiful surroundings, S.'s were nice to her and Mr. S. especially
spoiling her as much as he could and taking enormous pains to gain her
love and interest. He overdid this apparently for although they were al-
ways very polite and friendly together there was no real contact. S.'s seemed
to realize this better than Eva who liked being with them but admitted
she was being spoiled and bored. To the head-mistress of the school she was
in, had just said her school was too easy and she had better change over
to another school with higher grades, this was a good opportunity, and I
agreed with S's in all friendship - they were surprisingly nice and
understanding about it, one really shouldn't judge them by their deter-
mined not-writing - that Eva would better be with a lot of other
children and different school. Then, after long deliberations and con-
sultations with all kinds of people, I decided for Schaeffes's place, and
from all we can judge until now, it seems exactly the right thing for Eva,
I wrote you that after all she goes to the Public School now and I must
say I am rather glad things did turn out this way and that she is not
brought up on the super-individualistic methods of the Progressive School,
even if this particular one was supposed to be very good. - Eva looks very
well, unchanged, still a little bit on the stout side but not at all fat, and
is her old self again. As Mrs. Sch. writes she is gay and seems very happy
in her house, is friendly with the other children and there are now
quite a number in her age. The dresses I saw on her fit her perfectly - the
red velvet, the checked dress and the yellow Yella. Mrs. Salmon had got
her a nice new coat (and an awful hat with a feather which fortunately she
need not wear any more) and I bought her for outdoor life in Boston
a ski-suit, wind-and waterproof, blue with a red hood, and a pair of high
rubbers. That was all she needed. She has grown a little, but not too much.
Sch's try to lure her into out-door activities with various tricks. She does
not like that too much yet, probably because she is not used to it and
the others are better in winter sports and games than she is. But that
will change once this long winter is over. We had been longing for
winter weather, but we have already enough, it is too cold and windy to
go out as we can't put on snow suits in the street. - As Stefan wrote you about
my illness, I better report too. I had a bad cold with an asthma-attack, the
first since 2 years, fortunately I got asthma-syn here, and a week later it de-
veloped into a flu. I am very glad for I finally had my necessary fever
again for a few days and this will settle the asthma for months, I suppose.
Poor Stefan has been very patient and helpful and hardly at all a "Jewish nurse"
but as usual the fact that I was not available for work has made him more
anxious to work than usual.

[Randnotiz links:]
I will see what I can do about the
affidavit. It is very difficult and best luck
Thanks address now.

3
We changed over quickly to Sch.'s as the headmistress of the school
in New Rochelle had suggested a change to a higher school, and
I think we were right in doing so. Eva feels happy at Croton,
there are nice children with her and she seems on the best of terms
with Mrs. Sch. and all the others. There are about as many Ame-
rican children as refugee children, Jews and Christians and that
mixed atmosphere seems to us a good and lively one. We did
not see her while we were in Newhaven as this terrible weather
and a series of colds, asthma and grippe from my part kept us
busy in Newhaven, but we phoned several times and had frequent
letters from Eva and detailed reports from Mrs. Sch. Had she
written them in English I would have sent them on to you as
it would have reassured you that Eva is with understanding people
who like her and who think in our lines. - Next week Eva
has her Easter holidays and I am taking her to New York to be
with us, and I am looking forward to have her with us for
a little while. If it is possible I shall go with her to see the
Smollett boys. I am going to have her photographed, take
her to a reliable dentist, maybe invite Robin Gilbert and
take them both to a show and try to make her at home in
hotel rooms. At least we have a little kitchenette and so we
can pretend home life to a certain degree by preparing
breakfast and occasionally eggs or sausages. - We returned
to New York two days ago and are glad to be back. Stefan
worked well in Newhaven and enjoyed the library facilities.
But as we had to stay in the Hotel and the weather was
most unpleasant we decided to leave rather suddenly,
and New York seems very attractive to us just now.
We got your brother's letter today. I am sorry that
he has not yet his visa and I hope the Consul will not be
too thorough in the examination of the affidavit value.
If it is not accepted we will have to try elsewhere. His ex-
tremely difficult now but he is one of the very few for whom one
can guarantee. On the whole I am glad that he is not sailing
just now, later in the summer the weather and the outlook will
be more sure, we suppose.
So please do not worry about Eva. She is developing
quite as she should, is as nice and lovable as ever, and in fighting
her tendencys for forgetting to write, Stefan has to overcome the combined
Mayer- and Altman heritage. Best love and kindest regards to all,
Lotte.

Address for air-mail: c/o Viking Press, 18 East 48th Street, Newyork
- later mail: c/o Editora Guanabara, 132 Rua Ouvidor, Rio de Janeiro
                                                              (Brazil)

                                     42 West 58th Street
                                     New York City

                                     2nd April, 1941

Binder, Hamlyn & Co.
River Plate House
12 South Place,
London E.C.2
ENGLAND

Dear Mr.Wilmot ,

I wrote you already from Rio to ask you as
my accountant about my position with regard to taxation
as I have been away from England since last June.

I have not yet received your reply and, there-
fore, do not know whether I am subject to income tax for the
{entire} last year or not. Anyway, I would like to facilitate your
task by giving you once more a statement on my position.

As you know, I left for South America last
June and have given in Brazil, Argentine and Uruguay a
series of lectures which I am asked to continue. During the
dead summer season in South America I have been here in USA
for further negotiations and the publication of a book on
Brazil which is, as you will understand, of special importance
in this moment. Under the prevailing circumstances I do not
see any possibility for me to earn a living in England or to
make myself useful while there. On the other hand, in the
Western Hemisphere I can achieve both aims, as I hope that I
will, for the time being, be able to make a modest living and
also to be of some use to our cause.

In order to enable you to prepare an income tax
return, I asked my sister-in-law, Mrs.Altmann, to give you all
{except the American} the details about my income from royalties/and investments
{which I did send you} during the taxable year. I myself have not been able to get any
{directly together with} regular statements, travelling from one country of South America
{my travelling expenses} to the other without possibility of receiving mail regularly
{on the lecture tour} owing to difficult communications which, among other reasons,
may also have caused the loss of some letters.
                                     {(European income)}
You will not be surprised that my literary {work}
has considerably decreased in this year of war, as in all the
occupied countries my books have immediately been suppressed
by the Nazis, and my literary activity was hampered by travelling
and lecturing.

As to my lecture tour, I told you before my
departure about an arrangement with the Ministry that I would
have to support myself abroad by lectures and literary work,
and that an eventual deficit should be covered only up to the
amount of two hundred pounds.

pages.transcription:
- II - 2nd April 1941

So far I have managed to support myself and, as
you will see from the enclosed statement, the deficit incurred
until now is rather small. I hope that I shall be able to
conclude new agreements which will enable me not to have to
apply for any money transfer from England. Since I am away,
I have been dependent with my wife on my activities here only,
as also the last of my foreign investments have been called up
by the Treasury, so that the equivalent in pounds must have been
already credited to my account with the Westminster Bank in
London.

You will see from the enclosed statement, which is
made up on US-Dollar basis, that I had an income of $ 6,443.84 ,
while my expenses amounting to $ 6,550.00 were somewhat higher,
so that the deficit of $ 106.16, i.e.£ 26.10.-, is up to now
much smaller than anticipated in my discussions with the Mini-
stry.

I suppose that you will find the amount of $ 4,320.00
for living expenses and other disbursements self-explanatory.
This amount would mean that I and my wife had spent for board,
fares, representation, telephone, stationery and other similar
disbursements less than $18.00 in the daily average during a
period of nine months. As you will probably imagine the condit-
ions under which I have to live here and especially in South
America, these travelling expenses cannot be considered high
and could really not be reduced.

I further wish to mention that I have not made any
deduction for the ample secretarial and translation work,
because all this work had been done by Mrs.Zweig, so that I did
not need any secretary or translator.

I hope that my sister-in-law, Mrs. Altmann, who has
dealt with all my correspondence since my departure, will have
no difficulties in giving you all necessary details.

Would you please be so kind as to confirm receipt
of this letter in duplicate sending one copy of your letter (airmail)
c/o Viking Press, 18 East 48th Street, New York City, and
another c/o Editora Guanabara, 132, Rua Ouvidor, Rio de Janeiro,
as my future plans are still uncertain, when I have to return there.

Thanking you in anticipation for your assistance and
expecting your reply to this letter and my letter from Rio,
I am

Yours very truly

Enc.

as my future plans are still uncertain, when I have to return there.

Thanking you in anticipation for your assistance and
expecting your reply to this letter and my letter from Rio,
I am

Yours very truly

means again destruction of numberless individual lives and happi

pages.transcription:
Dear Hannah and Manfred, we are forwarding today the photos of
your daughter, lets hope, they will safely arrive. You will see
- they are excellent - that Eva is looking well and so your mothers
heart will be glad. Today she goes back to Accily Hall and I think
it is a good sign that she is rather eager to see her auntie Olga
again; she feels there perfectly at home and in all those good days
with her we heard not a single complaint about anything there. So we
are rather satisfied to have found the right thing. She ~~do~~ has made
some progress and I hope you will not regret that she has seen and
learned so much.
Thanks for all what you are doing for me. The consul has promis-
sed to me that a new power of attorney will be made in the Consu-
late here; I shall go there in the next few days. Please drop a
line also to Siegmund Warburg, and telling him that I have written
three times to him and once to Koerner and never got a reply. It
is really not my fault. And give Frietental all material help, I hope
I can send also to him a food-parcel.
We lose here much time by thinking what to do next. On the 15th
of May I shall have to speak at the great dinner of the Pen Club
one of this enormous dinners with 1000 persons which I have avoided
all my life long. But this time I cannot refuse as it is important
for our common cause. Somerset Maugham will speak - every one ten
minutes sharp - for the English, Sigrid Undset for the Scandinavian, Jules
Romains for the French and I for the German-speaking writers, the other
~~persons~~ {ones} get only 1 minute; I have to speak one half in German, the
other in English. All this will be relayed by short-wave all over the
world and I shall give you in time the exact hour, that you may hear
me in London. Will we have afterwards still time and occasion to
go to Brazil? Who can tell it? Lotte is now in competent treatment
and many tests are made to find out the real reason and center of her
asthma. I would not like to travel before she is perfectly fit. Love Stefan

[Rand links, vertikal:] I have written an obituary for our good Hermann Meine for
the "Anfanger" here and shall send it to his widow.

[Rand rechts, vertikal:] Best love (I will write soon)

The Wyndham Hotel 42 West 58 Street	5. April 1941
Dear Hannah & Manfred, I wrote you these days about my taxes
with which I have to worry you as you have the statements, I hope
you have {and will communicate} already my letter. Today what will please you more
- that we shall have Eva here for her holidays one week and I hope
she will enjoy New York more than she did before. We will talk a lot
about you.
Lotte has behaved badly against me, as I wrote you, and is now be-
having costly. As her attacks of asthma did not stop we were obliged
to let examine her thoroughly for I want for my work and travelling
a wife and secretary who keeps fit. Dr. Schür, whom I know from
London, (he has been the doctor of Sigmund Freud) has seen her
and now with a specialist he is making tests to find out the allergic
points. It is not a serious state as you know, but before we go
away I would like to have her examined as well as possible; I doubt
if we could find on another place such competent persons. Do not
think therefore that it is serious; I want only to prevent a setback
when we would have to travel again. Our plans are not at all fixed
up - who can decide in a time like ours? - but we will stay in any
case till to the end of May here in New York.
We have read here in the newspapers about attacks on Bristol and
I hope you have been had no visit of this kind in Bath, which is
so near. I hope also that 17 Orchard has no damage and that all
is going quietly as before. Here the preparations seem to be enor-
mous and we hope all that they will become sufficient et effective
in a short time.
Perhaps I shall have to speak here at a dinner at the Pen Club
(only a few minutes) on April 29th at the opening of the Euro-
pean Branch; if so it will be relayed by short wave and you could
perhaps hear me. I hate dinner speaks but I do not know if it will
be possible to escape. Kindest regards to you all yours Stefan Zweig

Newyork, 5.4.41
Dear Hanna & Manfred, I am still troubled by the ~~th~~ thought
that you misunderstood our first letters about Eva and probably
had a bad time thinking that not only was she in unsuitable and
uncongenial surroundings, but also on the other hand criticized
by us. I hope that our later letters-which you have surely re-
ceived in the meantime-have reassured you about both points,
and so that you feel content in the thought that now Eva is in
the right and pleasant surroundings, a kind of old-fashioned
family-life coupled with modern-but not super-modern education
methods and understanding, and that our feelings against her are
just the same as ever, and I believe hers for us too. She has
written us frequently, and is looking forward to be with us soon,
just as we are looking forward to having her. I am sorry we
haven't seen her during our stay in Newhaven as we had intended
to. But as Stefan wrote you, I have not been too well, and
that absorbed much time and energy and occasionally even forced
Stefan to look after me instead of being served and waited on
himself. But he did it nicely and willingly and hardly felt sorry
for himself. Now I am in treatment by Trend's former doctor,
get Calcium-injections, iodine, nose-drops, spend every evening half
an hour in the bathroom with the hot tap on to make it a kind
of steam-or inhalation room. Besides those allergic tests will now be
made and I am looking forward to learn against what strange
objects my poor body reacts so unpleasantly. But you must not
think that I was in a very bad condition and that there is anything
to worry about. Only the last years have spoilt me and I don't
want to put up any more with even moderate asthmatic conditions.
Eva will come next Thursday to stay with us
for a week, and as we have a radio, a kitchenette, an adjoining
room for her and I am not too busy at present, I hope she
will have a pleasant time in New York. I had thought of
inviting at least Robin once, but it seems that he is going
to stay with orthodox friends over passover. At the end of April
I shall go with Eva to visit Elizabeth one Sunday. She has a
girl of 11 and a boy, a year or two older, and I like her to
know at least one of her many cousins. - Yesterday I phoned
to Eva to make arrangements about her coming; I thought that
she might just be going to bed but instead she was just
going out (8 in the evening) to some school festival. The other

10. April 1941 Dear Hannah, now your little lamb is with us for the
easter-holiday week and we will do all to make her the time as pleasant
as possible. She has grown up and looks again like a ballet-dancer in her
short frock and this shall be arranged in the next days. It seems that she
likes her new home and we like her very much and we have the impression
that the surroundings and the way of living is absolutely what we wanted
for her; under our supervision she will write today a long letter for you
and I can imagine how eagerly you will read it. Please dont be worried
that she is away, I understand your feelings but dont forget that very
big ordeals are still ahead of us before the victory and that the feeling
to know her safe should be for you in the hours of longing a comfort.
So be relieved that she is either treated harshly nor spoiled, we hope
that we have just found the right thing for her.
I thank you so much for all the trouble you have for us. There
should before the taxation day some royalties from Cassels (perhaps
you can write him/and Paul Tabori (you will fix his adress/number
as we nearly a year ago just before I left the remittance of Hunga
rian royalties, which should be paid by an English publisher. Perhaps
you find still his letter or write him if it was not paid in July
or August; it may be that he has used my absence for not paying
but you can write to him that on behalf of tax purposes you have
to ask him about.
As to the power of attorney I will speak to the Vice-Consul of
the British Consulate whom I shall see Saturday in our house; he
is a charming man with great literary interest and we like him
personally very much.
I have started to work again and all goes his quiet way; would
it not be, that we always have to take new decisions we would not
complain. But also we do not know if and when we go to Brazil,
there are pros and contras and nobody knows what is right and
best in such an absurd time. Anyway, I continue to work and avoid
seeing people as much as possible. Lotte feels much better since
the injection-treatment and health is the most important as
but have which demand strength of nerves from us all. Yours Stefan Zweig

New York, 10. 4. 41

Dear Hanna & Manfred,
This morning your letter (March 25th!) arrived and a few hours
later Eva & two great pleasures one day. She has grown
quite a lot in those weeks at Croton, is her old self, gay
and lively and I believe glad to be with us. I have
just put her to bed after bathing her - at her own request -
and she is really growing from a child into a girl, even
showing faint traces of developing a bosom. We will have her
photographed for you next week and I think you will find
her a little thinner, although still well filled out, and
the face not more quite so round. I shall have to get her
one or two more summerdresses (the ones she brought over will
be lengthened by a little dressmaker) and a few pairs of
socks, otherwise she seems to have all she needs. Although
while she found it very nice at Salmon's (I am sure she never
was unhappy there) she feels absolutely at home in Amity Hall
and has a great love for Mrs. Sch. I think you took the
big words in her letter to you too seriously. She has de-
finitely been influenced by Frend, but what she has
taken over is only the friendly understanding and the big
words. In her education method she is as normal and healthy
as you could wish and I believe, if you could see her you
would find yourself in complete agreement about the up-
bringing of children. As to her or their own children, I know
the three small ones, very nice fair and blue-eyed, perfectly
normal children, and Marilis, the 20 year old girl who is
looking after the children and who has graduated in
astronomical mathematics!) a very pleasant girl. One boy is
in college, apparently working his way through. And one, a big
boy, from Mr. Sch's first marriage, is not quite normal and
they had to leave him behind. Mr. Sch. himself does not
seem to have an agreable temper, but as he has nothing
to do with the education and seldom sees the children
except at mealtime, he is without importance as far as I can see.
I would have more to write, but
Stefan wants to send the letter off. So best love and
keep well
Lotte

Dear Hannah and Manfred, we have your letter from the 11th
from Bath and have been happy to hear that you have been there
for a while (wishing you would remain there for good). Please
dear Hannah, do not worry about Eva. You may {love} believe in my
complete sincerity. We have both the feeling that you are an-
xious if at Ms[?] Klaeffer she feels allright and has sufficient
care. Please be sure that she has and we have been surprised
how much she likes the place, the surroundings and has be-
come attached to her, auntie Olga who is really a superior
person and just the right one to guide and to educate a
child. I feel so profoundly how you, poor Hannah, the more the
separation from your child is going on, become more and
more anxious about her. But remember that she is safe,
that she has excellent care and that we are near, that
my sister in law and others would in any case be at hand
and that she is happy, really as happy as she can be without
you both. We have all so many difficult things before us
that you should overcome your longing (which I under-
stand so deeply) with the consolating thought that her de-
velopment, her health, her life, goes on there without the
dangers at home. I {understand} [?] all your secret sorrows to be so
far away from her but I want to comfort you, that you
may at least be sure that she is in excellent care and the
photos will have shown to you, that she is in splendid
health and spirits.
As to your kind questions: please give Freudenthal
every help which is possible, I am so glad that I am
able to be of any use to the few true friends one
has. It would be opressive for me to think that he

pages.transcription:
would have to worry about money. It is so important
in those days to have at least not to be obliged to worry
about the daily expenses; please assist him with even larger
amounts than before (there will be soon a new amount
in the bank as some of my investements have been sold by
the treasury) and then there is still Frost, who can help and
from Cassels is my royalty due which I can have any moment.
As to the new power of attorney I shall go Monday or Tuesday
to the Consulate and will ask also, if they can send a
short story directly to Luso[?] for the newspaper (the original
as I dispose here of the translation). I have more prepared
than worked and because we have so much practical things
to order and Lotte has been out of work for some time -
I hope the treatment will be effective. The worst for us is
that we do not see clear, what to do. The others have established
themselves in little houses and started a new life, while we
are not sure, how long we shall stay and how to decide -
will it still be possible to go to Brazil? Will there still
be ships and planes? Perhaps when this letter reaches
you the United States will have already entered the war.
So we wait and waiting is not very appropriate for
concentrated work, but I have not been idle and have
different offers and chances at hand - you must not
imagine, that we are disturbed, we would only like not
to wander from one hotel to the other. But we know
also how grateful we have to be that I can continue
my work. We do not see many people, I am tired of
the monotony of the war - the Jewish - the aff[?] david talk;
with his thousand variations it remains sterile. I even
go not to theatres I feel not the right mood for everything which is amusement
while Europe breaks down under the leak of the heart and while you
and all our friends in England are in daily danger. Yours Stefan

New York, 18.4.41.

Dear Manna & Manfred,
Yesterday your letter of Apr. 4th. I hope you
extended your Easter holiday in Bath until the end of this
week, and I wish you would remain there permanently. We
fully realise what advantages the degree of an X-Ray specialist
would mean to you, but at the moment the risks of the brutal
and indiscriminate air-raids over London seem great and we feel
anxious. - Eva has gone back to Croton yesterday. She was
happy to be with us and enjoyed the week in Newyork, but
she was looking forward again to the children and auntie
Olga whom she likes very much and of whom she talked with
great genuine affection. I am very glad about that, for she
really feels at home at Amity Hall and from all she told us
and from what we hear she has just that kind of care
and education you would like her to have. Mrs. Schaefer
probably will continue to try to explain you Eva's development
by using big words, but this means nothing more than a well-
meant effort for psychological description and has no connection
with her actual relations to the children. On the whole I en-
vied Eva for going back to the countryside and she will
enjoy the garden. I shall go out there one of the next sun-
days and have a look on it in springtime. Sunday Eva and
I will meet in Yonkers which is just halfway to Croton and
visit Elizabeth and her 11 year old girl. - Yesterday I sent
you a number of photos by air-mail, registered, to Bath,
and I hope you get them very soon. We find them excellent
and I hope you will not mind too much that Eva's hair is
not perfectly groomed. She had slept on it the wrong night side
the night before and the hair dresses could not do anything
about it in a hurry. The photo in hat and coat was Stefan's
idea. Eva thoroughly dislikes the hat which was bought by
Mrs Salmon and which is perfect American fashion for a
child of that age, and she at first refused that you should
even see it. But she won't wear it any more and it just
gives you an idea what Eva looked like this winter.
I am impatient to hear what you think of the photos.
We have ordered more and she will send some postcards too.

X I am afraid you will weep when you look at them like a
"slosh-kind"

I am sorry, Manna, that the news of my various complaints
upset you. Stefan really looked after me very well while I
needed it, and the calcium injections brought me back to
normal very quickly, and there are even nights again where I
don't wake up at all. As I wrote before, I am now being tested
thoroughly about my allergies by a specialist for allergics. The
tests will be finished soon, and the doctor promised to send
Manfred a report. I asked him to do so as I suppose you
would like a medical report. It seems that the Americans are
ahead in all those tests and the treatments, and they have
reason to do so as asthma is a wide-spread disease in both
North and South America. The chances of immunizing through
a kind of serum injections seem fairly good and you will
hear in due time. In any case I am quite well again and
there is no reason to worry. - But how is the health of you
both in those times? I believe I enquired several times
but you never even mention it. That is far more important
because of the heavy strain of the war.
We are very glad to be back in Newyork and
Newhaven had at least this good effect that I like New-
york again. We live very quietly and hardly see anybody.
It is a little enervating not to know where we will
be in two months time, but although some reasons speak
for returning to Brazil I am against deciding for such
a journey just now. Kindest regards to all, best love to you,
Lotte

Dear Hannah and Manfred, only good greetings
for today. My publisher Cassel wrote me that my account
for this taxation year shows £ 382/7/10, so you can
inform my accountant Binder & Hamlyn and must not go
to Cassels yourself. The idea of your going-around in
London is oppressive for us - you cannot imagine our rage
about this indiscriminate slaughtering of peaceful people. In
what ages are we living? Please tell to the widow of Max
Hermann-Neisse that I have written a obituary for him here
which has been published today, I hope I can send her a copy

{Randnotiz links:} of it. Lotte is not yet quite allright but we hope the treatment will bring
her not only momentary but durry relief from her
asthma - afars. Love all Stefan

bereits im Abklingen, an ein Herunter-

denken. Ich sende Dir den -
Kaths wohlverpackt zu. Herzlichst
Euer Stefan

pages.transcription:
Newyork, 25.4.1941.

Dear Hanna and Manfred,
I believe that for some time now I have not
written you more than just a few lines or a page in a hurry, and to-day
it is again the same - I don't know whether it is the asthma-business
which makes me more lazy or the doctors with their injections and tests
who take all my time, in any case I don't seem to get round to do all I
want to do, and also the work has been somewhat neglected these last
weeks. Now at last the tests are finished and I expect that I can get
one of the doctors to give you a short medical report. As far as I under-
stand, they consider me a perfect allergic case, sensitive according to
the tests especially to dust and some of my own nose- and throat bacte-
rias. They'll start making injections with those things and say that in
most cases they have good results in immunising. Unfortunately for us
the result will not show up definitely before a few week's treatment,and
Stefan especially is anxious for a quick result. I have learned more
patience and am already satisfied that the calcium injections (although
only as long as they are continued) definitively help. It is of course
disappointing that this whole business which I believed to have got over
many years ago, has suddenly come back. But it is in no way as bad as it
was then, the treatment is more effective, and now I am hoping for the
new treatment. So don't believe completely Stefan's a little exaggerated
reports and remember that he has never known me with asthma and so feels
terribly disappointed that a few injections did not completely heal it.
Now that is enough of my health and I hope I shall not have to mention
it again. But as he started telling you about it, I wanted to make the
real situation as clear as possible.
About Eva. We sent you a number of photos - in our
opinion excellent ones - by registered air-mail last week (to Bath) and
hope that you already got them. I think they tell you more about her than
many descriptions, and you see from them that she has ~~xxxxx~~ grown taller
and slightly thinner, that she looks strong and healthy, and in excellent
spirits. Of course there are moments where - like all of us - she is
longing to be home and again with you - but we would be very disappointed
if she did not feel that way sometimes, and they really are only moments,
and she is absolutely happy and at home at Amity Hall. Marion Ullstein,
a thirteen year old girl - I am sure she wrote you about her - is her
best friend there, and these two, together with two other boys of about
12 or 13,feel themselves as the "big children" against the small ones,
which seems to be quite a nice feeling. I have met Marion when I was
in Croton and I liked her very much, also one of the "big boys", Rudi.
The other boy I have not yet seen. In the summer vacations some of the
smaller children will go away and apparently some bigger children will
come, Marion will also stay in Croton. I could have arranged to send Eva
to a camp for the summer, but it is hot everywhere, unless you go very
far away, and Eva herself said she liked it so much at Amity Hall, she
would not like to go away. And Mrs. Sch. will run the house in the va-
cations just like one of the camps, that is to say entertain and keep
the children busy with all sorts of occupations, games, excursions and
sports. When I have seen her again I shall be able to tell you more in
detail, Eva only told me a little of what she planned to do with them,
and also spoke of learning French and reading German. If Mrs. Sch.
wrote you about Eva's starting Latin, I suppose this too is in her plan,
and as she has x the doctor's degree in philology (Eva proudly told me
that she even knows Greek) this speaks for her ability and knowledge.
By the way, Evas friend Marion has been in school in Switzerland and
speaks English, French and German equally well. And Eva says that she
often talks to her in French at night and that she is beginning to under-
stand. The school system, as regards the teaching of languages, is
pages.notes: Typoskript.
Rückseite von Seite 1, durchscheinender Text.

pages.transcription:
2

quite different. Eva is now in the 8th grade, and until she gets into
the 9th grade (next February) she won't have neither French nor Latin.
The progressive school where I first intended to send her, does teach
French earlier, but nevertheless I am very glad she does not go there.
From all I hear - and I take every opportunity to speak with parents
about this - it is much better for her education to go to a real school
even though the other school had a very good reputation. The whole
school system is very different here from the English one, but altogether
I understand that in the Public School they have the best chances of
learning, and the one she goes to is supposed to be good. And in Mrs.
Sch.'s house they are sure to have more stimulation than in an American
home. - Sunday I have been with Eva to see Harriet's sister Elizabeth.
She lives in Yonkers, halfway between Newyork and Croton, and Eva was
brought to the station, travelled that half hour alone and was met at
the station again by me. Elizabeth has two children, a girl, Nancy, of
about 11, and a boy, Philipp, of 13, and as far as I can judge, Eva
liked the girl and vice versa, and they seemed both delighted at Eli-
zabeth's suggestion that Eva should soon spend a weekend with them.
I like the idea very much, Yonkers is very conveniently situated, except
the way to and from the station Eva can travel alone, Elizabeth and her
husband are really very nice, and I liked the children very much, too.
They are both lively and intelligent, as good-looking as Harriet's
children but much more natural and agreeable to my taste- and I suppose
to Eva's taste too. I think you too will like the idea to know pleasant
relatives near Eva in addition to us. As to Salmon's they are typically
American as all our other American friends in so far as you cannot get
any relationship with them except when you actually have something de-
finite to say or a definite appointment to make. Eva has been there for
a weekend and apparently they wanted to invite her for the Easter holi-
days. But when Eva said that she was going to spend those with us,
nothing more was heard of them in spite of several letters and an Easter
card and the pyjamas which Eva sent them. If I can judge from my ex-
perience with other Americans, especially Rose and Huebsch, Salmon's
will one day again ring up Eva and invite her - but there is not such a
thing as keeping up a relationship by just writing or phonecalle. -
While Eva was here, we had lunch with Franz Neumann, and he too promised
to drive out to visit her one day. I have the same idea as you that -
whether we remain here or not - Eva should have as many contact with
friends besides us as possible, it will make it more pleasant for her,
the more people she has to go to and who visit her. My sister-in-law,
whom from now on I shall call with her first name Stefanie is genuinely
eager to look after Eva too, to invite her, to go out with her and to
spoil her, and I believe, she even thought me rather cruel and careless
that I did not take Eva to a show every day. But I assure you that even
though Eva had to spend more time than I would have liked, accompanying
me to the doctor etc. she liked being with us immensely and we liked
having her with us just as much. But then she liked also going back
to the children and her normal routine, and this is just as it should be.
I must say I envied her, going back to the country. - I am glad that
you sent me Miss Baker's address. I'll ask Eva to write her soon and
perhaps add a few words myself. I am sure Miss Baker sometimes comes to
Newyork and it would be nice for both of them to meet again.
Now, inspite of my excuse at the beginning, I have written you
a long letter and hope you will retaliate with an even longer one.
Thanks for all your repeated birthday wishes. Fortunately letters take
hardly a fortnight lately, and I was happy to receive your letter of
the 11th April already yesterday, the 24th. I hope our letters reach you
just as quickly.
Love and kisses, and
kindest regards to the Rosemount and Regency Lodge inhabitants. Lotte.

pages.transcription:
Wyndham Hotel				Newyork, 29.4.41

Dear Hanna & Manfred,

Just a line to tell you that there will be
a dinner of the P.E.N. Club on the 15th of May where
Stefan, Sigrid Undset, Romains and Somerset Maugham
will speak. The speeches will be relayed by WRUL
Boston to Europe. and maybe if this letter reaches you in
time you can find out and listen.
Thanks for your cable the other day which shows
that you feel now reassured about Eva's surroundings
and her happiness there. Last Sunday, as I wrote you already
I met her at Elizabeth's house, and next week I hope
I shall be able to go and visit her at Amity Hall. It
must be lovely there now, and now the children surely
enjoy the garden very much. If I go I shall try to
borrow a camera and send you some photos of the house
and people in it. But first of all I am impatient to
hear from you that Eva's photos have arrived, I am
quite sure you will like them. They are natural (mother
will say that the hair could be done better, but you
know how it is sometimes with hair, it just went the other
way and even the hair-dresser could not make it behave)
and say and from the one with the coat on - which Eva
disliked because she is ashamed of having had to wear
such a hat - you can see that she has grown.
I hope you had a good time at Bath on
Easter and did not return to London too quickly.
By the way, could Lore remain in Bath? Eva and I
have been wondering how you spent your Easter days and
what the garden looks like and whether the cuckoo is back
already. I do wish we would spend the next Easter again
together. From us not much is to report. Stefan is working,
I have finished the allergy test, am supposed to react to dust
and own bacterias and the injections with this stuff are being
prepared. I am fairly well, but hope for definite results
of these injections.

I expect a letter from you these days - a clipper arrived to-day - and
shall then write more in detail.
Love, kisses, all good wishes,
Lotte.

pages.transcription:
Dear Hannah, we had your letter of the 25 April just on Lottes
birthday - she is now much better and I hope her recovery will
be a during and complete one. We have now decided not to go
to Brazil as her treatment will continue and I do not want to
expose her to new changes - on the other hand the political situation
is not clear at all and it would be risky to travel by boat. Here
we will have no difficulty to stay longer than our permit was (six
month) and we will go somewhere to the country and I hope to
work there better than here in Newyork. Here I have to write some
little things between to assure our living, I have to see some people
and to correct the English and French proofs of my book on Brazil
- when all this will be finished we want to retire ~~and not~~
more to ~~stand~~ the terrible heat here like last year (my goodness,
it is already nearly a year! and what a year!!). I do not know
if you will have heard through the wireless my ~~address~~ - I have
to say it in German for the European waves, in English for the
London radio, in English again before the public and so three
twice in the microphone, once before the eating crowd
times in one evening and it will be one of these enormous dinners
which I hate with thousand nerves; but everyone has to do his
duty and I try at least to avoid all phraseology of democracy
which will be poured over this evening by a ~~dozen~~ of other
speakers. You may imagine how we follow in the newspapers
all news about England and every air-attack let us think of you
- has Manfred already had opportunity to give his medical help?
He as a doctor will probably see more as everyone other. You should
keep a diary as it will be for coming generations an unforgettable
story - alas for us it is more sad, especially for our generation
which goes for the second time through this ordeal. Please give
Manfred my best wishes for his birthday, we are so sorry that we
cannot sit together quietly and happy and even not send him a
little present for this day. Thanks for all you have arranged with

pages.transcription:
my accountant. Mondadori was my Italian publisher but
my books have been banned already half a year before the
war, only when all this fascism will be over they will be
there printed again. I hope you have received the power of
attorney which was legalised here at the British Consulate and
which we did send by registered mail; I like to have my
things in order even in a disorderly world, it is the only
inheritance which has remained me from my father, this punc-
tuality and methodic order. - We will stay here in any case
till to the middle of June and you shall have regular news
from and about Eva who enjoys very much the stay in Croton
and is developing into a young lady out of the little child
you did send over. As to the things which I want to do for
me the first is that you buy for us - lavishly - a beautiful
birthday present to your husband as we could not do it
ourselves, secondly that you write to us if we can let you
send by ~~us~~ our friends a food parcel again and if you have
told
special wishes, I would have arranged it also for Frietental
but I do not know his new adress. Now I have talked enough
and want only to tell you that you may take out of
life what is to be taken and not to be parcimonious -
this war is now starting from this side and we do not
know how long it will take from our life. Kindest regards
to all of us. Yours
Stefan Zweig

pages.transcription:
Dear Hannah and Manfred, we are somewhat disappointed that Manfred's
exam is but in July, I had wished so much to know you both in Bath.
Meanwhile your teeth will be quite in order and you will feel relieved.
Do not worry about Eva's school. I hope it is quite right for the time being
and in my opinion school-education not so important as home-education
and most of all: self-education. Remember yourself how little we learned in
school of all what later became efficient in our lives and how much by reading
and self-instruction. Eva is in an intelligent milieu and likes reading curi-
ously, so I am not afraid. And for the next term we have plenty of time
to decide as we ourselves have to make decisions. Perhaps we will in the
meantime discontinue to live in Hotels (we are so tired of it) and go somewhere
near to the country provided we will and can stay here; the most important
thing is that you have full confidence in Lotte who is in a certain way
a second mother to Eva and loves her like an own child and you may be
always be sure that we take her education and development as a personal
matter. Lotte told me that Eva would like to have a bicycle, I however do
not favour very much the idea - the time of safe bicycle-riding has gone
and I think it is too dangerous now as all the roads are continually
full of deadly riding cars. I would not feel happy knowing her riding
along these roads, I think it would be better to let play her tennis or
other games which develop the body and are socially useful. Now we have
soon to decide where to go, we prefer to remain near to Newyork, the diffi-
culty is that we dislike Hotels and on the other hand have nobody
for housekeeping and no car, perhaps we will emulate our boy an old
one and tell it again in return. Thanks for the idea to send the Bal-
manuscript. But I could not continue without my reference books
and notes. I am working on my autobiography and one or two little slices
out of it I could sell to Readers Digests which is the best for our own stomach.
I did sent a short story through the British Consulate to Peter Smollet
for his party, I hope it will arrive safely. Lotte is really not suffering
any more but the cure tries to get a definite stop for ever: let us hope that
this ambitious goal will be reached. When this letter will reach you great
decisions - much more important ones than our own - will have been
made here and let us hope the best - how far are the quiet hours we could
pass together; I have always the same wish that you could have at least
Some restful hours in the garden and forget there the bestiality of our age which is not to be reconciled
with the beauty of the eternally peaceful country. And let me repeat: do not be pessimistic and
remind always that all this belongs in reality to you and not to us.
