pages.transcription:
Wyndham Hotel
42 West 58th street
Newyork, May 8th, 41

Dear Hanna & Manfred,
We have received your letter of April 25th and I am more
than glad that you feel now reassured about Eva. I went to see
her on Sunday and found her well and happy there, and almost
envied her for being there. The house is beautifully situated on
a hill, overlooking other hills and the Hudson river, has large,
if still somewhat neglected, grounds - we realise what it means to
bring even a limited garden back into shape after years of undoubted
neglect. We were all outside in the garden after singing folksongs
at the piano - Eva and Mr. Schaeffer included - and I confirmed
my impression that there are very nice children, especially the boys
and the girl near Eva's age and Mrs. Sch's 3 year old little boy
which is petted and spoiled by all. There is no need for you to
worry about the summer. First of all we have decided not to
go back to Brazil at the present moment but to postpone all
such decision until America's position which seems to get nearer
the war every day, is quite decided. We have vague plans at the
moment to go north to Maine for the summer months, but that
would not worry you as it is not far, according to USA standards,
we would remain in close contact with Eva and might even
have her with us for a while - for I am sure she would not
like to miss the holiday life at Amity Hall to which they
are all looking forward already. The bigger children are all
remaining there for the holidays and others may come, and
they are making all sorts of plans. There seems to be, however
a little misunderstanding between you and Mrs. Sch. I spoke to
her about Eva's learning latin and she said she never wrote
that to you. She or her husband could easily teach Eva but
as she is going to have latin next year anyway if she remains
in USA (and unfortunately, it looks like a long way at present)
she does not think it a very good idea as it would only bore
her once they begin it at school. As regards French, she is ex-
pecting a girl of about 20 or 22 shortly, who has been brought
up in France and will speak French with the children. And as
Eva's friend Marion and her brother speak perfect French too, I
think the prospects for Eva's learning are very good. - Eva had
a very good report for Easter which I am sure she copied for
you. We were happy to learn from your cable that the photos
had safely arrived and that you liked them.
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief auf Hotelpapier. Sehr gut lesbar.
Rückseite des ersten Blattes, leer.

pages.transcription:

I was terribly sorry to learn that you, Hanna, had trouble
with your teeth and that you have to undergo such a long and
disagreeable treatment. I hope that you are already finished
with it when you get this letter and that you had a well-
deserved rest in Bath in Manfred's company. By the way, how
does your heart stand all this terrible strain. You never men-
tioned it with a single word and I am anxious to learn about
your health more anxious than you need feel about mine.
For I have all the best medical attention and can have all
the rest and quiet and treatments how and when and where I
need it. And over there, rest and quiet in any case cannot always
be easy to find. - We are impatiently looking forward to the day
when Manfred will have finished his exam and come out to
Bath for good or at least find a hospital job in the country.
I have read that the 40 year old have to register for military
service now, but we do not know how soon they are actually
called up and whether physicians will have to do anything out-
side their medical profession. At any rate Manfred ought to take
a good long rest at Bath with you, if possible. You know we
like the idea of knowing you there although it is always with
regret that we cannot be there with you.
Now, Manfred, I think it's just about time to
congratulate you to your birthday and from all my heart
I wish you many happy returns, to be celebrated not only
in Hanna's but also in Eva's and our company. Eva made
me a lovely present, flowers cut out in coloured paper and
glued on cardboard and I am proud how nicely it is done
and how pretty it looks. It is a shame we cannot send
you a present from here, but maybe you see something
which we might have liked to give you and get it in our name.
We are looking forward to Mr. Voge's arrival who, I hope, will
see us immediately and tell us a lot about you.
Kindest regards and best love
Lotte.
Two days ago we sent you the power of attorney
by registered air-mail. Please confirm receipt.
By the way, we have not yet received the
birth and marriage certificates which we may require
for one visa or the other. Did you send them already
or was it not yet possible. Don't take any special trouble,
just let us know about it.

pages.transcription:
Hotel Wyndham 42 West 58 Street New York		12. V 1941
Dear Hannah and Manfred, we have just your letter from the
2 May, mail is now much quicker and this we take as a good
sign - There are still things like Hess' flight out of Germany which
let us hope that in the Nasi-Empire not all is so perfect as they like
to let us believe. You in London and England have to share the
bitterest part but I hope you have the conscience that your sufferings
and your courage can and will alone save this world. We follow
on the radio and in the newspapers anxiously the events and I must
not tell you that all our thoughts are with you. I wish Manfred
could finish his examinations soon and have some rest! You
too would feel much better - your nerves must be wrely shared[?]
by his dentist-treatment. I know how one feels during such a
treatment, how one hates his own head, his whole body. May the
thought you be helpful that Eva enjoys her life at Croton very
much and that she really is in best hands; Mr. Schaeffer did
win her full confidence and love and as she is really interested
in her progress you can expect the best results. We will visit her
very soon - this week is rather up with a hundred things. My
speech had to be cut from 10 minutes to 6, I have to speak in
German and in English for the European radio transmission. You
cannot imagine what pettiness authors develop on such occasions,
everybody is offended, one because he got only 2 minutes, the
other because he has not to sit on the parade-table, the third be-
cause one had not invited him personally - they cannot under-
stand people like Lotte and me who would be happy not so sit
for show and prefer to leave to them all these little things that
seem so ridiculous in a time where horses are smashed, inno-
cent people murdered and the greatest decision of mankind is
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief auf Hotelpapier. Die Tinte ist violett. Die Lesbarkeit ist gut, abgesehen von dem Wort 'wrely shared' (evtl. 'sorely shared' oder 'sorely shaken'?).

pages.transcription:
at stake. Sometimes one wonders that those are the same people
who really wrote beautiful verses and show in her books wisdom
and psychology.
I did not cable to you about Joaquim Torres. I liked to
leave it to you; it is not important to care about him, one
will never hear from him again, but if you thought it better
to acknowledge his letter you may do it. - Lotte is here still in
treatment for some weeks but only twice a week and we hope
it will be effectif. She feels much better and we hope to go for
two months somewhere to the country not only on behalf of the
heat in New York but also because one looses so much time here.
We see not many people but very interesting ones and make
no public appearance whatever except on this one dinner. Most
of my collegues are in California, from English writers there live
here Somerset Maugham, Cronin, Bertrand Russel, Auden,
some of them for good. I have an invitation for lectures
in Cuba in November - the voyage paid and even
a good fee for lectures - but who can say if it will be
possible to Cuba at this date? The most important for us is
to know you both at Bath and to have a rest; we feel our-
selves not very important in whatever we do and you must
never worry about us or Eva. Altogether it seems as in the
long run the turn will come, the preparations here in
America are accelerated from day to day for the necessary
relief of your burden! Kindest regards to you all! Yours
Stefan Zweig

pages.transcription:
Wyndham Hotel
42 West 58th Street

New York, 14.V.41

Dear Hanna a Manfred,
Your letters arrive now fairly regularly
every Tuesday, and on this day I automatically wake up earlier
in order to read your letter as quickly as possible. I am terribly
sorry for you, Hanna, that in addition to the already heavy
time strain you have to suffer such a long and painful treatment
and I do hope it is over now and that for years to come you will
not have to worry any more about your teeth. We count the days
until we get the news that Manfred passed his exam and that
you both have a good rest in Bath. I was happy to hear that
you had received our and Eva's letters about her stay with us
and that you liked her photos. I'll send you the two which
Eva dedicated - on our advice - to Granny and Raumann's who
certainly are pleased with them too. And as I suppose
that you will like to have duplicates, we will send you
those in postcard size by and by. They are all ready, and
if you want Eva to send them to someone else, just let us know.
We have plenty of postcards for such purpose. - I hope Eva's
and our birthday letters for you, Manfred, arrive in time and we
would be glad to learn that Hanna got you a lovely present for
us. Maybe that food parcel has also reached you by then. I
sent it more or less as the shop prepares them for such purposes
without knowing whether such parcels are at all welcome to you
and what you really would want. You must let us know if
we should send more - it is quite an organisation here - and
what you would like to have. - I did not see Eva this week,
we were busy preparing, translating, altering, correcting,
shortening, retranslating Stefan's speech for to-morrow's dinner,
and Eva was invited to spend the weekend with a friend of
hers in or near Groton. So you see, this is a visible proof
that she has made friends, and Mrs. Sch wrote that they are
very nice people. I hope to be able to go to Groton again
next Sunday and shall then try to borrow a camera to make
snapshots of the house and children and the Schaeffer family.
I hope Carmel had a good rest in Bath. She must have had a
very strenuous time all those months and I am always glad that
our house is at least good for something. I feel a little guilty that
I did not see her children for such a long time, but I was too
busy with myself and Stefan's work and in the Easter holidays when I
wanted to invite at least Robin to come with Eva to the Circus,
[Randnotiz links, von unten nach oben:]
he was just gone to live for a week with John. Rose and Benes are doing all they can
for the boys and Robin loves them but John is a lot of trouble and seems determined to dislike
America and not to adjust himself in the least. It really is not their fault but I
am sorry for all of them and Carmel.

pages.transcription:
Dear Hannah and Manfred, to your letter I want to tell you my fear, that Hannah
has an exagerated feeling of responsibility concerning the house in Bath. I am
of course happy if she takes a few days of rest there, but I do not wish that she
has the worries of a house-mother. It is quite indifferent to me, if the house is
kept somewhat better or worse and the Rainmans will look themselves to it -
you cannot imagine how indifferent I have become to all material things and
how far the house is from my thoughts, how I have resigned ever to see the books
any more; concluding my autobiography I have said fare well to all the past. For
me one thing is important - to concentrate after the many month of travelling
and the depression through the war. I have lost all pleasure on entertainment,
we have even not been a single time in a cinema and I am so thankful to Lotte
that she does not protest against this rather monkish form of life. The idea
to stay now for half a year without to move is for me a relief; may be that
I shall be disturbed from outside, but all is here ~~really~~ much easier, much
indifferent and I would not mind to live for ever such a retirer life, for-
getting the world and forgotten by her. For you this war is what the other was
for me - an interwall - and just his terrors and difficulties will let you long
life more afterwards, especially if you have back your daughter more happy
than ever and full of experience. I my self can no more live in transitory
forms, I must know, that I have not to change and will not have worries
Here is for the moment the maximum of possibility of complete retire-
ment and thats why we do not want to change. Believe me that I think
quite clear and if I do not fulfil your wish which would give you to the
Bach before Eve, it is because I see the possibilities of some complications
which may arise; we all must have patience now and I for my part would
not complain even if our small life here would continue for many months.
I am glad to have left Newyork. I can work here better, life is easier and cer-
tain primitiveness have her great charm. As to the material matters I insist
that your expenses for travelling etc should be paid back to you regularly;
if there should be no more cash dont worry, we will then sell of some
the investements; it is important that you and your family have all you
want. I wish we could send you parcels from here but till now we could
not find an opportunity. I know that the food situation has improved a good
deal, but if you would know how cheap sugar, caffe' is in Brazil you would
understand your desire to send over some specimens. Give Victor my kindest
regards, he may excuse me that I do not write him - but not-writing letters
means always that I am writing books. Let us hope that this winter (here begins
the summer now) will not be too hard and if some good signs to not deceive me I hope it will
be the last winter of the war and all our expectations fulfilled. So cheer up - to
us, the old ones, to resign and not to worry. Stefan

Dear Hannah & Manfred, I have just your kind cable. You have
nothing missed, all these lectures are without importance and
~~are~~ altogether we minutes instead of tea. Lotte was sitting
on the grand table between Somerset Maugham and Conte Sforza
I suppose she has proved a brilliant conversationalist. Today I
have time to write {you} as she has gone to Croton and you will get
from her farther news about your pet. I believe that the asthma

sleeps without to wake up a single time. And that she likes
to stay a little longer in the morning hours has nothing to do
with her asthma but it a kind of 'Blitzgift' she brought into her
marriage. I do nothing to drive her out only I refuse to make
the morning coffee myself. Now we are wondering where to go
during the months of heat. It is not at all easy because we
who have no car are something prehistoric in this country -
all is adapted for driving. Then ~~all~~ is so far away and Lotte
has probably to ~~go~~ form and to look if she finds something con-
venient. I personally has liked to stay here provided we had found
a hotel with air conditioning, but the very few, which have such.
roofs are too expensive and too fashionable for my taste. Even
if I would calculate that four hours saves for work every day would

of Claridges - I never did even in the times when it was
possible. Again and again, we can make ~~not~~ ~~disturb~~ 
plans and who can do so in this moment - since years
we believe always that next month next year one shall see
clear but it seems that we shall pass the greater and

Lotte had a very nice letter from Miss Bales, she has the intention
to go over for her long holidays but Lord Halifax himself advised
her not to do so - it is practically impossible to travel nowadays
within time-limits and it is not advisable. We were so sorry
to hear from her that also our dear Bath had on holy Friday a
hint of air-raid; but I am convinced it is a better place than
London and we are anxious to know you there. Manfred will
want his rest after the examinations and yourself Hannah, you
must be somewhat worn out. In Bath you can at least rest the
whole day long in the garden, while London like every big town
also does not allow to relax; you will have telefone and
guests and whatever. - Now to Friedental. I am in touch
with his friend Margaret Raiser who is very active to get him
an affidavit and I do the best for my part. Here it would be
easy to get for him something to do. The most important
is now to have the affidavit ready and to try for a passage
- also for Heinrich Mayer we have made inquiries about the
validity of his affidavit. To Friedental we did send a
food parcel, let us hope that he will get it, meanwhile I expect
you will have got yours already. It is a pity that one has
to take those ready-mades and cannot choose, but it seems
that there is an arrangement to use only one type of
food-parcel to avoid all specifications of weight and cus-

are waiting already to hear from me and this you shall
through Lotte immediately she comes back from Croton
I understand how heartbreaking it must be to you not to

pages.transcription:
Wyndham Motel                                Sunday evening, May 18th, 41

Dear Hanna & Manfred, I have just returned from Croton
and have nothing but the very best and satisfactory to
tell you about Eva. She feels fine, looks very well, loves
Amity Hall and the country round it (which
with its rolling hills has really some resemblance with Bath).
Yesterday Mr. Kiefer visited her and they went for a drive
and walk. I suppose he will write you about his impressions
and I am confident that his report will contribute further
to reassure you about her surroundings. Today we went
for a visit to Fueloep-Miller's, our friends - I believe you
have met them in Hallam Street - who are in Croton over
the summer with a 3 months old baby whom Eva admired
very much and whom she is invited to visit. As they are
on best terms with Schaeffer's I suppose that will be easy.
If Eva's letter from today should be a little shorter
than usual, you must blame it on me because I left
an hour later than usual. Both Eva and I had a nice
letter from Miss Baker, and she promised to call me up when
she comes to New York. - Salmon's are silent and in spite of
various letters not a line is to be got out of them. There
is nothing to be done - and I don't think it is important.
They mean well - when they happen to think of Eva - but
they are unreliable and have no manners. And as Eva
is now in very good hands and we do not intend to
leave the country we do not need them. - Eva will have
written you that she spent the last weekend with a friend
in Croton. Mrs. Sh told me that the girl and her parents
are extremely nice and Eva enjoyed it. She brought some
photos and I enclose a small one. - Some other visitors to
Amity Hall took me back to New York and I felt quite
grown-up, discussing the children and their various
little problems, summer holidays, etc. - I hope you have
at last finished with the dentist. You are to be much more
pitied than I. I am much better and the twice-weekly visit
to the doctor means no more than a few injections - three at
one time, a "mezihe", as the doctor calls it.

pages.transcription:
Dear Hannah and Manfred, we are missing very much your letters but we
know it is not your fault - there are now terrific gales which sweep
the country and many of the planes have to wait. Here it seems that
the United States are going fast into help for England and finally all
the obstacles are cleared away. But I know you have the heavier part to
bear and you may imagine with what feeling we read about the attacks
on Bristol, so near of your house. At least you have not to worry about
your daughter, it seems that she likes her new house very much - she
writes always we should come to visit her, but unfortunately it is
not so easy as she thinks. We have 1 hour 50 minutes to Newyork, from
there to another station, from there to Croton, from there with a car
to her house and we have no car; it cannot be done in one day.
and Lotte has been ill for ten days, we have lost much time and have
still to go to Baltimore for two days. And we hope to have her here
in Newhaven in April for a few days - we are afraid she will not
know what to do here, as there is nothing except the library and no
distrea at all. We hope however that she will be a little recruited
of you and having opportunity to talk about you abundantly. -
Alltogether we feel very often very sad, - the first war took five
years of my life and this one, a hundred times more violent,
will take all bright and quiet way of living away from us for
years and years. And I shall soon be 60 years old. This living in
Hotels, which we not afeable at all, and in foreign countries be-
comes in the long run very oppressive; just our generation has such
an unlucky time! Some times I wish I had also to pass examinations
or to do some public work; what means literature today against
the dramatic of our daily history! As soon as we have news from
you, you shall hear more from us. In the mean time kindest regards
to all from yours
Stefan Zweig

Wyndham Hotel
42 West 58th Street
New York

24. 5. 41

Dear Hanna & Manfred,
We just received your letter of May 13th and
hasten to reply before we begin the daily work. I am very glad
that by fulfilling your engament[?] and visiting Harrogate you
missed one of the heaviest attacks on London, but I pity you,
Hanna, that the torture at the dentist's was prolonged for another
week. At this moment, however, I hope that you are already en-
joying the quieter atmosphere of Bath, having no more dentist to
be afraid of, and all the advantages which the garden can offer.
Now first the replies to some of your questions,
Eva. I shall make more detailed enquiries about the school and
the prospects when returning to England to continue school or
university. For that purpose I shall enquire at the Childs
study Association where I met a lady who has lived in England
for some time, had a school of her own in Hamstead and has
children who go to school here. As her job at the committee is to
advise parents and guardian about education she can certainly
help me. I will also write to Miss Baker from whom Eva and
I had very nice letters and who, being in one of the most
expensive and exclusive colleges, will be in a position to
give reliable information. - About the two schools in Croton:
the private (progressive, that is very modern) school and the public
school where Eva goes now, I had made enquiries before
deciding to settle Eva at Mrs. Sch.'s. The information I got
from Mrs. Sch. and other people was that both schools are good.
The reason why I first decided for the private school was -
in spite of its ultra-modern education and teaching methods-
that most of the children of Amity Hall go there while only
3 or 4 go to the public school with Eva. The private school has
been for a long time very generous with scholarships and
Mrs. Sch. prefers it, as far as I can make out mainly for
the reason that the "art" classes are so very good and
because she is personally on very good terms with all of them
while with the public school which is a school about the
size of the Bath school, also a very new and modern building,
is of course more impersonal. Where she learns more in the
old-fashioned sense of the word, is difficult to decide.
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief auf Hotelpapier. Die Tinte ist blau-violett. Die Lesbarkeit ist gut.
Rückseite des ersten Blattes, leer.

pages.transcription:
2)
The private school which has only a hundred pupils in
all and where the children are taught in groups of 6 or 8
is of course much more individual and it may be that in some
cases a much more rapid progress is possible. On the other hand
it is doubtful whether their method of giving the children as
much freedom as possible in their work and make them do things
by trying to get them interested in it and never force them to do a
thing in the given moment, will always work. - I discussed
all those problems with everybody I could get hold of at that time
and I am still at the same point that both systems have their
definite advantages and disadvantages. - Both schools lead up to
the college which is something between high school and uni-
versity, and I do not think that except in a few very snobbish
schools public school education would be a disadvantage.
As to languages I wrote you a few weeks ago. In her present
school Eva will get French and Latin next February, and she
has a good chance at Amity Hall where they will have a French
councellor - that is a person who is something between a teacher,
playmate and matron - and where her friend Marion speaks it
fluently. - That they should think her "inferior" in her school
I cannot believe; this must be the personal opinion of one
child and she certainly does not take it seriously, for she neither
mentioned it to me or to Mrs. Sch. and from what she tells me I
had always the impression that she likes going there. There is
one teacher whom she does not like - but that will happen in every
school. - One thing may be a little hard for her and the
other public school children at Amity Hall, and that is that
the private school closes already next week whereas the public
school continues another month. But as the school finishes
at 3 anyway she still has the whole afternoon with the others.
About your brothers affidavit we made an
enquiry last week through Washington's Visa Department and
they may let us know in due time how his matter stands.
But they are slow and it may also take weeks before we get a
reply although we asked them to make telegraphic enquiries.
I am glad that Bath and Rosemount are as
pleasant for you as ever and I do long for the moment
when we will all be there again, together. But when will
that be?
Love and kisses, keep well and
take good care of yourself,
Lotte.

pages.transcription:
New York, June 1st, 1941
Dear Hanna & Manfred,
There was no letter from you last week and
also from our side there is little to report. We had a letter
from Eva that she is well and everything is fine, and next
Sunday I hope to be able to visit her again, and perhaps
Stefan will come with me. If Sunday were not his best and quietest
working day, he would accompany me more often, but as we had
so many little business things to settle which take lots of time
without bringing profit he hates to lose any more time. This
weekend we had to go to Atlantic City - the super-Brighton of USA -
to visit a lawyer-friend who advises us in our personal decisions
and our next plans. I wrote you that we had given up the return
to Brazil for the time being although life down there is much
cheaper, easier and quieter. And I am glad to remain near Eva
and to convince myself regularly how well she is settled in Boston
and how much she likes being there. From Salmon's none of us has
ever heard again since many weeks and we have decided to forget
about them. They are the type of people who only see what is
under their nose and who do not think. And fortunately we
do not need them. - Kiefer's have visited Eva a fortnight ago, we
are near - and will not leave New York before the end of July. -
Franz Newman as well as Berner's (Rose Wohl's brother-in-law) have
taken out their car again after the winter storage and promised
to visit her, and Elisabeth is only expecting the school holidays
in order to have Eva for a few days. From mother I have
not heard for a few weeks, and I attribute it to the fact that
she wrote by ordinary mail the last months. She must have
been very happy to see you both again. Stefan had two more
or less private letters from Eisen, and is somewhat disappointed
that his friend Ruben is not in his house as he expected after
earlier news. He fully understands the difficulties under which
he works, but he requests you not to give him any more help
until he has spent all his money he got for this purpose.
From my friend Lotte I heard that she was in the country
with the Raeburn family but that she intended to leave
them in June and to return to London. I suppose she will
then communicate with you at least by phone. - I wrote
you last time that we were trying to find out from through
Washington whether your brother's affidavit is sufficient
but we got no reply so far. Authorities here work very slowly, just
as the whole tempo here is not at all "American" as we imagined
it in Europe.

I do not think that you missed very much because you
could not hear those Penclub dinner speeches. For me it was
quite interesting and entertaining because it was my first
big public dinner, sitting at the celebrities' table between
Somerset Maugham (who was very nice at not at all stiff as I
imagined him to be) and Count Sforza. Most of the European
writers whom we ever read were present and I hope it was not
disappointing for the thousand people who paid 3 dollars each
for this privilege to see that writers really do not look
different from other people. There were lots of speeches, and
fortunately, on account of the radio, the speakers were strictly
rationed in time - Stefan, Jules Romains, Maugham, Dorothy Thompson,
Sigrid Undset between 6 and 10 minutes, the others who spoke in
their native languages to two minutes each. Then there was
the inevitable auction to raise money for refugee funds and
we were surprised that really a number of people publicly
donated three and four hundred dollars each. They raised about
5000 dollars and that will be just sufficient to pay the
travelling expenses of 10 persons from Europe as they can only
get out by the most phantastic routes - via Russia and Japan or
via Africa and Martinique and only a few lucky people via
Lisbon direct to USA. Unfortunately the possibilities for affi-
davits become more and more limited among the people we
know, and we have not yet succeeded in finding one for Friederike.
I wrote to Jan in this respect so you need not give him my
earlier letter at all. Should he come to you again for help
you might let him have ten or fifteen pounds and tell
him that with this the money you had at your disposition
is exhausted. - I hope you all keep well and that you
are definitely through with the dentist. By the way, you never
mention how your heart stands all the strain. Do tell me whether
it gives you any trouble. This is much more important to me
than my own health about which you seemed to worry quite
unnecessarily for I can do and really do everything that can
be done for it while you certainly neglect those things.
By the way mail is now much more regular and therefore
it is worth while, and we would be glad, that you always inform
us by cable a week or ten days before when you go to Bath. -
I hope you did not mind that our birthday telegram was sent collect.
I felt a little doubtful about doing so but Stefan said you
would understand. Kindest regards and best love and kisses
Lotte

Hotel Wyndham
Newyork, June 2nd, 41

Dear Hanna
I return the enclosed forms signed and quite
agree with you that you should be able to take any necessary
steps or precautions. Your last letter (from May 21st) proves that our
thoughts still conform. As soon as we had mailed you the power of
attorney we regretted that we had omitted to specify it also for
safes, and on the other hand we wrote you just yesterday that
Stefan is not quite happy with Eisen's effusive and evasive
letter and that it seems to us that he puts Stefan's interest
behind that of newly acquired friends and clients, in an
understandable and yet disappointing instinct of self-interest.
I am very glad that you too are now convinced that Eva is in
satisfactory surroundings and somehow I am absolutely certain
that all along you would have acted in the same way about
her as we did. You, too, would have made the arrangement
with Salmon's last year under the special circumstances and
the personal and general uncertainty then prevailing, and you,
too, would have transferred her to Amity Hall on our return.
And you, too, would still now be uncertain whether the Public
or the Private School has greater educational advantages. Miss
Baker promised to let me know when she comes to Newyork and
I hope to discuss this question with her, as well as with
several others. As the Private School will not reopen before the
end of September there is plenty of time also for you to write
me suggestions and your opinion, although in the end I am afraid
you must still leave the decision to us. I can understand how you
miss Eva - I judge it from the fact how much I miss you -
but somehow for this very reason I enjoy so much having
Eva here and looking after her as well as I can. In a way it
is a compensation and gives me the feeling that our old life
has not been completely disrupted but continues, for the time
being, over here. (Stefan will criticize these last remarks as being
imprecise, but after all I am no writer and I hope that even
you will understand what I try to say and not speak again of
"burdening us with Eva's care". - I am terribly sorry that this
torture at the dentist is still dragging on. Both you and Manfred
will have earned a long rest in Bath, and I hope you get it soon.
please turn over
love and kisses Lotte.

pages.transcription:
I had to-day a reply from Washington that they do not more cable enquiries
to their embassy in London, but that they have written them and asked to
send me a report about the status of your brother's affidavit - in clear
language that probably means that I shall never hear from them.
For why should the London consulate take the trouble to write me a
letter when they refuse to give an answer to the people themselves?
Probably too many people have tried to find out how things stand
via cables from Washington and they therefore stopped this practise.

pages.transcription:
Dear Hannah and Manfred, there are not much news about us,
Lotte is a bit better but I hope that when the systematic
treatment begins she will be perfectly alright. Now summer
is approaching and we have not yet made up our minds
what to do. I hate to go to the country here as in the
hotels of this kind I would find no place to work quietly
and all is so far and we have no experience what would
be convenient to us - The others have now taken houses
in California because the climate is perfect there, but
we as visitors cannot do this. Newyork is terrible
during the summer and an air-conditionate apparte-
ment would be the only possibility but the prices
are fantastic. Going to Brazil would be the best but
we see not yet a possibility or probability in case
of Americas entrance into the war to come
back (except immigrating what we would of course
avoid.) So we see not yet any solutions and time
flies (with black wings). And you may imagine how
I am longing to sit somewhere quietly and to work
in continuity. The terrifying doom comes nearer and
nearer and I must hurry to do what I have to do
- but who can act today after his own wishes? For
your friend Fridlauer dont worry, he has already announ-
ced here that he writes in Brazil the biografie of the
President and I suppose he will be soon
here to meet all the others Fridlauers. You underrate
him, there is a hint of genius in him to overcome
all difficulties and the darker the waters the better he swims. I
his tenacity and courage. We are not fit enough for such
times with our "alergic" moral conscience.

Rückseite des Dokuments, leer.

pages.transcription:
Hotel Wyndham 42 West 58 Street
2. June 1941
Dear Hannah we have been for one day on Atlantic
City to discuss different matters and to {get} also an im-
pression if such a place would do for the coming months
of heat. It was very pleasant now but {it will} be unpleasant
when the great crowds begin to come; so we have to look
for another place; it is not easy for old fashioned people without car.
About Eva, you will have the best news, she feels perfectly
at home {in Croton} and I shall not forget your wish that she
shall learn French during the holidays. I had two long
and very friendly letters from our friend Eize but there is
something in it which does not please me; he has since
a year not notified a single precise thing and I see
that the drawing from which you gave me news he has
afterwards sold to somebody other. I can well understand
his situation; it seems that he cannot resist the tempta-
tion if some new friends come now who were not so inter-
ested in art as myself and have discovered her inclination
but now, he forgets his old friends and also the promise he
gave to them. If he would have written straightaway: I
could not do anything this whole year for you I would
have been clear. But I cannot get rid of the idea that
he whenever a better offer comes for the same things
he reserved months and months ago for me he gives
them away with profits and forgets what {he has let him down?} Perhaps I
am wrong but there is something evasive in his letters
and I wonder if he has given {you} clear information;
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief auf Hotelpapier. Tinte violett. Die Zeile 'he has let him down?' ist eine Einfügung über der Zeile.
Rückseite des ersten Blattes, durchscheinender Text der Vorderseite sichtbar. Leer.

pages.transcription:
The situation in the book market is not more the same than
a year ago and that is why I tried to reserve me in
time the material for my work. I did not write to him
myself because {it may} be a mere suspicion
of my part and as I know how hard he works, how diffi-
cult his life must be; perhaps you can make it out and
act without to let him feel that I begin to feel a bit dis-
appointed. I want to believe always the best of my
friends as long as I have no absolute proof of the
contrary. Wednesday we have our great 'spring cleaning'
- I have invited all those people I had to see to our
cocktail. It is impossible to make visits here {individually} 
by it takes too much time and the distances are too
great.
You never wrote me dear Hannah if there any
books or letters of interest came all this year long; I
do not want of course the whole list {and busy that} if anything
of personal interest would arrive you will let me
know it; altogether our correspondence is very small
now during that all writers are already {have} arrived here
I hope you will {have} with brillant teeth a brillant
summer in Bath and enjoy after Manfrets examina-
tion the well merited rest. Lotte is much better, she has
lost a litte weight and I will do my best to let her
regain all his ounces; if we only could sit some-
where quitely and be out of this Hotel and hometic
life! Yours faithful
Stefan

Rückseite des zweiten Blattes, durchscheinender Text der Vorderseite sichtbar. Leer.

pages.transcription:
8. June 1941 Hotel Wyndham Newyork
Dear Hannah, we just returned from Croton and I hurry to say you my
impressions as they are beyond my expectations. I found Eva grown-up,
sunburned, gay and happy; she is there loved with everybody, has with
Marion an excellent companion, takes care of the little children with real
passion and seriousness, loves very much her auntie Olga and the house. You
would have enjoyed to see her riding a little very tame pony which is now
for the whole summer in the house and most friendly with all the children.
We went in the car with Ron Wohl, the Berners and the little Robin who
knows Eva still from London; they all were surprised how beautiful the
place is now in summer time, overlooking the whole valley and very breezy
even in the hottest days. They will have soon tents there and allowed
as a special reward to sleep in them if they like — it is a kind of
life I wished to have had myself in my youth, free and amusing and
I feel it does Eva a lot of good. She has been always in company
of adults and learns now to deal with all the really important things
like housekeeping, care of little children, gardening and comes in con-
tact with life much better than with us who are only intellectuals (and
mostly disappointed ones). Lotte is really happy that all works so well as
she feels that you would enjoy to see your daughter so pleased with her
daily life, so healthy and so far from all the troubles and difficulties
of this damned time. It is also egoistically for us a great advantage that
she feels so thoroughly at home here because we can go with much better
confidence somewhere to a summer place - we have not yet decided where,
but I do not believe that we will leave before the first weeks of July as I
would prefer that Lotte continues her treatment as long as possible with
Dr. Shor. She feels much better but her activity, her „pep” as they say here
was a little hampered all these last months and I hope if we could find
a quiet place somewhere it would do her good; in summer Newyork is
like a furnace and even after Rio it would be a hard test to remain
here.
As to my material things I hear that some outstanding royalties
from Hungary will be paid directly to Paul Tabori in a few
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief von Stefan Zweig, violette Tinte. Sehr gut lesbar.
Rückseite des ersten Blattes, durchscheinender Text der Vorderseite sichtbar. Leer.

pages.transcription:
weeks, I shall give order that they shall be directed by him to my bank
and as soon as they arrive there, please inform me; it should be about
32 Pounds. As to Cassells I am convinced they will pay as soon as they will
be able to do so. We are now revising the translation of my book on
Brazil. The proofs will go to Cassels and I hope he can publish it next
year provided there is still enough paper available.
And now give my best wishes to Manfred for his exam and
do not forget to inform us by cable about the happy event which will
give him the well merited holidays - may: holy weeks, holy months -
in Bath. Altogether airmail is now much more rapid than before
and ~~though~~ {thanks to} that we feel you somewhat nearer to us. Kindest regards
to you all. Yours

Stefan Zweig

Dear Hanna & Manfred, We enjoyed the afternoon yesterday with Eva,
and I hope that the photos we took will come out well and give
you and Carmel some pleasure. Her vacations will begin earlier
than expected, practically already in a fortnight, and will last
until the middle of september. We are still uncertain when and where
to go for the summer, but I suppose we will have Eva with us
for a few days still here in Newyork. There are one or two little
things to be done about her teeth which the dentist could not fix
when she was here last owing to the holidays. - Our life continues
unchanged. Stefan is working at the autobiography, we are revising the
translation of the Brazil book, and last week we had a large cock-
tail party collecting all of Stefan's native friends, collegues and
acquaintances. It was nice, apparently so much so that nearly all
people remained not only for a cocktail but for more than two hours.
Twice a week I get my injections of dust and bacterias (separately) and
occasionally adrenaline in oil, and all this, together with the little
things one has always to attend to - this week for instance trying
to exchange the typewriters, getting summer shirts for Stefan, looking at a
house near Newyork, interviewing a prospective help, business talks,
having photostats made of several documents - keeps us busy.
I hope you are both well, that Manfred is not
working too hard and will soon get his degree and that you Hanna, have
nothing more to do with the dentist. We saw your last letter to Eva
which took only a week.
Love and kisses, Lotte

pages.transcription:
I hear Hal an old friend of mine Guido Baron Fuchs
is in great need after Harry been interned for some months
he is also a great friend of Sir Frankenstein. Please send
him to Baron Fuchs in my name a few words to Manor Farm,
Upper Quinton,
Warwick

Hotel Wyndham                                Newyork, 17.6.41.

Dear Hanna & Manfred,

To-day was mail-day and we got a letter from
Korner but none of you, and as we had nothing from you last week
we were very much disappointed. Eva showed us a letter from you
when we visited her last Sunday, but ~~that~~ that is not the same.
- I hope that you are all well and that Manfred's exam is soon
over. Please inform us by cable of the result. And then go to
Bath and remain there, both of you. We feel that the house has
a certain justification of existing if you are in it, and it ought
to be nice now in summer. We do not yet quite know where to go,
but it will not be far from Newyork, probably, and we shall continue
to see Eva and have her with us for a while. To-morrow I shall see
her teacher, Miss Baker, who is passing through Newyork and will
come to see me. It is a pity Eva cannot be here, but her school
does not finish until next week, and right now they seem to have
examinations. I shall also discuss the school problem with Miss
Baker. - From us there is little to be told. We work, with lazy,
tired or excited periods in between, according to weather and news,
and besides that cocktail party we gave and where we had the whole
crowd here, we do not see many people just now. - I wrote you
that we had an answer from the Visa Department in Washington that
they do not more send cabled enquiries about the status of prospective
immigrants, so we must wait until your brother gets his reply in the
regular manner. Let us know at once if his affidavit is sufficient
or if not, which sum would be required as a deposit here. Maybe we
could get his sponsor to put up a deposit because this would mean
saving considerable time compared with trying to find an additional
affidavit etc.

As I hope to get a letter in a few days time,
I only send this as a preliminary note until I can reply to what
you write. With kindest regards to all,

Dear both, really there is not much to tell,             fondest love and kisses,
we live quietly and are ashamed that we have
food and leisure, while you are in foarba, we are
Lotte
furious when we see how much to {here} waste our spent; Lotte is much
better and the treatment has already clearly shown where the real source
of her ,alergic' cealhes are and we hope the best just because her reactions
to the injections have been sometimes rather violent. Now we have to look
where to go for the summer. It is not easy because houses in the country are
very expensive and as we have no car we should be near to a station and
all what ~~is~~ is near and has easy access is overcrowded especially in the week
end by millions of cars - no possibility for walks as Manfred loves them so
much. We hope to see Eva again next week, she feels happy as she really
merits it and I am glad that you feel now sure about her. Yours Stefan

c/o Vikingpress
18 East 48th Street
Newyork.

I will write Sunday or Monday after visiting Eva.
Today I enclose two photos, one with Mrs. Sch.
who frowns against the sun. Love, Lotte
20.6.41.

Dear Hanna,
First of all I want to tell you that you better address letters
to us from now on c/o Viking Press, 18 East 48th Street, Newyork, if we
do not cable you another address. For we will probably leave Newyork about
the middle of July and go somewhere to the country because it will be too
hot in Newyork. Up to now we do not yet know where to go and it is every-
where the same trouble: we have no car and so far no one who could do the
house-keeping for us. But we are confident that something will turn up soon,
- don't worry, as one would say here. Today one request. I just received
one of those many enquiries which usually lead to nothing, about the film
rights for "Burning Secret". Unfortunately these rights do not wholly belong
to me as a film has been made seven or eight years ago by a foreign company.
But I had already negotiations about this in London with a refugee lawyer,
Justizrat Rosenberger whose address I unfortunately have not with me. Please
be kind enough to look up our correspondence in the big folder "Films"
which you should find under the heading "Burning Secret-Brennendes Geheimnis"!
I would be very grateful if you could find out his present address and
perhaps you could even cable it to me. I am very, very sceptical if anything
will come out of this vague agent's enquiry, but I would like to have in any
case the possibility to communicate with him.

Just in this moment while I am writing this, I get your cable of
the 19th and thank you very much. You know how much I appreciate Eiseman.
I had only become uncertain because he kept writing me letters announcing
more detailed ones without sending them.

Yesterday we have been for the first time to a concert in the
enormous Lewisohn Stadium. We were at the same table with the son of the
donator of this wonderful gift to the American people, and surrounded by
the big Jewry like the Warburgs, Loebs etc. It was quite interesting as a
contrast to the Schnorrers which are our daily surroundings.

We are confident that you will send us a cable immediately Manfred
has passed his exam, as you know how happy we will be for you both that he
will then have his well-deserved holiday.

Sunday Lotte will go to Croton to see your
little lamb (not more so little now) probably together with
my sister in law and she will give you the usual report.
We are so glad that she feels happy there having all the
funchois {being} at once a child and a kind of mother for
the younger children in the same house, friendly with every
body and especially with her bosom friends Marisa (and
she is already able to have a bosom friend thanks to her
quich devopement into a young lady.) Kindest regards and
love to you all
Stefan

[Randnotiz links:] Lotte is quite well and only so lazy to write.

pages.transcription:
Liebe Hanna!

Nicht nur, dass wie Stefan schreibt,
alles Deinen Wuenschen entsprechend geordnet wird,
sondern es war bereits vorher schon bestimmt, dass
ich am 27. nach Llandudno fahre und dass ich Mama
wollene Nachthemden schenke (die sogar bereits beé orgt
sind). - Wie es Mama geht und was sie moechte, geht
glaube ich ziemlich klar aus beiliegendem Brief von
ihr hervor. Ich bin der Ansicht, dass wenn ich Ende
Dezember hinfahre und Manfred oder Hans vielleicht
im Januar oder Februar, sie dann Maerz oder April
auf einige Wochen zu uns kommen soll. Dann ist es
Ende April, und ich glaube, weiter hinaus kann man
heute noch nicht disponieren. - Auch an Tante Ines
Geburtstag hatte ich nicht vergessen, und ich kann
Dir sogar verraten, dass sie diese Woche zu Be-
such bei Cissy ist und spaeter wahrscheinlich auf
ein paar Wochen zu Beaty geht.
Fuer die Kinder habe ich hier noch etwas
Strickwolle besorgt, teilweise zu reduzierten Prei-
sen, und ich persoenlich warte nur bis nach Wieh-
nachten, um zu versuchen, ob es in Londoner Sales
noch Tischtuecher und Handtuecher gibt, da selbst
die kleinsten weissen Damasttuecher rundherum auf
den Boden haengen. - Die Struempfe, die wir im
September in jenem Schuhgeschaeft bestellten, sind
jetzt gekommen, und ich habe sie genommen, auch fuer
Dich, merkwerdigerweise noch zum alten Preis, dafuer
wahrscheinlich in der Qualitaet reduziert.
Der Teppich liegt im drawingroom und eine
Stunde nach dem Legen haben Marta, William und ich die
beiden Sitzgarnituren von library und drawing room aus-
gewechselt, was unvergleichlich besser aussieht.- Eva und
Ursel hatten an jenem Nachmittag ein Kind eingeladen,
Judith Caro aus Berlin, respektive Essing rschule, und
Eva entschuldigte sich bei Judith, dass es so unrodent-
lich war - wir waren gerade beim Teppichumraeumen und
Ausprobieren.
Woosters Leute sind gluecklich aus dem Hause.
Stefan verteidigt ihn, aber zweifellos war an dieser Kette
von leakages Wooster schuld. Bei einer guten Firma darf
eine Kleinigkeit passieren, eine Stelle am Dach kann man
uebersehen, aber drei duerfen es nicht sein und nicht
dazu noch die anderen Schlampereien. Wooster hat es mir
uebrigens selbst zugegeben, nachdem er zuerst auf die
pages.notes: Typoskript. Brief von Lotte Zweig an Hanna (Hannah Altmann). Seite 1.

pages.transcription:
Liebe Hannah, alles wird Deinen Wuenschen entsprechend geregelt,
Lotte zum Geburtstag exediert und wir wohl erst an Neujahrs
genkent zurueck ins Haus gestellt, ich widerum hoffe sehr, dass Ihr
mit der Bahn faehrt - da Manfred so wenig Urlaub hat, soll er doch
nicht die Zeit auf den duellen und gefaehrlichen Strassen vertun. Fuerch-
te Dich uebrigens nicht - Eva ist durchaus nicht das fette Meerschwein-
chen, das Du in Deinen Angsttraeumen siehst, sondern bloss "mollert"
wie man in Wien sagte (wo dieser Typ sehr in Gusto war) - lass es Dir
von Smolka oder Jos ins Hochdeutsche uebersetzen. Wa Wooster haben
wir noch immer nicht die Rechnung, er laesst uns Schonzeit - Arbeiter
sehen wir nur bei andern Leuten (und da mit Vergnuegen). Ein
Schinken ist Euch zu Ehren bereits bestellt, ich haette lieber vom Nach-
barn ein grosses Schwein nach altem Brauch geschlachtet, um die
lieben Gaeste zu ehren. Auf jeden Fall (auch wenn Ihr nicht
kommt) kuendige ich Herrn Unger das Bett fuer Ende der Woche.
Also beeilt Euch, man spuert doch die Riessitat dieser Zeit hier
weniger als in London, das mir uebrigens ueber Christmaschine
immer odios war, Alles Herzliche von Eurem
Stefan

p.t.o.
pages.notes: Handschrift (Stefan Zweig). Seite 2.

2
freundlichste Art unverschaemt war und mir zum Beispiel
beim letzten Rohrbruch im Conservatory, als ich anrief,
ich wollte nicht Mr. Flint, sondern einen expert, der
alles nachprueft, den Vormann der painter, Mr. Rickard
schickte, ebenso, als ich mich ueber die leakage am
Heizkoerper beschwerte, die die Hallendecke hinunterkam,
mir zuerst erklaerte, "he undertands that Mr. Zweig
keeps on turning it off and on". All das war schon eine
grosse und unnoetige Schweinerei und er hat es auch zu-
gegeben, als er sah, dass ich auf seine Scherze nicht
mehr einging. - Immerhin, bis zu Weihnachten wird
hoffentlich alles in Ordnung und auch das Silber wieder
da sein, und Stefans insistence, einen handyman im Haus
zu haben, hat sich durchaus bewaehrt. Er verkittet
Maeuseloeecher, macht kleine Schreinerarbeiten, repariert
Tueren, hobelt sie ab und wird uns auch anstreichen, war
wunderbar zum Moebeltransportieren, saegt Holz, und neben
seiner Vergesslichkeit ist sein Hauptfehler, dass er
wahrscheinlich in paar Monaten eingezogen wird.
Jenes Bettdeckenmuster ist sehr schoen,
und ich warte sehr darauf sowie auf die anderen repa-
rierten und neu anzufertigenden Decken. - Ich denke
auch sehr daran, wenn ich schoenes Leinen bekomme, mir
selbst noch paar Tischdecken mit Hohlsaum zu machen.
Die paar Decken, die wir bei Jolly gekauft haben, sind
mein ganzer Vorrat, und hier habe ich wenig Attraktives
gesehen ausser diesen bunten Kaffeedecken.
Evas Dicke ist ungeheuer uebertrieben.
Sie ist noch genau so, wie wir sie uebernommen haben,
und es fehlt nichts als ein neuer Schuss Wachstum.
Jenes Bild fuer Mama werden wir machen lassen gleich
Anfang naechster Woche, wo man zu normalen Zeiten mit
ihr in die Stadt kann. - Heute sind sie bei jener Judith
wegen des Anzuendens der Chanukkalichter, und William
holt sie ab.
Mit Marta habe ich mich vorlaeufig so
geeinigt, dass sie, wenn ihre Kinder so wie unsere
bis zum 11. Jan. Ferien haben, erst nach meiner Ruecke
kehr von Llandudno am 1. oder 2. faehrt.

Alles Uebrige muendlich und hof-
fentlich bald. Ist der 22. definitiv oder kommt Ihr
nicht doch ein paar Tage frueher? Bedenkt, dass Manfred
noch viele Spaziergaenge nachzuholen hat. Herzlichst Lotte
von Raumanns eine uebersahlige mitzubringen, aber das
kriegen wir auch hier sicher in Massen.

Die Hühner kommen dieses Tage und sind laut Angebot "strong, healthy
and in good condition". Hund haben wir noch nicht und auch keine
Katze, Hühnerstallen sollen nicht gut sein, sonst hätte ich euch anheimgestellt,
pages.notes: Typoskript mit handschriftlichen Ergänzungen am linken Rand und am Ende. Seite 3.

pages.transcription:
Besorgungen fuer London weiss ich
sonst keine ausser einem outside
thermometer, das auch - oder nur -
Reaumur oder Celsius zeigt. Stefans
haengt glaube ich noch vor dem Hallam
Street Wohnzimmerfenster.
Solltest Du zufaellig Leinen
für Decken sehen, noch schoene Stoffe
oder gute weisse Handtuecher zu
billigem Preis - ich habe meine
mit Perdenkornmuster und Hohlsaum
sehr gern - so hast Du Vollmacht.

pages.transcription:
New York, 25.6.41

Dear Hanna,
We have finally found a house for the summer,
which meets all our requirements as „house-workers“ and car-less
people, which is nicely situated and even very near Eva. It
is
7 RAMAPO Road
Ossining, N.Y.
and ten minutes drive from Croton and there is even an
hourly bus-service between Croton and Ossining. I advised
Stefan against cabling the address (which will be valid
from July 1st to Sept. 1st) because you would certainly
think that Ramapo Road is mis-spelt. Actually it is
an old Indian name. One of the great attractions of
the house - besides being nice and near to Eva - was
the fact that the maid will stay on with us and is
even glad to remain, just as glad as I am to be able
to take her over. As we move out in 6 days you can imagine
that we will be busy, packing, arranging things, seeing some
people and trying not to see others and so on. It is 50 minutes
by train from New York and we shall come in now and then
- certainly I because I can thus continue my injections
without changing the doctor. I am glad about this for a
few weeks ago I had some strong reactions against my own
and apparently quite powerful bacterias, and I feel better to
be with a doctor who has experience and is not surprised by
such symptoms which as he says are rather favorable and
even desirable. - I went out Sunday to see Eva and
my sister-in-law came with me to visit her. She found her
looking splendid; she is sunburnt, strong and has grown.
It was only a pity that it was such a rush owing to
the house-hunting, but as we will now be very near to
each other this little disappointment was worth while.
We have not yet heard from you this week although we
had a number of English letters on Sunday. Now it is soon July
and then Manfred will finish his studies and you, I hope are
through with the dentist. We shall then enjoy the idea of knowing
you both in Bath.
Love, kisses Lotte

next address:

7 Ramapo Road
Ossining, N.Y.

Newyork, June 26th, 1941.

Dear Hanna,

We just got your letter of June 18th which is not
quite clear to us because it refers to your letter of the 13th
which has not yet arrived. I am extremely sorry that you had
to run about and to have all these discussions for us. You know
that when we left it was our intention to come back soon and I
left everything in your care, perhaps not in such perfect order
as I otherwise would have done, believing that I would soon be
back again. Owing to the enormous distances I have had no direct
mail about business matters since a long time and therefore not a
very clear idea how things stand. But I am convinced that all is
in best order and that if there have been any questinns, they have
been settled satisfactorily. Everybody's affairs are nowadays
frightfully complicated and I am sorry that I had to burden you
with ours while you have no doubt enough troubles of your own in
these difficult times. As to my publisher I am terribly sorry
that they had such a mishap, and I shall write him directly how
sorry I am. We will now go to the little country place we wrote
you about yesterday - the above address will be valid until Sept.1st
but do not address any more letters there after the first week of
August because they sometimes take three weeks - and there we will
do nothing but work hard these two summer months. After that we
shall again have to decide what to do. I have again offers from
South America for lectures in Cuba, Brazil and Argentine and so
on, but who can tell what will happen in those few months in times
like ours where every week brings new and unexpected developments.
Let me repeat how thankful we are to you and I need
not assure you again of our love and gratitude.

Yours,

Stefan Zweig

Your letter arrived in record time today - 7 days
from house to house. Your other letter has not yet come
and we are guessing what your references to the Edinburgh trip
and other things mean. But we will no doubt receive it
very soon. From next week we are near Eva, and that will
give us pleasure and you further reassurance

Love, Lotte

pages.transcription:
Ossining 7 Ramapo Road
State New York

1. July 1941

Dear Hannah & Manfred, I am writing with pencil
as all things are already packed - Lotte has worked
for two days as there are always a lot of books,
papers manuscripts coming together in six months
and we cannot more carry all this continuously with
us - we have left in Rio already all Brazilian
books and here in the hotel a second part of it.
It is not easy as I have a kind of office to
move with me, letters, documents, typewritten copies
adresses, contracts - you can imagine how we
are longing to have a kind of house!! But this
will never be as long as this war continues, it
is possible that I have to go in the autumn for
lectures to Cuba and perhaps again the other
countries - for the moment we will retire
to the little house and I shall try to work there
continuously on my autobiography which will be
a long and I hope very substantial book (the
great difficulty is that I have only to rely upon
my memory as I have no letters, no diarys from
all those bygone times.) As we took over the maid
Lotte is still packing, packing, pasting - I wish I
would see us more thanks for ten years!

in this little house we hope to have time - here
one looses much by going to Restaurants, meeting
people. Eva is quite near and thanks to the Lops'
auto we shall see her every few days. Many thanks
for your conversation with Willmot, the idea was
absurd that such an amount should have been
earned - those times are gone for ever and I am
very satisfied that we can make our modest living.
If I say modest I am well aware that even the
smallest restaurants here give such an abundance
of food that we are often ashamed when thinking of
Europe where thanks to this devil of Hitler 20
to 30 millions in Poland, Russia will die by
starvation. We get frightful letters from France
all these people want affidavits, money, re-
commendations and alas, we have no power at
all and every day we get new and new demand
it is heartbreaking. It is frightfully hot, New York
a real furnace and if Croton and Ossining
are in themselves no cool places there are at
least the evenings refreshing and one can go
in shirts and pants. Here it is the humidity and
the smell in the air which make it intolerable and
the houses are baked the whole day and therefore
still hot during the night. Thanks for all Stefan Zweig

Stefan is just busy working, so I send
the letter without word from him.

7 Bamapo Road
Ossining, N.Y.
4.7.41

Dear Manna & Manfred,
I had the idea of writing you the very
first day of our arrival here as long letter, but the heat
made me lazy and took all my energy. We are now quite
settled until the end of August and I thoroughly enjoy being
in a house again and even the housekeeping. The maid is
a great treat for me and I almost feel like the time
we got Rhoda. Why I should feel like that I do not know
myself for I certainly did not work hard or a lot in the
hotel, and the Wyndham, being a small and mostly residential
hotel is not as impersonal as most of them. Anyhow, I am
glad to be here and out of New York which was already very
hot, sticky and smelly. The situation of our house here is in
certain ways very similar to Mrs Leckie's house in Bath.
It is not the house itself which is much smaller and alto-
gether different, but its position on a hill with a steep
driveway, and a very awkward angle to the garage, but a
good garage so that I involuntarily thought when we
saw it: that will be a good garage when Manfred comes
with his car. Thinking of that house in Bath I miss
Martha much, of course - not to speak of your visits. But
we can visit Eva instead and Monday I shall take her
to New York (we both have to go to the dentist and I
must get my weekly supply of bacterias injected) and I
shall keep her with us for a day or two. I don't think
much longer, for there is nothing whatsoever to be done
or seen in Ossining. Sing-Sing is in Ossining, but one rather
tries to forget this fact. - Did I write you that Miss Baker
came to see me in New York? Her visit was interesting for me,
but I was amazed how talkative she was and how naive she
still is. She still was not quite resigned to the fact that she
could not go to England just for the summer holidays - this
in a time where it is impossible to obtain any kind of passage
except for solid and urgent business or political reasons. - A few
days ago I sent a small parcel, mainly sweets to Manfred, hoping
that it will eventually reach him. I also sent one to Ursula whose
birthday must be very soon. A small amount of duty may have
to be paid for both. I also sent you 'Life' and 'Vogue' by ordinary
mail.

[Randnotiz links, von unten nach oben geschrieben:]
I was not quite sure which kind of magazine interests you, whether literary, fashion,
or more serious ones. Let me know please and please send me once in a while
a newspaper or magazine which might be of interest for me. I should love to see an
Evening Standard. Love and kisses.

pages.transcription:
Dear Hannah & Manfred we are eagerly expecting your cable
that Manfred has passed his examination and you will has
the well-earned rest in Bath. I wish you would feel happy
there - as much happy as people with human feelings are
able to be in these horrid times. I personally am extremely
depressed by the prospect how many people will suffer before
this beast Hitler will be down but this will on the other
hand be the only possibility to make life worth living. You
are so much younger than I who has no more much time
for waiting and very often I am a bad companion for
Lotte with my black thoughts - but how could it be other
wise in such a time especially if one cannot be active and
useful. I am writing now the story of my life, it will be
a rather long book and I shall try that the end of it will
not be too sad and depressive. Most of the refugee writers
are already here in the country some did find small
possibilities and altogether it is only for those who can
assimilate themselves and write what one likes for read
here, exciting stuff or sensational news; just the best
have the smallest chances, those who take responsibility
for every word. I hope Willi[?] has been able to arrange
all, in the future you would perhaps sometimes apply
to Frost or Wooster for extraordinary occasions. Thanks
also for the news about our faithful bookseller Eidemann[?],
you understand that I was somewhat puzzled that he never
gave me directly news but I know very well what an honest
and reliable friend he is. Now enjoy your holidays, I was
so glad that you had for a whole month quiet nights in
London and I hope you will have rested physical and
mental rest in Bath. Please give my love to all, also

[Randnotiz links, von unten nach oben]:
to Belauin[?] and Roland to whom I will write soon. Yours
Stefan Zweig [?] [?] [?] [?] [?]

[Randnotiz rechts, von unten nach oben]:
Just your letter from June 21st thanks!

pages.transcription:
7 Ramapo Road,
Ossining, N.Y.
6.7.41.
Dear Marta,
I often think of you and of the year we spent
together in Bath, but now more than ever because we are
again in a house for the summer, after a too long time
of hotel- and restaurant life. There is some similarity to
Mrs Leckie's house as regards position, but neither house
nor landscape are to be compared with Bath although
Ossining is rather pretty. There are no walks round here
and nothing is to be seen - unless you have a car and go
for rides along pretty roads. I am trying to find someone
with whom I can go out in a car, get some practice and
knowledge of the traffic rules and then take my driving test
again to be ready if one day we should decide to live in
the country for longer. For although a bus passes near here
one is lost without a car as most people live away from
bus or railroad lines. I was able to take over the maid with
the house and that simplified everything, of course. She can
cook meats and vegetables and is willing to do more but
any kind of desert which does not come out of a tin or is not
made just by adding water to some ready-made mixture, is
quite unknown to her. But this does not matter very much.
I shall try to pass on to her what I myself still dimly
remembers of the art of cooking and there is in the house a
book with recipes. In any case we enjoy very much being
out in the country. There is a nice lawn round the house
it is about as secluded from the road as Mrs Leckie's house,
there is a porch for Stefan to work on he need not dress and
I can go even to the village in slacks. Two other advantages
are that we are near Eva and not even an hour from New
York. It is not much cooler than New York in day time, but the
air is nice and if it smells, it smells of flowers and grass.
Today we have Eva with us and to-morrow I shall go with her
to New York and return her to Croton on Tuesday. We would
have liked to keep her longer but there is really nothing
whatsoever for her to do here except to read. I hear that you are
always busy and at least not lonely. But it seems strange that
Love is now in Bath and that you may not be there. Life certainly plays
unexpected tricks on us nowadays, and God knows where we will be in
3 or 6 months time. Anyway, we had that year in Bath which I thoroughly
enjoyed and I have the good feeling that you too felt at home in Rosemont.
Kindest regards to all, yours,
Lotte.

Kindest regards and love from Stefan

pages.transcription:
c/o Vikingpress

12. VII 1941
Dear Hanna, and Manfred,
We have not heard from you this week but I suppose
a letter is on its way. Now we are every day expecting
a cable telling us that Manfred passed his exam, and we look
forward to knowing you in Bath for a long and well-deserved
rest. It really looks now as if that parcel Eva and I sent
together in April, has been lost. I sent another one to London
about 2 or 3 weeks ago, and a small one to mother and Ursula
whose birthday must have been one of these days. They come
all from Altman's and you may have to pay a small amount
of duty. - We have had Eva with us last Saturday until
Tuesday, and I was with her in London on Monday to see the
dentist. I shall take her once more Thursday next, and then
she will be finished. There was not much to be done. Eva
looks splendid, very brown and strong. She liked being with
us and read the whole book "The Microbe-Hunters" by Kruif
while she was here. If there are no special holiday events
in Amity Hall we will take her again for a few days
before or after we go to New York. - Stefan is working very hard
partly because he wanted to work, partly because he is depressed
by the facts of war in their humanity-destroying consequences,
partly because there is nothing else to be done here. It is nice,
green and quiet out here, but that is about all. If you
have no car there is nothing to be seen and nothing to be
done. This and many other, more important reasons may
decide us in the not too far future to return to Brazil.
For how long we can not say yet. Should we not return to the
States within a few months and the war go on and on, we might
want to take Eva to stay with us there. I need not say how much
I would like to have her with me, but I am afraid she might
find it much harder to adapt herself to Brazil. It would mean
passing from one extreme to the other, from the most liberal
education methods to old-fashioned ones, not to speak of the
new language she would have to learn. I enquired about
schools before I left Rio; there is one American school which

pages.transcription:
c/o Viking Press
18 East 48th Street
New York

Ossining, July 19th, 1941

Dear Hanna, We had today your long letter of July 8th
and are very happy to know you in good spirits,
probably even happier now that Manfred is with you
after his successful exam. None of us doubted of course
that he would be successful, nevertheless we were glad
to get the confirmation and to hear that he is resting
in Bath. I hope that Marks managed to get really
good photos of you and Manfred for I must confess
that I don't like those which Eva has. I don't know
whether you are allowed to send snapshots of Rosemount.
It would be lovely to have them, too, although I still
have every detail in mind very clearly, and especially in
the month of June every day another event came back to
my mind very sharply. I may even allow myself to confess
just once that moments of acute homesickness occur
from time to time and that Miss Baker's idea of
returning for the school holidays was not bad at all,
if rather naïve in present times. - We are leading
a very quiet life here in the country, disturbed
only by world events and the ever acute question,
where to go and what to do next. I used to like
decisions at short notice, but nowadays this is
rather inconvenient. - It is nice to be near Eva,
and were we not so handicapped by being without
a car and therefore a misance to all who have one
we would go to see her still more often. I spent an
afternoon at Amity Hall last week, had supper there,
and Eva was allowed to stay up much longer, and
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief von Lotte Zweig. Tinte blau/violett. Sehr gut lesbar.

pages.transcription:
to accompany Mrs. Sch. who drove me home. It was still
more thrilling for her because Mrs. Sch. showed me
the new house they are going to take from September
and Eva was the first child to see it. It is really
a most beautiful place, a big old Tudor house,
situated high on a hill with glorious views on the
Hudson, large grounds and as Eva said "just made
for Amity Hall" and nearly as beautiful as Rose-
mount. She is thoroughly enjoying the holiday,
they are kept busy with games and sports, go swimming,
play tennis etc, sleep in tents (next to the house)
and there are a few more girls in her age now.
You need not fear that she has outgrown all her
things. I had her summer dresses lengthened in spring
and they still fit her. Besides I got her one or two
cotton dresses for the garden which are very cheap,
and I don't think she needs anything until winter.
I shall talk it over with her and Mrs. Sch, however,
and write you what she could use for the winter.
As regards your questions about my housekeeping
I am sorry to have to disappoint you because I
got a white and not a colored maid. She is neat
and efficient and knows plain cooking, and she
gave me some excitement by disappearing for two
days on account of complicated love affairs. She came
back, however, and my landlady came and talked
to her about the moral side of the matter until she re-
pented and promised never to let me down again and
to conduct her own affairs strictly during her time off.
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief von Lotte Zweig. Tinte blau/violett. Sehr gut lesbar.

pages.transcription:
2)
I am glad that the Rosemount garden supplies you
with lots of fresh vegetables and fruit and I hope that also
the chickens do their duty. I am sure Mr. Miller keeps them
as fit and happy as he can. I hope that Marta can have
a good long holiday in Bath, and it will seem strange
to her to return as a guest into a house where she
belonged from the beginning. Victor, too, would cer-
tainly be happy to come back for a while. We were glad
to hear that Manfred seems satisfied with his state of
health, he wrote otherwise and his letters were very sad.
This last year has certainly mixed us up thoroughly,
and it would have seemed phantastic a year ago when
we had just arrived that now I am keeping house
in Ossining that Fuelop-Miller's would come over in
the evening and Stefan read them a chapter from his
autobiography, that Eva would live a few miles
away, and that Jules Romains and other people whom
we had not expected to see for years to come would
come out here to visit us. My hope is that just as
phantastically fast the changes for the good will
come before we dare to expect it. It is a rather
difficult moment for us now, because we do
not know and are yet unable to decide whether to
remain here, whether to leave the States and come
back later or whether to return to Brazil. This un-
certainty and all the problems involved with the
decision are a little hard on the nerves and Stefan
feels it more strongly than I do. It makes him work
more and more intensely and that keeps me busy.
The good thing is that since a few weeks I feel
quite well again and that the treatment finally
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief von Lotte Zweig. Tinte blau/violett. Sehr gut lesbar.

pages.transcription:
seems to take effect. I had rather strong reactions for a
time temperature and even asthma attacks, and that pro-
bably accounts for my being a little thinner. But I
feel well now and have again learned to appreciate
consciously physical fitness. I still get my injections
of dust and bacterias once a week and go to New York
for that. At the same occasion I take Eva to the
dentist (she will be finished next time) and I also showed
my doctor a wart which Eva had developed and which
has meanwhile been removed. At this occasion my doctor's
wife who is orthopedist, gave Eva some exercises against
her tendency for flat-footedness, and if she is clever she
can turn these exercises into games with the others,
picking up marbles from the floor and writing with
the feet.
I hope that the Wilmot business is now
settled satisfactorily and we feel terribly sorry that you
who cannot know all our affairs should have to
work them out. Whatever new questions may unexpectedly
arise, please don't let them worry you, just remember
that you could not possibly know about everything and
that everything can be cleared up eventually. Wilmot
certainly is hard to know at first and it takes some time
to discover that while he seems to sit and hardly listen
to you, he is in reality thinking hard and trying to
help.
Have a good rest and holiday, both of
you and give my kindest regards to all. I
am so glad your brother found some decent work
at last.
Love and kisses,
Lotte
