pages.transcription:
Dear H. & M., I am happy to know you in Bath, We tend to often of the
Coast/there are more and more moments when I would like to go back
I am a very bad companion for poor Lotte. The idea to wander around for
years always packing and unpacking without any stay, without my books, without
space and service is oppressive for me who is longing with to years for some rest.
Our idea was to go to Brazil, we have even made reservations (four weeks a lead
is necessary - meanwhile there [cause] are a lot of new regulations, exit permits, questions
and questions, our situation is frightfully complicated - in every respect! - being
only visitors here as friendly aliens and perhaps not as naturalized only, on the other
hand we did not immigrate on behalf of the citizenship - 'not fish nor flesh'
as one said in your mothers house and with the obligations and worries of both sides.
Brazil had the advantage that I could stay as long as I wished and have all
possible opportunities; what here will become in case of war is in any case
not agreable, we cannot take a flat and I hate this packing and unpacking, this
life which is contrary to all concentration with its daily decisions and deli-
berations. And I see no end of this for years and years. The only advantage
of my depression is that {it} make me work; here in this little house I have
done more in three weeks on my autobiography as otherwise in three month,
not leaving it from morning to night without to see anybody; in three days
I hope (in the autobiography) to be through the first war - I wish I would
be through the second one in three months! What has become out of me,
the fanatic traveller and passionate globetrotter! I cannot imagine how I
shall continue if in August we have to leave again (we have reader only for
two months; yes, it is in earnest that I sometimes think I would be better
on my table in Bath even if I has only to eat carrots. I am so sorry for
Lotte that I cannot give her brighter hours and only manuscript to copy
and to copy, that I could not give her a quiet life as modest as it may
be. The others here have all settled only we cannot and sometimes I wonder
how this will continue. Now enough of my worries (we have still some others
in stock) and thanks for all your trouble. Please do not bother yourself with
all that you cannot know about all, even myself could not remember everything
The most important remains that you have a quiet summer and that Eva
is happy and healthy there - I feel how you are longing to see her and I
would like to bring you back her as soon as possible. And who can tell what
the next months will bring; my curiosity is satisfied for good events and I would like
to oversleep the next years. Thanks for all, also to love in the better days
kindest regards from yours Stefan

address letters to
Vikingpress, 18 East 48th Street
New York.
Ossining, July 21st, 41
Dear Manna,
Once in a while I must write a letter which
Stefan does not "censor" before I send it. I am a little
worried about him at present, he is depressed, not only
because it is really no pleasure to lead such an un-
settled life, always waiting {short-term} what will happen the next
day before making another decision, but also because
the facts of war which is now becoming a real mass
murder, and the seeming endlessness weigh upon his mind.
I hope this mood will pass soon and I wish I had some-
thing of those people who can talk others into cheer-
fulness and somehow inspire courage and hope. My qualities
are rather that I can stand any kind of life without
complaining and feeling sorry for myself, but I cannot
talk him out of his present mood and can only wait until
he gets over it himself - as he usually did in previous cases.
Fortunately this does not prevent him from working but in
the contrary induces him to more and more work. And I
hope that he will feel better when the decision which
has once again to be taken now between the States and
Brazil, has finally fallen. Both countries have their great
advantages - here are some really good friends of real
intellectual niveau, and the libraries, down in Brasil
life in itself is pleasant and interesting and the
country stimulating for Stefan. The people are extremely
nice and cultured, but cultured somehow in an old-
fashioned way, and intellectually there is a difference
of niveau so to say. - It is difficult to decide and
lots of things are to be considered - not the least the
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief auf weißem Papier. Tinte blau/violett. Gut lesbar.

pages.transcription:
enormous distance and the fact that travelling with
all the necessary permits, visa and the journey itself
will probably become more and more difficult.
Sometimes we wish we were back in "Rosemount" in
spite of everything which made us leave it, and we
wonder sometimes whether this would not be the best
solution. Rationally it probably is not and probably Stefan
would again feel useless or be given an unimportant
job which others might do just as well, and besides
this it is nearly impossible to get home without special
official priorities. It is just a dream and only to be hoped
that one day circumstances will allow its realisation.
But it was not the reason of my writing to
inform you of our present mood - which will probably
have changed until you get this letter, so don't give
it much thought! - What I would like you to do
occasionally, is to get into touch with Cassell
(maybe you can get Newman Flower, the proprietor on the
phone) whether they are willing to send the manuscript
of Balzac to the Vikingpress (Mr. Huebsch). Stefan says
he does not want it, but I am convinced he will
be quite happy when he gets it or knows the Viking
Press has got it at his disposition whenever he will
have finished his present work. So please try to send
it - if possible through Cassell's because they have less
difficulties in sending a manuscript to another publisher.
Later on - better not at the same time as it is {as Balzac}
something quite different. I would like you to send me
a copy of the bibliography of Stefan's books. There are two
parts, one the printed book which is not quite so
important, and the typewritten additions which your
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief, Fortsetzung. Gut lesbar.

pages.transcription:
2
brother {typed out} for me in several copies. It would be
useful for me to have, and there is no special risk
of losing it as - just as in the case of the Balzac manuscripts
copies still remain with you. When you send this either
through Cassell or direct to me write clearly on it what
it is "bibliography of books published in translations etc.
by..." so that the censor sees at once what it is all about.
This is all what I have to tell you today.
And please don't worry because today I admit that
Stefan is passing through one of his black moods and
that we wish we were home and had never left. These moods
will happen once in a while and they will pass and when
you get this letter probably our plans for the next
months will be definite and we will feel better
accordingly.
We went to see Eva yesterday. She looks
and feels fine, loves Mrs Sch and Amity Hall and
Mrs Sch loves her. When you see her again you will
not find her changed at all, only grown and probably
a little more grown-up. I should hate to leave her
when we go really to Brazil, but only because I
shall miss her. She really is in excellent care for
soul, mind and body and is treated exactly as you
would treat her and has full confidence in Mrs Sch.
The new house they are taking is perfectly beautiful
and as Eva says "just made for them". -
One good thing is that we are not isolated
from friends here - Schaefers and Fuloep-Millers in
Croton, Stefan's first wife by pure chance also in Ossining
(as a matter of fact she was already here when we decided
to take this house) and the strange thing is that we are
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief, Fortsetzung. Gut lesbar.

pages.transcription:
almost on better and certainly more normal terms {with her}
with Stefan's brother who is absolutely egocentric. I
remember a conversation I had with you once with regard
to the relationship of first and second wives and husbands,
but it all seems perfectly natural and normal and
maybe the great difference in age makes it easier.
I like to think that you and Manfred
are now taking "holidays" in Bath and wish you an
uninterrupted pleasant time. Are there already
prospects for Manfred to get employment on account
of his new qualifications?
Love and kisses to both of you,
Lotte

pages.transcription:
Liebe Hannah, Du wirst es vielleicht barbarisch finden,
dass ich Lotte nach vier Tagen zurückfordere. Aber sie
hat eben verabäumt die Dinge vorher in Ordnung zu
bringen. Plötzlich sind keine Coks da, die Zentralheizung muss
abgestellt werden, weil die verabäumt hat solche zu be-
stellen oder jedenfalls sich zu überzeugen wie viele vorhanden
sind. Ich persönlich weigere mich solche zu bestellen, weil
wir (Du und ich) sie bereits allzuviel verwöhnt haben, dass
wir die Dinge ihres Hauses für sie ausdenken und mitwirken
sie muss wissen, dass auf mich nicht mehr zu zahlen ist
und sie selbst vorsorgen muss.
Ebenso geht es nicht, dass sie länger die Last auf deiner
Schwester allein lässt. Frau Martha tut alles was in kann
in aufopferndster, in bewunderungswürdiger Weise. Aber ich
habe ein zu gutes Auge, um nicht zu sehen, dass sie ermü-
det ist (kein Wunder!) und endlich einen Tag Ruhe braucht.
Sie wäscht die Kinder, macht ihren Frühstück, kocht, räumt allein
alle Zimmer auf, hat den ganzen Tag das Heu und Her der
Arbeiter, das Getrage und Gelaufe und macht das Bett vorher
ohne dass ihr für einen Tag das Kochen oder Aufräumen ab-
Seit Tagen hat sie ihren Nachmittagstee ausser mir
genommen wurde, ich kann das nicht länger ansehen
- es ist Pflicht Lottes entweder ihr für einen Tag das
Kochen jetzt abzunehmen oder endlich für Hauspersonal

pages.transcription:
zu sorgen, wenn man schon selbst nicht richtig zupacken
will oder kann. Sie muss sich klar darüber werden, dass
sie eine Verantwortung mit dem Hause hat. Alles Erlaufen
muss jetzt nach dem die Grundlagen da sind, auf das Notwen-
digste reduziert werden, bis alles in Ordnung ist. Mir ist
weniger wichtig in einem Zimmer, ob der Teppich braun
oder schon orientalisch ist als das das Zimmer geheizt ist.
Vor der Schönheit muss die Ordnung kommen. Es kommt jetzt
nicht auf Gläser und Untertassen an sondern das endlich
der Hausstand ruhig läuft - alles andere bleibt Nebensache.
Ich kann es nicht dulden, dass deine Schwester mir
übermüdet - nur das Hämmern, Klopfen, Fragen, Thran[
Tür zu und Tür nicht zu macht einen wirklich nervös selbst
wenn man Strichleitern statt Nerven hat; sie ist noch nicht
eine Stunde spazieren gegangen in den ganzen Wochen. So
geht es nicht weiter.
Dies nur zu zeigen, dass ich kein Barbar
und Gewalttäter bin, wenn ich Lotte am Samstag
zurückfordere. Herzlichst Euch allen

Stefan

pages.transcription:
Ossining, July 25th, 41
Dear Hanna & Manfred, I just received your letter of June 26th
and a letter from mother of July 18th. I hope you are both
still in Bath, and probably there are some visitors with
you. I hope Marta got permission to come and spend a good long
holiday, although I have a suspicion that she won't be able
to resist the temptation of bottling fruit and vegetables. -
I am very happy that you are now really convinced that Eva
is in best, loving care and in surroundings which are just
what you think right. She thoroughly enjoys the holidays
and although she always wants us to visit her often and
long, she is not too eager to spend whole days away from
Amity Hall - which I think is a very good sign and should
greatly reassure you for the case that we should really
go to Brazil. Elizabeth who will come for tea next week
with part or the whole of her family has invited Eva for
a few days the week after, and although she likes to
go there she says she does not want to be away from
Amity Hall for long. I shall probably go over and see
Eva to-day, because for the weekend we shall have the
visit of Dr. Bondi - one of those many Bondis you disliked
mother to tell stories about. We have seen him quite
frequently recently in his business quality and as he was
very nice and helpful and reassuring Stefan wanted
to let him have the pleasure of a weekend out of town.
He has a clear logic lawyer's mind, and that is good against
Stefan's too productive imagination sometimes, and although
he is as ugly as Marks he seems to be quite nice. -
Our plans are still undecided but it looks as if in
the end we will go to Brazil. In any case we are bound
to come to a decision very soon and that will end this
disagreeable state of indecision and continued considerations
what to do best and why and when and where next to go.
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief von Lotte Zweig. Tinte auf Papier.

pages.transcription:
By the way, a friend of ours, Camille Honig, a young Jewish
journalist who has been in Australia for some Jewish-British
war collections is returning to England shortly. We would
have loved to send you something through him, but when
we met him last it looked as if he would go by clipper,
and so we just asked him to ring you up as soon as he
arrives in London and promised him that you would
invite him for a weekend to Bath should you not be in
London just then. You will like him. He comes somewhere
from the Eastern Ghettos, has worked his way up and knows
a lot about art and literature. He is married to a non-Jewish
wife of a good English family, and has left her here with a
few months old baby. We have been together several times,
and I am sure you would like to get direct news from us
just as I would be happy to meet someone who just
spent some time with you. We had a letter from him
yesterday that he will probably sail in a few days, so
it will take weeks at the best before he can call you up.
He returns because he has to enlist for military service,
and I hope he will have time to see you. - Don't worry
that my treatment is still going on, it was meant to be so
from the beginning. The injections have been reduced
to once a week now and I am getting the top dosis of
1ccm. Gradually they will be given once a fortnight
and once a month only and after 6 or 12 months
it will be stopped and then I am supposed to be immune
against asthma. In any case I am quite well now, just
as I was the last years, and if I had some disagreeable
weeks, I have learned again to appreciate deeply the
fact of mere physical health. And once we shall have
settled down somewhere for more than two months,
be it here or in Brazil we shall be quite happy again.
Nothing is worse in the long run than being undecided,
and that is what we have been too long now, always
waiting for the next weeks to bring solutions from outside.
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief von Lotte Zweig (Fortsetzung).

pages.transcription:
2) I hope you wrote a little in detail about your exam
Manfred! All I know is that you expected it to be dif-
ficult and that it required lots of time and studies.
Did you find the examinations difficult, were there
many others with you, were they all doctors already prac-
tising, and how many of them passed? Do you try to
get a hospital job now, and how are the chances? Or do
you expect to be called up soon? And will it be in your
quality as specialist do you think? - Do tell us about
all this as well as about your progress in chess and piano,
and never be afraid of writing too long letters. -
I was interested to hear that Edith Hoffman has married,
and surprised that her job at the Burlington still is
in existence. - We had Wilmot's letter and only expect
some information about the securities which have mean-
while been recalled by the Treasury, before answering
his questions which are very easy to answer once you
managed to understand his rather complicated way of
writing. - We continue to work hard, Stefan much harder
than I do for I stick to my principle never to work
after dinner if I can help it and he works until late.
My household does not take much time on the whole. I
make the menu, order everything by phone except the
meat which I like to see and for which I walk over
to the butchers 5 minutes from here, and the maid
does the cleaning and cooking. It is enjoyable to be
able to choose in which room to go and to have a room
of my own for my work, complete even with writing table.
Sometimes I occupy myself with the garden which con-
sists in mowing the lawn, and then I always remember
William and how we used to wonder that it took him so
long to mow those two terraces. Lots of wild rabbits help
to keep the grass short and they are amusing to watch and
I am glad that I have not to eat them as one of our guests
suggested.
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief von Lotte Zweig (Fortsetzung).

pages.transcription:
I wonder how Marks' photographs of you, Manfred
and Rosemount turned out and I am impatient to have
them. It will be only a poor substitute for being with
you and talking with you, but there seems to be hope
that some day in some distant future we will be together
again - and how much will we have to talk and how
many nights will we have to sit at the fireplace until
far after midnight to get everything talked over!
Kindest regards to all and best love & kisses
to you
Lotte.

Dear Hannah & Manfred, we are not yet decided
what to do and you will hear soon of us.
I am rather depressed - This life without
a real home, this wandering around makes
me melancholic and it relaxes as this would
go on for years and years. Lotte feels much
better and I would wish a better husband for
her. I have done my autobiography till
to my fiftieth year and I am wondering
if I shall continue because the third
part would be rather sad and oppressive
We had here a very quiet time; I have
worked the whole day and Lotte looks al-
ready much better. Kindest regards Stefan

pages.transcription:
c/o Viking Press 18 East 48 Street
July 31st, 41
Dear Hannah & Manfred, many thanks for your letter. Eva is just
here for a visit and I hope to induce her to write some lines - no,
she really likes now to write and is a big and intelligent girl.
Now about us. We had finally - after more than a year - a little
house with a maid for four weeks and this and on the other
hand my deep depression did let me work like seven devils, I
have finished in this month my autobiography, written it with
my own hand so quickly that Lotte could not yet follow. Now I will
leave the manuscript for two months and we shall see later if
I will have to change. In any case I have no hurry to publish
it, I wanted only to have it ready. It goes till to the first
day of the second world-war. We shall let send you a copy
of the the Brail book when it comes out in September. The
small book on Vespucci will appear much later. As to Hilmot
please tell him that your task was only meant to be a temporary
one; if new ~~difficult~~ questions arise we shall deal with them
ourselves. The idea that you should have to go to London and
loose your time is oppressive to me; I know how much you
have to do and that physical and psychic rest is necessary for
you. So never worry about our worries we want to take care
of ourselves. When does Manfred start his practice as Xray
specialist?
About our travelling plans you will have our news soon. We
are ready to start in August because we have to be there in
the lecturing season but there you can never tell till to the
last moment in such times if there are no changes. We would
do our best of course to come back here after some time
- what I want, badly want is some rest and New York is not
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief von Stefan Zweig. Tinte auf Papier.
Rückseite des ersten Blattes, durchscheinender Text der Vorderseite sichtbar. Leer.

pages.transcription:
the right place for it. I have worked hard and want a little
dolce far niente. If you would have been with us in all these
months you would understand this much better - this wandering
this eternal indecision for the next few months was exhausting.
Now I would like to give these {indeed} times to our friend
Kormendi. I got his book and want to thank him. To Rose
Mann please say that I am not more interested in books in
the next time, as I have no opportunity to read books and to
admire drawings; perhaps later again! I like to avoid all
which complicates - I have but one wish to sit quietly and
to write my own books, to know you without worries and not
connected with my own, to see your child growing up and
in excellent hands, to dream from peace and to give Lotte a
happier life than she has with her old and depressive husband
You will hear from us soon. Enjoy the summer as much as
you can with Manfred and all your friends and your sister.
Yours truly

Stefan Zweig

pages.transcription:
31.7.41

Ossining.

Dear Hanna, dear Manfred, I can only add a few lines today
being busy with supervising Eva's writing, knitting typing
and the maid's first try to make potato salad (still a special
treat for your child). I had her come here yesterday, for I
had Elizabeth for tea who came with husband and her two
children. I like them, and Eva who is invited to spend a
few days with them the week after next will certainly
enjoy herself, once the two girls have given up her very great
politeness of the beginning. - We are working hard and Eva
had to help too, sorting out a few chapters. At the pace at which
Stefan is working I could use Ursula as well. - I am glad that
parcel arrived. I only sent one more, containing chocolates and
cocoa, about 6 weeks ago to London, and a small one to Ursula
and mother each. It is not possible to send cigarettes as far
as I know, also not fresh fruit. - I hope it will soon be
decided whether we stay or travel south again. Stefan will
fell[?] much better once things are settled.
Love to all, Lotte.

pages.transcription:
Dear H. & M. now we are nearly ready. Our hearts are not light at all, we
do not know when we shall return as we have been here only on visitors
visas and all depends if America enters the war. Altogether it has been
a very strenuous time and especially in the last times we did not feel
happy at all. Perhaps Brazil will help us with his beauty - but I doubt
more and more if I ever shall see Bath again. Sometimes we thought
to leave everything and to go back, but I feel I shall never in my life
have more a real home - had we emigrated here like the others we
could have said, here we begin a new life, but I was bound by my nationa
lity which has and will give us still many problems. Now about Gil-
bert. Please dont take too much worries about my complicated affairs
which in future may become still more complicated, I do not want
that you take any responsability and will advise him to direct every-
thing to Dr. Artur Bondi whom your family knows from London, because
we do not know if we have not to give lectures later on in Argentine
and it will be difficult to reach us. And in the long run all will be lost
whatever one had and I am prepared to live in future from what
one earns, Brazil is much cheaper and we will have a very sober life
if possible. My book on Brazil will be forwarded to you by the Viking
press in September, I hope it will reach you safely, The Brazilian
edition is already out and the French and Spanish in preparation.
My dear Hannah and Manfred, sometimes I feel very depressed,
and doubt if we ever shall be together again, I wish only that you
shall see your child grown up and more sympathetic as ever - I
always am frightened to read that this war will take still more than
a year, this war, which has destroyed so much of our lives - I know
there are millions and millions like us, but everyone feels his own
life. I hope Manfred will have much to do in these next months
in his x ray departement - I have worked hard which means always
that I am not in a good mood. Lotte is physically much better now and
perhaps we will have in Brazil a better time: only if this nomadic life
would come to an end, I would like to live in a Negro hut in Brazil
if I should know I could stay there - and you, you have to care for
two houses. Let us hope at least that you, the young generation will

[am linken Rand, vertikal geschrieben:]
still have the reward for these enormous efforts - for me it is too late
and I could no more enjoy the victory. And you and your child will
see a better world! Yours ever Stefan

pages.transcription:
New York, Aug. 6th, 41

Dear mother
I have again received two letters
from you almost at the same time - one dated
June 7th and the other July 25th! Your birthday
letter to Eva I send to Mrs. Sch. to keep it
until that date - also Mamma's birthday letter
has already arrived and Mrs. Sch. is keeping
it back.
We have returned to NY yesterday.
We are not yet decided what we shall do and
whether we shall really return to South Am.
But for all these difficult considerations
and deliberations it is better to be in NY
in spite of the heat, Ossining was not far,
but travelling in and out almost every
day is more strenuous than being here. It
is not so bad in NY just now. We have
rooms with cross-ventilation, and if there is
any air at all, we get it. - It was a pity
to leave Oss. just when we had got used to it.
It was pleasant and I was glad to be near
Eva, and we had nice friends in the neighbourhood.
Well, it can't be helped and before you write me
again, inquire first at Manfred's where we are. We
shall cable them as soon as we know ourselves what
we are going to do.
I hope you enjoyed Jan's visit and keep well
yourself. Kindest regards and best love
Lotte.

pages.transcription:
New York, August 6th, 1941

Dear Mamma & Manfred, Our mind is nearly made up, and
if nothing unforeseen happens, we shall leave for Rio
on the 15th. Well - you will already know by cable, when
you get this letter, what finally happened. - We have returned
to NY yesterday. There is so much to be done before such
a journey, so many things to be arranged, so many formalities.
I saw Eva nearly every day before we left. She regrets
that we are leaving, of course, but she is so much at home
at Amity Hall that she will not really miss us. While we
were at Ossining and saw a little more of the Sch's I had
occasion to see that Mrs. Sch. really loves Eva and does not
considers her just a „baarder“. And that Eva loves her you
know already. Mrs Sch. gave me a photo, a better one than
the snapshot I sent you, and if Stefan does not write too
much, I shall enclose it. - It was a pity of course to have
to leave Oss. so quickly and early, but there is not much
time - fortunately - to look back and reflect how nice it would
have been if... Many things would have been nice, if not...
I shall write you soon again, I am in a hurry
today as you may imagine.
Kindest regards, love and kisses
Lotte.
Did you accept that hospital job, Manfred?
How do you like it and what have you to do
actually? X-Ray treatment??
Dear Manfred, we have so much to do and all is so difficult. We do not
know if we can leave because what can happen still!! I would be glad if
I could sit somewhere quietly for a few months, I am extremely tired and
a bore to Lotte and myself. The war was too long for my nerves with all
this travelling around and I feel my age. Thanks for all you do. But now
something I insist, that Hannah {she has made} [?] for all the troubles she has with
my house a compensation which covers also the expenses for [?] and
that she gets it immediately. I do not want that she does it only by
friendship, I have a very bad conscience against her. Please do this soon
and be sure that it is reasonable. We have seen Eva, she is grown up and
in excellent mood, she is now there already an important person and loves by all in the town
even Mr. Shaffer has a special liking for her. Stefan Zweig
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief von Lotte Zweig (und Stefan Zweig am Ende), violette Tinte. Der Text am linken Rand wurde nachträglich hinzugefügt und verläuft vertikal. Die Zeile 'she has made' wurde über 'Hannah' eingefügt.
Rückseite des Dokuments, leer.

pages.transcription:
New York, Aug 11th, 41

Dear Mamma,
Yesterday your letter of July 27th with the
photos which I will give to Eva in a little album as
you suggested. I liked the one of you with Manfred very
very much and would love to have it. Please send it to us,
I suppose already c/o Editora Guanabara, 132 rua
Ouvidor, Rio - for we have now the tickets and nearly all the
necessary papers and probably leave Friday. Just as last
year it was the worst to come to a decision; now that it
is made and only unforeseen events will change our plans
we feel better and more ready and willing to go. -
About Eva you need not worry - I probably shall miss her
more than she will miss us in spite of all her liking of
us. And I am very glad that we spent the last weeks
so near to her and saw her frequently. To-morrow she
goes to our cousin Elizabeth for a few days and
I hope she will like it. We shall certainly see her
before we go and Yonkers is even nearer than Croton
should we suddenly have some spare time in these
last few days. It is a pity to leave almost on her
birthday but I shall try to leave her some nice
present and she will have a party at Amity Hall.
In a few weeks they will move to the new house
and I suppose the "big" children like her will
have an important part in it. Mrs. Sch. will get
a prospectus with pictures so that you will have a
fair idea what the new place looks like. It is a
grand property, a beautiful big house and perfectly
suitable for an establishment like that.
Yesterday Foges suddenly phoned and we were
with him for more than an hour. He brought your
regards and tried to tell as much as he could. On
the whole I found, however, that he knew most about
Marte about whose excellent qualities he was quite
enthusiastic. He must have dined there frequently!
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief auf weißem Papier. Tinte violett. Sehr gut lesbar.
Rückseite des ersten Blattes, leer.

pages.transcription:
2)
He intends to return in September and will report to you, I
suppose. But I hope that before him Mr. Honig will have
called upon you - he knows us better and we were together
quite frequently while he was here. -
We are terribly busy these last days and besides
this have some shopping to do as all clothing is either
not good or expensive in Rio. And it is typically Ame-
rican that it is already difficult for me to find
summer dresses. The sales started when we were away
and the shops are practically sold out and at this very
moment busy with selling furs and winter things. For
Stefan it is easier because the mens' sales began
much later and are still on. About the sudden crisis
in silk stockings you may have read in the papers. It
was quite a panic when the silk import from Japan
was stopped, the women rushed out to buy and hoard
and it is with a kind of horror that they foresee the
necessity of wearing cotton stockings. I cannot get very
excited about it and actually bought less than I would
otherwise have done as the prices already nearly doubled.
I suppose if you get along without silk stockings, the Western
Hemisphere will also be able to do so. By the way, I
carefully studied what you wear on the photos but I did
not recognise anything except the checked grandmothers-sheet
dress. However I recognized Millers antoize trousers and
suppose they are still the same pair. This reminds me to
write that of course you have full authority to give away
and make use of mine and Stefan's clothes. I hope you have
done so already! - I am terribly sorry that Mr. Wilmot keeps on
bothering you with our affairs. We never meant it to be thus
but thought that all you would have to do would be to
furnish him all the statements and documents that come
in without worrying about any details, especially as you know
much less about our "business" than he does. - I am anxious
to hear whether Manfred already has his new job and where and
how and when it is. A pity it could not be in Bath.
Warmest greetings Lotte.
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief (Fortsetzung), Seite 2. Tinte violett.
Rückseite des zweiten Blattes, leer.

pages.transcription:
Dear H. & M. We just are returning from Croton where we visited
Eva the day before our departure and we went even with her to
a bar after with Philip Miller. We regretted to leave her
behind but to let her start in a new language would be too much
and especially as we have the impression that she feels perfectly
right and is very happy there. Mr. Haeffner is absolutely reliable
and the new house is just a dream - you cannot imagine
what an enormous park it has the Mr Cooks at Bath. They
could only take it over because the taxes for private owners
are too high.
Thanks so much for all the trouble you took again in
their discussions. I like Gilbert and hope he does his best,
infortunately I am pretty sure that I will have some day
complications with his boss. I can understand it as his
financial position is difficult, and that he will become
more and more disagreeable. Thats why I wanted you to
let things go and to keep away and not to loose your time,
I do not want that you have to do with all this - {here} I
will have a friend of mine to discuss all possible compli-
cations. You have your own worries.
It is interesting that you told me about the possibili-
ty of a house for Manfred new Xray practice. Nobody
can tell if it is wise or not, for a house in London it
means certainly a risk as long as the war goes on and
in any case one should take a mortgage on it. I understand
so well that he as a doctor and specialist cannot live
always in a flat - a small one is impossible, a large
one too expensive. Of course you should buy it in your both
names jointly as nobody can tell what may happen to
one or to the other in these times; my friends Wooster &

[Randnotiz links, von unten nach oben geschrieben:]
Please send the Penclub a contribution for the Congress fund
in my name, perhaps for L. as 7 cannot be present myself

Rückseite des ersten Blattes, durchscheinender Text der Vorderseite erkennbar, aber kein eigenständiger Text.

pages.transcription:
Prof would do all to be helpful to you with any kind
of advise as tolles husband [?] is not able to help
you directly. You understand that I do not encourage you
neither discourage you - all is risk now, mere chance if
a bomb finds its way this street or the other street. But in
any case it would be something for your daughter one day
and if you have happy hours only in outfitting it, you have
already had something. We are all gamblers today with
whatever we do, wherever we go, wherever we are - the
great game is not in our hands. Personally I would be
glad to know that you {both} own a house again even with mort-
gages and that Manfred can have his Xray apparatus and
his other medical work in comparatively safely.
I am glad that you meet the Kormendis. His play is
excellent, also Tilop Miller was enthusiastic about it
He know no better author - play and I hope he has a
good agent here in Newyork. If not I would advise him
to send over more copies to prominent people - I am
sure that if anybody with influence gets it into his hands
it will be produced at least at the radio
About Freeman I wrote you already that for the moment
I am not interested in books etc. I want to avoid all
what complicates matters - they will be complicated enough
as what goes one. All what I want is to forget everything
I had and everything I was formerly and to try again
to write new books for the old and forgotten ones - the
autobiografy is quasi finished and I hope quite an interes-
ting book. The other on Brazil will be sent in 4 weeks
to you directly by the publishers. Please remember Hannah

[Randnotiz links, von unten nach oben geschrieben:]
To charge all the expenses out she had and I want that she is rewarded
regularly for all the true cost. Steel Celler comes from the Coat
we will have more here. Yours Stefan

pages.transcription:
Dear Hanna & Manfred,

Friday, Aug 15th 41
It is a few hours before sailing
time and we shall both be glad to get under way,
although I am a little worried about sea-sickness because
it is rainy and windy to-day. This is, however of minor im-
portance and the main aim is to get settled down there
as quickly as possible. We went to Boston last night to
see Eva, and we tortured her by bringing parcels to Mrs.
Sch. (Your books and birthday letters are all there and
waiting for the birthday). But she had a treat in various
ways. First we went over to let Stefan have a glimpse of
the new Amity Mall. Then - already past bedtime - Fullepo
took us over to Ossining to say goodbye to Mrs. Zweig N°1,
Eva went with us, and in addition to that attraction was
taken to a bar and treated to a coca-cola and ice cream
- at 9.30 p.m.! So I hope she will always remember that
there is something nice in our leaving and not mind too
much. - Her slightly high-brow letter style is, I believe, her
own; and maybe it can be traced back to Manfred, maybe
it is just the sign of an effort to write well. On the whole I
would call the surroundings more child-like than highbrow,
although with an intellectual tendency for those only who
are inclined that way, and since my own childhood I
have not seen children who managed to get themselves
so dirty in the garden than there. But they all get clean
again in the bath at night and Eva and Marion etc,
the big girls, even wash their own dresses because
the laundry is not very good. Even I, who do certainly
not belong to the washing sort of women, have got so far.
You would never believe what a laundry can do to your
things, they even managed to turn Eva's Bath school dresses
from blue into a pretty pale green! Well this is America
and Rio is not much better on the whole. They wash better,
because machines would be too expensive, but they cannot
yet dry-clean. Again, there are minor matters in a mad world
like ours.
L.T.Z.
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief auf zwei Seiten (hier Seite 1). Tinte violett. Die Unterschrift 'L.T.Z.' steht für Lotte Zweig.

pages.transcription:
We were sorry to hear that Manfred's holiday
is already over, and you did not mention whether he
already got a job in his new capacity as Xray specialist.
I can understand that you do not want to live in a
flat for always, and I think the idea of taking a
house is on the whole very good. I am sure Wooster
or Frost would help you with the first cash payment,
but we both think it would only be worth while if you
can get a mortgage on the rest - from a bank or corporation
as it used to be done - and pay them the interest as
rent. Besides this of course only a buying in your joint
names is to be considered. Any other arrangement could
complicate matters one day. I remember those houses
in Ingram Avenue very well and also similar, but
smaller ones in St. Johns Wood. - With regard to the friends
you mention I it seems that you mostly associate with
yours now and neglect your own. But maybe this is only be-
cause you tell us only about ours. I would like to know,
however, what became of all the others, doctors, Joss etc. -
I got a little album for the photos you sent me and this,
too, is awaiting Eva's birthday. Mrs. Sch. was still considering
yesterday which special treat for Eva's group would be the
best to celebrate the event. - I wonder how Marta will
feel on her "visit" to Rosemount. Tell her she must write me
about it. - What you write about "Fantasia" was our impression
too. We left after the first part feeling quite dizzy. Besides
that and some very old Chaplin films we have seen nothing. But
on the boat we will have, I hope, a few good new films.
Well this is all for today and the last letter from USA,
at least for a while. It was a difficult decision to take,
and I had to think so hard as never in my life. I never
missed you as much - though I always miss you - than in
these weeks.
Best love to you all
Lotte.
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief auf zwei Seiten (hier Seite 2). Tinte violett.

pages.transcription:
Dear Hannah, we start this
letter on board of the ship, the rest will
follow from Rio where we hope to
find your news. I am
sorry to say it but we are frightfully spoiled
here on the ship and it is the most wonderful
voyage one can imagine - I wish you had
only one day out of our twelve, The air
warm and a marvellous breeze all day,
Sunbaths and waterbathes, nice people,
Brazilians, Argentines, Suisse, Dutch which
all are good and old readers of my books
from tomorrow (after Barbados) I
shall get a state cabin to work in. It
was really necessary and a rest after
the hot days of Newyork, where poor
Lotte finally nearly broke down - I have
done there hard work to make some
money, minor but amusing work and
we had to see many people, Unfortuna
tely just the last two days, when you
cabled about Heiner were the worst, I
had to see a doctor on behalf of an
attack of sciatica and some other thing

[Randnotiz links, von unten nach oben geschrieben:]
just recieved your telegram as board
in your [?]

[Stempel oben links:]
AMERICAN
The Good
Neighbor
Fleet
REPUBLIC
LINE

[Gedruckter Text oben rechts:]
VIA AIR MAIL
ON BOARD
S. S. Argentina

pages.transcription:
Lotte lost a filling and had to rush to a
dentist, than we had to go to the Custom
House and when our ship left Lotte was
so tired, that she remained the whole
next day to bed, But what a splendid
rest cure we have and I suppose that
Brazil will not remain behind our
expectations. Our friends expect us
there in the kindest way and I have
invitations for lectures from Uruguay
Argentine, Chile, Venezuela; I suppose
all will go all right and we would
be perfectly happy as seldom in a
voyage would not the idea of the
war destroy much of our feelings.
We get on the ship nearly no news
just a few lines - The Americans
are terribly indifferent to all what
happens, they help but they have not
the right compassion and not enough
foresight - we were glad to leave
Newyork because we could not stand
longer this "jolly mess" in such a time

[Randnotiz links, von unten nach oben geschrieben:]
Now Lotte will write you more, kindest regards
Stefan

[Randnotiz rechts, von oben nach unten geschrieben:]
We have charming people on board, all the ambassadors of the [?] are
my chess partners

Liebe Hannah, ich glaube dass das lexicon für £15/-|-
das verhältnismässig billigste ist und sein Geld wert ist, schon
weil es mir für Manfred in Freude und Bildung nützt.
In jedem „behoweten“ Bürgerhause stand ein Conversations
lexicon, nur dass es dort nicht benutzt würde, während ich Man-
fred schon unablässig auf mir wieder wandeln sehe: Du wirst bei
dieser Gelegenheit auch das Alphabet üben können.
Mein zukünftiger Balbobart hat eine traurige Vorgeschichte. Seit
Friedental hier ist - der selbst mir immer wieder dank sein
Wissen erstaunt, besonders auch in praktischen Dingen - ist mein
Ansehen im Hause beträchtlich gesunken. Ich erscheine neben ihm
als Ignorant, werde verhöhnt und wegen krasser Unbildung ver-
spottet. Um mir wenigstens einen dünnen Schein von Respect
zu retten, versuche ich es jetzt mit einem weismelierten Bart. Bis-
her haben mir zwar schon mächtige Stoppeln aber keinerlei Ehrfurcht
vor dem Alter eingestellt.
Lotte sende ich bei erster Gelegenheit. Ich hoffe sie bringt Dir
ein selbstgelegtes, - Pardon, ein von den eigenen Hühnern ge-
legtes Ei als Gastgabe mit. Herzlichst Euer

Stefan

X man muss nur vorsichtig sein nur nachsehen was „good condition“
heisst, wahrscheinlich nur „ganz gut“ der andere beschreibt sein Exemplar
als „fine“ was etwas positiver lautet.

pages.transcription:
VIA AIR MAIL
Aug 24th, 41
ON BOARD
S. S. Uruguay

Dear Hanna & Manfred,
We will soon
be in Rio and I am glad that we took
the boat which was very restful while
the plane journey would have been most
tiring. Eva will have written you that Mrs.
Sch. brought her down to the boat to see
us off which was a thrilling way to begin
her birthday - taking the train for NY long
after bedtime and returning about 2 in
the morning. It was Mrs. Sch's birthday pre-
sent to Eva - I would never have dared to
suggest it to her for she is more than busy
the whole day long. That she had the idea
and made this trip with her at night
should be a further proof to you that
Eva is more than just a „boarder“ in
Amity Hall. They have already taken pho-
tographs of the new house and you might
soon get a brochure with them. Eva missed
being photographed with the others because
she was at Elizabeth's house in these days.
- We had an agreeable trip and a good
rest, I refused to work and also Stefan
did not do much. In Rio, I shall imme-
diately look for an apartment or small
house so that we settle down at least for
a few months.
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief auf Briefpapier der Moore-McCormack Lines (S.S. Uruguay). Sehr gut lesbar.

pages.transcription:
I hope it will not take too long
before we hear from you there and
that it will be only good news. Has
Marta already been in Bath and how
did she feel as a guest? And has
Mr. Honig who went back to England
a month ago already been with you?
We told him to come and see you if
necessary in Bath. We were with him
quite frequently and liked him well.
- I am afraid my letter is not very
coherent, but I am writing in the
lounge, have heard the BBC News and
American news while I read, not to speak
of the people who pass etc. Anyhow
you know that my thoughts are with you
most frequently. Now it is nearly two
years since the beginning of the war and
I remember those days most vividly.
& these days on the boat, lying in the
deck chair all day long, I often indulged in
day dreaming and wishful thinking and I
imagined how I would have enjoyed it
could you have been next to me in the
deck chairs. As this cannot be just now,
we must keep contact by letter, and so
please write frequently.
Best love and kisses
Lotte
pages.notes: Fortsetzung des Briefes auf der Rückseite. Sehr gut lesbar.

pages.transcription:
Dear H. & M. now we have to economise VIA AIR MAIL paper
as the airmail takes from Rio only 5 grammes. We had
an extremely quiet voyage and are both
again restored after the heavy strain of Newyork
- I have never been so down as S. S. Uruguay
in these last weeks and Lotte too has not been too
well. What we want both is some months in
a quiet place and not hotellife; we hope to find
this near Rio. In America you feel already
the war in the atmosphere, the preparations
are tremendous and life became still more ex-
peansive than it was - I believe we have seen
for the last time the splendour and the luxu
ry there as this war will unfortunately be
a very long one and the expenses are simply
fantastic. We have here with the sister of
Morgentau, who has the whole financial prepa
ration in hand, her husband is from here
and arched since many years in Newyork;
I start already learning better Portuguese
as I shall stay at least six months here -
we do not know when it will possible to
go to the States and if it will be the right
thing for us who are longing to have rest
from travelling; it was hard for us to leave
Eva behind but we feel that she is better
here with her "auntie" Han with us
who do not know where to we go; perhaps
I have to lecture again in Argentine. I be-

pages.transcription:
c/o EDITORA GUANABARA
132 RUA OUVIDOR
31.8.41

Dear Hanna u. Manfred, We have well arrived on
Wednesday and are glad to be here in a somewhat
quieter atmosphere. Nothing has changed while we were
away, we have the same room in the same hotel, the
which Stefan spends most of his time working, and even the food is
still the same. Two days after our arrival we went to Petropolis by
car - a little more than 1 1/2 hours on a beautiful and well-kept road.
and looked for a house. It is altogether more difficult than we thought
because all the old or wealthy families have houses of their own
and very few houses are to be let. Tuesday we will go there
again and there is hope that we may find something. In that case
we would move up to Petropolis in about a fortnight and come
down to Rio once or twice a week. There are plenty of busses
between the two places and also a railroad of an already
venerable age. Going immediately to Petrop. and settling down there
has the great advantage that we need not move again when summer
begins in December. Petrop. is the summerresort for all who want
to remain near Rio, more so than Brighton and Eastbourne were for London.
While still in Rio we gradually see our friends again and shall
also take Portuguese lessons. We read fluently and understand already
fairly well, but now we also must begin to speak it. - Through the
long boat trip of 12 days Newyork seems already very far away
and besides missing Eva (and Amity Hall also a little) I do not regret
having left the States again. It is strange: all the Europeans down
here in South Amer. dream of going to the States while many of those
who are there would find it very difficult to adapt themselves and
wish they could leave and live in South Am. - Arriving in Rio we found
your letter of Aug. 8th forwarded from Newyork and I hope we will soon hear
from you again and hear more about yourself and Manfred's work.
Best love and kisses Lotte.
We are now four days here and feel allright - happy would be too much because I
cannot adapt myself to this nomadic life without a home and without books, we remain
Europeans for ever and will feel everywhere strangers. I have no, pep like the American
say and also writing will be difficult after the autobiography - all I have to tell
is so far away what America likes to read and to hear. Lotte is somewhat better
but we dream always to be fresh and enterprising and cannot more fix the
right "elan" - the war is too long for me and still far from his end. Our
life in Petropolis (at here) will be a solitary one because we do not like
mon society and I have refused to make public appearance for the next
time - we will study Portuguese to feel more free and I hope to continue
to work. Newyork we had too many people and here not enough of

Friday, Sept 4th, 41

Dearest Mamma, Please stop worrying about us, we will
be alright and even if things do not always go for us
as we would like it and if we complain once in a while
don't take it too seriously. Those last weeks in USA with
all the indecision were difficult, but now that we are
here we are going to settle down again. We have already
found a house in Petropolis which suits our purpose
very well. It is small - bungalow style - has a large terrace with a beautiful
view over the mountains, you climb up to it from the street on a
number of steps, it has a small garden and is tolerably furnished.
We are satisfied to have found it, as it is not at all easy and
most houses are either dreadfully ugly or dreadfully expensive.
The servant question, which as I am told is also difficult, also
promises to be solved for us for the time being as the couple
who look after the house at present will probably remain
until I find what I need. Being without servants is in so far
very disagreeable here as in Petropolis the kitchen stoves are
exactly of the type of children's toy stoves and have to be looked
after all the time. We hope to be able to go up to Petropolis
next weekend and intend to come to Rio fairly frequently. It is
still very quiet in Pet. and the air reminds one even of a european
spring. - We shall cable you the address as soon as we definitely
go up there and I repeat it here 34 Rua GONCALVEZ DIAS
Petropolis, Brazil
but please note that it is only for cables. Letters please continue
to address to Editora GUANABARA, they will be forwarded
immediately from there by a professional messenger which is safer
than trust them to the change of the little railroad and delivery
in Petropolis. - We had a letter from Eva and Mrs. Sch. Both write
how beautiful presents she got from everyone and Mrs Sch wrote that
Eva was well and cheerful. It seems that they have already moved
to the new house and I hope that you and I soon get details
about the life there. - I must close now, first of all our Por-
tuguese teacher just arrived and secondly the mail for to-morrow's
clipper closes in a few minutes. - We have received
today your letter of Aug. 20th and Mama's of Aug 22nd,
not so bad really, just a fortnight.
Love to all, best wishes
for the solutions of the servant question in Bath,
Lotte

pages.transcription:
Dear Hannah & Manfred, we have your letter of August 20th today Sept 4th I am sorry
that the house in Bath gives you so much trouble - especially as
I doubt more and more that we shall ever see it again. Please do
not spare yourself and do not too much work, the coming times
will ask from us all our strength. As to Lotte's box I wrote
you already that you shall not worry too much; I am convinced
that I shall have with him serious discussions and I do not wish that you
shall be mixed in my personal troubles. Thanks so much to have given the
manuscript of my Balzac to Lotte; it would be wonderful if I could
get it one day and continue my work! You are really too kind! You cannot
imagine how I am longing to work quietly. Lotte will write you about our
intention to go to Petropolis; I want absolutely a few months rest and
in any case I shall not give any lectures before spring. We cannot see
any more trunks, suitcases, we are tired of hotels, of changes. -
I wish I could report to you that Lotte is quite right. Unfortunately she
has seldom a quiet night and I hope only that the treatment will finally
give her complete recovery. It is perhaps also the nomadic life with its
changes of climate and surroundings which was not favorable to us both
I have finished the autobiography in the greatest strain only to
finish it before leaving New York and will now work on it quietly. At
least six month we hope to stay in Petropolis - you know how I like
to travel but now we feel we have overdone it. It will be an absolute
relieved life without society, theatres and (the only thing I miss) without
books and we even do not start to think what we shall do afterwards.
Here in Rio the first news we received was that the poor Count Hoya
died on the consequence of an angina (streptococcic poisoning) -
Fritzi's have flowers but we have not yet seen him. He has made a
book on the president and will get much money out of the funds:
you know how I admire his ability. I have seen so many of the best
in New York unable to earn a cent that I find it masterly how he
always invents new possibilities to live largely. Give Edelmann my
kindest regards. My indifference against books etc. comes from the
conviction that I shall never see them and I wish you would keep
them as the best of them for you. We are all very confident in
the final victory, more, much more than ever before but there is no
[Randnotiz links:] doubt that it will take some time - some years perhaps - as the enormous preparation of
the United States will be in full swing but from now on there every day is for Britain
and you in England will have still much burdens to bear. I wish you well.

pages.transcription:
Rio, Sept. 13th, 41.

EDITORA GUANABARA
WAISSMAN KOOGAN LTDA.
LIVREIROS E EDITORES
RUA DO OUVIDOR, 132
TELEPH. 22-7231
RIO DE JANEIRO
END. TELEG. EDIGUA - BRASIL

Dear Hanna & Manfred,
No news from you yet this week,
but so far two letters from Eva, they are already in
the new house and she writes very cheerfully. Of
course Mrs. Sch. will report to you now every few
weeks, but you must excuse her, I believe, for the
last weeks and a few more to come - they have not very much furniture to move
and to instal, and I suppose the noble house will be rather shabbily furnished
at first, but nevertheless the noble house will be rather shabbily furnished
at first, but nevertheless it must be an immense amount of work to change over
from one house to another with about twenty or more children. - From us there
is not much to report. I had a cold and did not go out much the last week, and
Stefan spends four to six hours daily at the dentist's. Our only regular "work"
were the Portuguese lessons every day, a rather boring business, as we both
have no love for this language and rather resent it - Spanish would have been
so much more convenient and easy while we are quite sure that we will never
master the pronunciation of Portuguese. Anyhow, it has to be done, the Brazi-
lians naturally prefer their language to French in the long run, and keeping
house absolutely requires Portuguese. About the house in Petropolis I have
written in detail in the enclosed letter to Mama, and you will hear more about
my experiences when we will be up there. - I have thought over what you wrote
about mother coming to Bath for a visit, and there is for my opinion not the
slightest reason why she should visit there while you have household and servia
troubles. I can understand that whe would like to return to London and that she
prefers being near Manfred, you and her friends to just personal safety which,
I have come to think, is not worth too much trouble and isolation. On the other
hand I would have acted like you did, declining all responsibility and advising
rather that she stays on where she is. But I do not see any reason why she
should go to Bath now, and I am sure she does not even want it. She has had
country life enough for a while, she does not need a rest, and what else does
Bath and Rosemount offer now that neither nor Eva are there? So do not worry
about this now. If mother really returns to London - she did not mention this
intention to me and I did not write to her about it - and again has spent a
winter there, this problem might arise, but how much will have happened until
then?! - I hope that you are both well and that Manfred will soon find the job
he wants. Do not bother too much about us and our problems, every European is
bound to have his worries in one way or the other nowadays, and if only the war
goes well, everything will have been worth while. So do not worry if Rosemount
has to be neglected for a while, and don't let other affairs of ours take too
much time and thought. We know you manage everything as well or better than we
could do it, and we only hate the thought to burden you with our affairs, you
must have enough of your own.

                                             Warmest greetings to all and love to you
                                             Lotte

pages.transcription:
Rio, Sept. 13th, 41
Dearest mother, I have received your two letters of
Aug 19th (addressed to NY) and of Aug 22nd and hope to have
good news from you again soon and to hear that you can
stay on in the same house which you seem to like.
We have taken a home in Petropolis and will move up there some time next
week. It is quite small, really only a bungalow and separate servants
quarters as all the houses are arranged up there - I suppose still a remnant
from the days of slavery - but we like it. It is built halfway up a hill
and has a beautiful view on mountains from a big covered terrace where
I suppose Stefan will spend his days working. You walk up to it a number of
steps through a nice little garden which as the landlady promised will be
full of hortensias in summer. Behind the house immediately is the hill, but
a few steps further up the gardener is just preparing a small plateau and
he promised to build a little summer house as well - so I shall take this as
my residence during the day, and maybe later on, when the season begins
I shall change place with Stefan so as to hide him from unexpected visitors.
I have been very lucky in so far as the landlady has solved the servants'
question for me. The gardener and his wife will continue to live in the servants
quarters and he will look after the garden, act as handy-man and do errands
if necessary. He works in a factory and does all for us after his work, and
besides their living in my place I shall have nothing to do with them -
they do their own cooking etc. During the day a cook-servant will come and
do the house-work and cooking. All our friends, meaning well
without doubt, have been warning me how difficult it is with servants in
Petropolis. Those from Rio do not go up there because it is too primitive
- the cooking is done on old-fashioned stoves which have to be heated
with wood, the servants quarters are very primitive etc - and the servants
in Petropolis are supposed to be lazy and inefficient. But I am not
frightened. I know that as the gardener lives in the house I shall not be
left quite alone with all the work and I believe that after England and
USA I do not expect too much from servants. In any case we are very
glad to get settled for a few months at least and to live a quite retired
life. We both have at the moment no desire at all to see people or to go out
a lot. Even here in Rio which we both love so much, we go out very little
and are satisfied with the view from our terrace which makes up for all the
defects of the hotel which is clean and has good service but which is run too
much on the principles of the Haushaltungsschule, especially with regard
to the food and all possible economies. - So far we have both still been
rather tired and I was at home with a disagreeable cold for some days.
So we declined all invitations for receptions, cocktails etc. and just saw
privately a few friends. We have Portuguese lessons every day and can speak
although with many mistakes, almost all that is necessary and even
carry on a conversation in Portuguese if there is no other way out. But it
is rather an ugly language and a great pity that just this country does not
belong to the Spanish group. Spanish is so much easier for us and so much
more beautiful as language. - The above address remains valid even when
we are in Petropolis.
Love and kisses
Lotte.

pages.transcription:
Dear H.M. we are going to Petropolis in two days and hope to live there quietly
for some time. Before I have thought much what you had to suffer at your
dentist as I had no less than two protheses to get - now I am
a real Englishman having my artificial teeth to take out every
evening. It was an excellent [?] dentist who really worked
wonder in making with his craftsman those two big protheses
in six days instead of six weeks and without any pain for me.
Now this is done and if Lotte would get rid of her asthma we could live
and work quietly after the long months of troubles and strain.
I have met here Manfreds brother in law. He arrives here a year ago, was
between in the United States and has the intention to stay here for the
next months, at least half a year. Last year he had still all his obli-
gations against his former boss, but he hopes as he is stabilised here
and has his permanent stay granted since November 1940 that he
will be free of his former obligations for the coming year. You cannot
imagine how it complicates his situation to be at once bound to
the new firm, the American one and the old one and he hopes that
one day he can clear his situation against the former one. He would
like to ~~take~~ rent an appartement for good - we ourselves have taken
the tiny house in Petropolis for seven months only but if it pleases
us we can take it for longer so that we have also a permanent ad-
ress and residence. It is possible that I shall give some lectures
in Argentine in spring, but we will keep meanwhile the residence;
it contains altogether 3-4 tiny rooms with a large terrace which
will be my real working room and we shall have a black servant girl
who lives near the house and if they prove as good as they are cheap we
will rejoice. Most important for me is now to finish the autobio-
graphy which is practically ready but wants revising and enlarging
and than to try to write again some short stories or a novel, some-
thing substantial and if the Balzac manuscript arrives I shall be
safe. Thanks for all dear Hannah and please use evening in Bath
as if it were yours; I hope this winter will be better than the last
one and in the great decision the odds are now on our side and
whatever happens, a world without Hitler will be a better world. Yours
Stefan

pages.transcription:
c/o EDITORA GUANABARA
132, RUA OUVIDOR
RIO DE JANEIRO

PETROPOLIS, (BRASIL)
(34, RUA GONÇALVES DIAS)
3.10.41

Can you find out - perhaps via Hirschfeld,
Lotte Sch. I have not heard from her since
June in spite of various letters addressed to
the Raeburn address in the country, and am worried.

My dear Mamma,
We have just received your, Manfred's and Victor's letter
of Sept 7th and nobody can understand your feelings about it and things in
general better than we do, who on the other side of the question have just the
same alternating periods of being depressed, reasonable, and sometimes opti-
mistic, sometimes resigned. And we know from own experience that in such moments
of depression the only reasonable answer - that we should be glad that our fears
were exaggerated and our precautions perhaps superfluous - does not help to make
one feel better. But I hope that in the meantime you have already got out of
that mood, that now you have fewer things on your mind and no urgent questions
to settle. I can imagine how long it took you to come to the decision to send
Ursula back to her parents although on the other hand it seems natural that
they should have her at their home again instead of living separately.
I hope, especially for your sake, and also because Miller seems a part of Rosemond
that he is better again and fully appreciate that you continue with his salary
so that he can afford to be cured effectively, instead of trying to rush back
to work. But I am sorry that in this moment it gives you an enormous amount of
work and little pleasure, and I do wish I could be with you and do my own
share. Instead I am sitting here in our little bungalow, learning again how to
cook by showing the maid how to do it, and in spite of the language difficulties
am having an easy time of it, being busy mostly re-writing parts of the
autobiography for Stefan, and when the weather - in rare moments so far
is good, we go out for walks. We are already quite settled here, Stefan has
his barber, his coffee-houses, his writing-table, and I know my shops and
already most of the household- and shopping expressions. No need to say
that sometimes it is a phantastic thought to live in a little mountain town in
Brazil, but we are quite happy here and certainly did well to come here in-
stead of remaining in the States. I do miss Eva, too, it was so nice to be near
her and to be with her every few days, but I don't think she misses us
very much, she feels as much at home in Amity Hall as she did in
Bath without in the least forgetting about her real home and parents.
Stefan's first wife saw Eva the other day. I believe she invited her, I have
no report yet from Eva about it - and she wrote how well Eva looks,
and with how much love she talked about auntie Olga. - In the mean-
time you may already have got the Brazil book and will learn more about the
reasons of our love for this country. Strangely enough we have now for
the first time again a number of books in our own language, there are two
lending libraries in Rio and here we met a Mr. Sternberg from Berlin who
has all the usual modern books which one had to have. And as the chess
takes also some time every day, we are quite busy even without all the
people who promised to visit us here. To-morrow I believe Paul will come up.
The last time I saw him and Marika in Rio they looked unbelievably
modest bourgeois and normal. Marika was cleanly and well dressed with care-
fully groomed hair, doing needle-work, playing chess with Stefan, and Paul too
seemed quite harmless and just friendly. Kindest regards, fondest love,
Lotte

[Randnotiz links, von unten nach oben geschrieben]:
Tell Friedenthal we found here in the lending library his volume "Marie Antoinette"
and have read and re-read it with greatest pleasure and regret more than this
new novel is not yet finished.

pages.transcription:
Dear H. & M. I can really confirm that we have here in our little bungalow
absolutely the life I wanted after the strenuous times in New York etc. I have as my
real workroom a large covered terrace in front of the beautiful mountains, the
neighborhood is very primitive and therefore picturesque, the poor people are so nice
here as you cannot imagine; our black housemaid is silent, diligent, clean and
grateful to us as she learns to see things she never has seen in her life - {she begins to sing now} for
them potatoes are already a luxury and fish an unknown animal. She takes our
empty tins at home as a treasure and uses them there as glasses but nevertheless
she is clean and it is the intern civilisation and humanity I admire so much here
in this country. Lotte is busy; you would not believe it as we make very few walks
and see no people that the day runs so quickly away, that we are quite surprised
to be here already three weeks. I am happy that she likes this kind of life as
much as I do; I am only not quite satisfied with her health. She has cheated
me first in having no dowry, now in loosing weight by her demure[?] eating, which
is somewhat better but every night there are one or two dialogues between her and
a dog in a house far away. Whenever she begins to cough the dog begins to bark
as the air is quite still and transmits every sound in a great distance, I
insist that she now makes a cure to get some embonpoint, because here life
is so quiet and easy that I wish she should take provisions for the bad times
which are expecting us in the future. Altogether I cannot tell you how happy
we are to have left New York where our life did not belong to us and we had all
sorts of problems, while here we live forgotten and forgetting the time, the world
(but not you) Fräulein is as always the object of my most fervent admiration,
the earns here with his larger book at least twenty times what I with my book,
having all entrenchous[?], connexions and that was not easy coming here without
to know anybody or a word of Portuguese. How I regret that I did not move
to Brazil five years ago, you have no idea of the fantastic modernity - a house
which was worth 100 £ five years ago cost now 500 or even a thousand, but
life is still cheap, all the native things in excellent quality as people have not
yet learned to use substitutes. And we told you already what we say, overpaying
the usual rates - 5 dollars a month to our maid while in America one has
to pay 60 or 80 and she takes there two holidays a week. I do not generally
be mean, but you understand what a relief it is to know that one can
still live cheaply somewhere and will not be dependent from newspapers and
agents. How you would like this country, so colourful and peaceful in such
a time. - Let me tell you that your letters are expected with the greatest
interest - I hope this winter will not be too hard. Give Hermann my love, I should really write to
him, but it is not the higher postage but the feeling that every letter takes much
longer than one does not so easily [?] love and greetings to all! Stefan

pages.transcription:
Liebe Hannah, ich komme diese Woche zuver
lässig, vielleicht Donnerstag. Aber sei nicht
gekränkt wenn ich nicht bei Euch wohne. Entweder
 fahre ich abends zurück oder ich übernachte
im Hotel neben Paddington, um gleich mit dem
Frühzug zurückzufahren, ich will nicht zwei
Tage verlieren, da ich doch in der Pariser und
der Naturalisationsangelegenheit gewiss noch zwei
oder dreimal ohnehin nach London werde fahren
müssen. Es ist nicht zarte Rücksicht auf euch, son-
dern grobe Selbstsucht, die euch euer Tantes Heim
keinmal vernachlässigen lässt
Eier verzehr. Der Gärtner ist sehr streng mit uns,
wir sollen nicht mit „seinen“ Hühnern wedeln
und ich fürchte er wird uns bald auch verbieten,
den Garten zu betreten.
Jedenfalls melde ich mich und hoffe, wir können
abends bimmeln, falls ich alter Bauer das nicht
schon verlernt habe. Herzlichst Euer Stefan

pages.transcription:
From Wilmot I had direct infomation. As far all is in order, let us hope the same
for the future.
About the business and financial arrangements you had to make for us with
Wilmot etc. I suppose Stein will write you himself. I feel sure that you
have done everything at lest as well as we could have done it ourselves,
and I am afraid you spent as much time and thought on it than Stefan would
have done. Many, many thanks! Thori wrote us a letter some time ago, that
he is not allowed to have any relations with people in Hungary and that the
money the Hungarian publisher has or had in England is blocked, so that no
payment may be expected. Ax - Now I have written more than my share and must
leave the rest of the page to Stefan. Please send the two first sheets of
this letter on to mother so that I need not repeat myself.

Dear H. & R. we like our stay here very much. It is life like our
parents and grandfathers had and the people are so extremely nice and
ever clean in their great poverty. Food is still not artificial, the baker
bakes his bread and his excellent cakes himself and our life-expenses
are one third as those in America. Others would call Petropolis out of
reason a frightfully dull place but for somebody like me who wants
no other thing than to work and to read quietly, to enjoy walks in the
beautiful surroundings. it is the perfect thing I cant imagine the variety of types and chara-
teristic topics in the Brazilian life, I enjoy it enormously after the
monotony of American streets. Dear Hannah, you will understand that
one gets more and more sceptic against a civilization & seeing the gloss
results of it and that this peaceful, more primitive, more natural life
has a quite new attraction; the only weak point are books but I have
bought a Shakespeare, a Goethe, a Homer and with this and some other
which I can lend from others one can live for a certain time especially
if one writes his own ones. What I miss are reference-books when I
need some details and in urgent cases I have to wait 4-6 weeks to
get information from Newyork. As to the material things I feel much
more free and careless than there; I have certain things and fears which
worried me very much and which I cannot explain to you as they
are too complicated but I repeat that from here all looks much
more indifferent and we become more and more able to forget the
possibilities of the future. This war takes such proportions that all
positions and all fears are futile, every thought of a post war life
and consequences of former mistakes is wasted. I do quietly my
work and hope to be through my autobiography in a few weeks
having completed still in Ossining the record draft - Lottes health
is somewhat improved and so we have not to complain; I wish you

[Randnotiz links, von unten nach oben geschrieben:]
could see our little bungalow in the mountains
Elegante (in reality a tiny room but nicknamed open café, in which I am nearly the only
white man and Lotte the sensation as never another white lady would enter
such a popular place) Perhaps we shall even get a dog! knows Stefan

pages.transcription:
Dear H. & M. I would not have believed that in my sixtieth year I would sit
in a little Brasilian village, served by a barefoot black girl and miles
and miles away from all that was formerly my life, books, concerts, friends
conversation. And we feel extremely happy here, the little bungalow with
its large covered terrace (our real living room) has a splendid view
over the mountains and just in front a tiny cafelaus, called „Café
Elegante“ where I can have a delicious café for a halfpenny and enjoy
the company of black mule-drivers. Life is here very cheap and you have
no opportunity to spend, I am working and in my idle hours I play the
master-games of a big chess book - one feels far away from all and
even the war. It was really necessary for us to stabilize for longer time,
we were both frightfully tired, Lotte more by her asthma and myself
by psychic depressions; here in the solitude we hope to get new strength
and alas, we will want much strength. The news from Europe are
so depressing, thanks God not the military ones but those from the
occupied territories - I am afraid, millions will starve while here
all is in peace and full prosperity. There is here now a quite new
nationalism starting, Brasil feels that it will become important
in war and peace, but the people themselves are very nice. We try
to speak Portugiese and it is difficult for me because of my Spanish
which interferes continually. - From Wilmot I have a letter and
I see that he tries to clear my position for next year. Altogether
I regard everything as lost and won't be glad if you can't enjoy
of all as long as it is possible - nobody has an idea what
enormous economic changes this war will produce, also America
will be another country after the war. For you, the younger genera-
tion all this has practical interest, not more for me - in four
years or even in three I will not be able and willing [?] to
adapt myself to the new world, it belongs to your daughter, who
I hope, see and enjoy better times. I wish we could send
you some chocolate or coffee and sugar, which is ridiculously cheap
here but we have not yet found out any possibility. I repeat
my wish, my urgent wish, that you may use all clothes, under-
wear, linen, overcoats and also whatever we have there - it has
not secure to reserve it for years and I am sure I will never use all this. You do
only a favour and you will see that I feel much better with this idea.
I have then to regret of what I shall never see more.
