pages.transcription:
Dear Hanna + Manfred,                                Rio, 31. XII. 40
We very much hope that you have spent not only Christmas but
also the following week until at least New Year in Bath and that
you both had a thorough rest. I have heard that the winter is very
cold in Europe this year, and I hope there is a good livable shelter
in your new apartment. We are living just the extreme of your
life. It has now become very hot - exceptionally hot, as we are told
- and we have taken an attitude of defense against the heat.
The days are not too bad, although to-day where the temperature
inside the house has been 33° celsius at 11 in the morning, we
sought refuge in the air-conditioned bar (which usually does not
open before nightfall). The evening and nights which are hot and
airless are a little hard to bear sometimes but the thought of
you all over there does not allow us to complain as the
others do. On the whole we stand the heat very well and Stefan
is grateful to it as he is losing weight without any special
effort. We have again thought of going away to the mountains
but decided that it is not worth while and that we better
leave a little earlier than we originally intended.
About our plans I do not want to tell you too much because
we may change them again. We intend to go first to the
north of Brazil and visit Bahia, Recife and Belem.
It will not be much hotter than here, and as this journey
will not cost us anything - except receptions, signatures
and innumerable photographs - we will already be half the
way up to the States.
Kindest regards and New Year wishes, Lotte.
                                Rio 3. January 1941
Dear Hannah and Manfred, your letter from the 24. November
has just arrived, you see, it takes sometimes five weeks and
you may be sure that we have written every week to you and
even sometimes twice a week. We have really the feeling that
we must talk to you even by distance and if one or the
other letter is belated or lost, it will never be our fault.
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief von Lotte Zweig. Tinte auf Papier. Sehr gut lesbar.
Rückseite des Dokuments, leer.

objects.confidenceNotes: Der Text ist sehr deutlich geschrieben und weist keine nennenswerten Leseschwierigkeiten auf.

pages.transcription:
Dear Hannah and Manfred, thanks for your cable, I hope our friends will get the
Argentine visa as the minister in persona was so kind to cable twice to
London; should he go to Argentine he has to pass per Brazil and I shall see him
there and give him every help, also in Buenos Aires my friends will be useful to him.
It is now quasi impossible to get any visas; for Edemann I will try again in Cuba
about a fortnight when Cata's daughter will arrive here. We will have here in the
great hall of the Foreign Office here a memorial-celebration for him on Monday,
presided by the Minister of Foreign Affairs and I will speak there in the name
of his European friends - (in French naturally.) So we are always busy and we have
to ~~keep~~ defend us against too many invitations; I personally don't like not
to leave our room from where we have the most marvellous views in the world
and till now the weather is splendid and not at all hot so that I have even not
yet worn my tropic clothes. - About Eva you have the news from Lotte, that we
have no news at all directly by her. I am nearly convinced that the Salmons do
everything to let her forget her family and to cut off all visits. I am not a
great admirer of my sister in law and would dearly exchange her against one
like you but I must admit that she has tried her best, except with that one letter of Eva a very friendly letter to look after her. Also our-
selves had never a line from Salmons it seems that they like Eva so much that
they will not cease give her bad. In any case we wrote her a energetic letter.
Please do not worry about all that. She is safe, that's what matters. And all
post-war things are so obscure that we better do not to think about - we have
to live this time through and the most important remains to live and to keep
fit for all the nice surprises which are expecting us. - From all our London
friends we have not heard a word, Friedlaender has not yet arrived here
and the only thing he would be useful to me would be to hear about you
and your daily life. I hope that Manfred and you will after the days of
work retire to have some rest at Bath, I cannot repeat too often, that we
want to see you not only in good health but also with good temper
and unshaken nerves. I know how Manfred likes his duty as a doctor,
but a doctor has not only to render healthy his patients but also himself.
Now we have more than one month or two to make our plans, if we

Rückseite des ersten Blattes, durchscheinender Text der Vorderseite sichtbar. Leer.

pages.transcription:
About our next plans, Lotte has already written to you,
~ if all goes right we shall be end of January in Newyork
and when this letter arrives you will have our adress - but
you can always write also to my publisher c/o Vikingpress
18 East 48 Street. The voyage will be a hard strain as we have
to be first in Bahia, Recife, Belem on the Amazonas - look at
the map and you will see the distances. From there we will
fly to Miami and from there go by train (30 hours) because
I prefer not to change the climate too quickly from 40° plus
to 20° minus. Yesterday I was surprised by Friedlaender's visit
he is here with wife and child and a "nurse", I have not
spoken him but by telefone and see him tonight. I am plea-
sed that he did not come earlier - how we are leaving alrea-
dy and he can tell his stories to others. He came in the last
moment as I hear that all visas will be stopped. I hope
Friedental got his; the consulate must have not only one
cable about him but two; as the consul refused it first to
Fandhoff who was mentioned in the same cable, he called
again the order for both. All what you say about the new
summer house - beauty in Bath has created mixed feeling
in us, pleasure and the doubt, if we will ever be able to
enjoy such quiet life. But let us not worry about the future
- all I hope is to find a quiet place for the next two or
three month to work and you will have a report about your
daughter. Mail is much quicker from the States than from here.
To America you better send cables with paid reply as we
will be short of cash but I hope that like in Argentine I
will by lectures and articles find easily my way. About a
second lecture tour to South America I shall decide there

Kindest regards to you all from yours Stefan Zweig

pages.transcription:
LYNCOMBE HILL,
BATH.

8. Dezember 1939

Liebe Hanna,

Ich bin eben zurueck und muss Dir
erstens herzlich fuer Deine Gastfreundschaft
danken, zweitens fuer meine Depressivitaet mich
entschuldigen. Aber es waren wirklich zwei voll-
gestopfte Tage, ueberdies durchspickt mit kleinen
Aergernissen, und der Londonder black-out wirkt
jedesmal auf mich wie ein Gang durch Katakomben.

Ich will Dir nur kurz berichten,
dass mein Angebot fuer den Teppich durchgedrun-
gen ist (inklusive der Unterlage), und sie wae-
ren sogar allenfalls bereit gewesen, ihn hier
aufmachen zu lassen, was wir aber selber koennen
(ich will keine Arbeiter mehr im Haus). Zweitens
will ich Dir melden, dass die Kinder vortrefflich
aussahen, Eva kam mir dadurch, dass Lotte gestern
kochte, sogar abgemagert vor.

Nun wegen Deines Urlaubs. Trachte
fuer Deinen Mann doch noch ein oder zwei Tage mehr
herauszuholen und fahrt keinesfalls mit dem Auto.
In der Bahn ruht man sich aus, und die Strassen
scheinen mir jetzt im Winter nicht ungefaehrlich.

Den Fahrplan wegen Llandudno wird
Lotte gleich studieren.

Herzlichst Euch allen

Stefan
pages.notes: Typoskript auf Briefpapier mit gedrucktem Briefkopf. Unterschrift handschriftlich in violetter Tinte.

pages.transcription:
Stefan ist müde und abgespannt zurückgekommen
und ich glaube froh, wieder in der Kleinstadt zu sein.
Wir hatten lebhafte Tage inzwischen, gestern tropfte der
Hahn des Heizkörpers im landing in die Halle hinunter,
heute brach ein Rohr im conservatory, dazwischen lief
geschäftig Stone mit Farbtöpfchen, und es ist nur ein
kleiner Trost, dass es mir gelang, Wooster klein und
bescheiden und nach Ausreden suchend zu bekommen.
Hoffentlich war das der letzte Zwischenfall, wir haben davon
langsam genug, Ende der Woche kommt Anita auf 3-4 Tage,
Die ferien der Kinder fangen nächsten Freitag an. Herzlichst
Lotte.

objects.confidenceNotes: Der Text ist sehr gut lesbar. Die Transkription folgt den Regeln der diplomatischen Umschrift.

pages.transcription:
Dear Hannah, we have frightfully to do before leaving - like in Newyork all
things rush together in the last moment. As to our friends; I hope Eidemann will
get his visa as my friend the minister Cator has guaranties for him, I did not dare
to promise it to him {but I believe it is quite sure} for Credental I will do my best and have already arran-
ged something with my publisher. For Barcla I can do nothing as it is my Ameri-
can publisher who has the only right to act and I am only his guest. I am very
glad that I shall not be here when Frinhaber arrives here, he will spoil the
good situation we all enjoy here by his feverish activity. In any case I avoid
to introduce him, he will do this himself (for some time) with his stories. I
understand however that he wanted to find another position and as far as
I can I help everybody in this regard. We are thinking continually where you
may be and what you are doing - please do not worry about Eva, my sister
in law wrote that she feels extremely happy, has a lot of friends and will start
skating next month, a pleasure which we could not afford to her in Bath. We
are very glad that Heiner can finally go to America, I would like to take for
my my tails (I have taken only the smoking with me) and if he hears from
some new music (here you get nothing at all of this kind) I would be grateful.
I hope he will not leave too soon, the idea of travelling in winter - true has
something frightening - I would not like it myself. We do not know more
what winter really is, every day sunshine - sometimes a little too much -
and blue sky; how you would like the view from our windows.
I see that in your kindness you make the servant and cook for all people
in Bath - what are the others women doing? Please advise Manfred to take
as much rest as possible in Bath. Could he not work there in an hospital? I
am afraid he overdoes his duty.
Kindest regards to all; also to Eidemann, who will I hope, find interesting
things and you give him certainly all help he wants. And yourself please
dont worry about money and dispose freely as I can by my lectures come
through without any difficulty - it is true, it means a great strain, this
lecturing in three different languages (or four even) but I have no right to
complain. Love to all from yours
StefanZweig

pages.transcription:
Rio, 11.I.41
Dear Manfred & Hanna,
Today we had your letter of Dec 18th and we are
sorry that you are worried about Eva. Obviously Salmon's determined
silence towards you and us is strange and that Rose Wohl behaved
in the same manner does not make the matter any more agreeable.
But you need not worry any longer. By the letters of my sister-
in-law you can be assured that Eva is well and apparently
quite happy there, and when you get this letter we will already
have seen her - and Salmon! I'll see to that - and decide what is
best for her and take her away if it should seem advisable. That
we should love to have her with us, I need not emphasise, but
that we cannot yet decide as long as our own plans are only made
from three months to three months. But you can rely upon us that
we shall not leave Eva at Salmon's if the surroundings are not
right. As to the school I cannot say anything until I have been
there. But I am afraid the American curriculum is somewhat
different from the English, and should we be able to take her with
us to Rio the difference would be still greater. But we will see to
all that and it will be easier now than in summer where all
the schools were closed. If we will have to take Eva away and for
some reason or other must again place her with others, I'll try to
find a continental background. Huebsch and Einsteins I shall
consult again, but I don't think that either one could take her -
it is not only the question of wanting to take a child but more
than anything else the problem of space - flats in New York etc
and elsewhere are usually just big enough for the family without
any room for guest or even servants. That may be also part of
the trouble with Berners and Carmel's boys. They lived in a tiny flat
with Rose, - two rooms and sittingroom all rather small - and the flat
they have now moved into is hardly bigger. I do not want to defend
their behaviour, and I certainly was disappointed that they never
even sent a postcard about seeing Eva, but as far as I can remember
it was Carmel who cabled that she wanted to send the boys, not they
who offered to take them and Berner's were not completely delighted
that Rose was taking them. That would explain not their behaviour
but their attitude to a certain degree. - We were glad to learn that
you were spending more than a week in Bath, and Belzim certainly
was an agreeable visitor although I cannot quite imagine where you
had him sleep. Have you many left already, and do you take
someone else in their place? Give Kanner my thanks for this
letter. I do believe I wrote them some time ago, but I am not
quite sure about it myself, the heat makes one stupid as well as lazy.

pages.transcription:
Dear Hanna & Manfred
Rio 12.I.41
I wrote you yesterday, but on re-reading your letter I felt that
I have not quite answered it. First of all I want to reassure you
that we will do everything to see that eva gets to live in the right
surroundings and that we would like nothing better than to have
her with us as soon as there is some chance of continuity in one place
on our part. In any case we will see eva immediately after our
arrival, - and we will report at once. secondly, We are very pleased that
you like to receive our letters and that you feel as well as we do,
that the distance and the complete contrast of our lives has not really
separated us. And please watch out that you don't acquire your brother
habit of not writing without thanking. There is really nothing to thank
for, you take care of our house and even of our friends and it is a good
feeling for us that in between you get some pleasure and rest out of it.
Furthermore I must remind you of the many years I spent with you
accepting as a matter of course (I did not then realise that you might
have acted otherwise) all you had and sharing your life. They were
happy years for me and I have begun to feel quite sentimental
about your leaving Woodstock Road, and so it is nothing more than a
just reciprocity if you now accept just as naturally whatever occurs
between us. - What you write, Hanna, that you wonder whether I could
keep pace with my husband in Argentine, was quite right. As a matter
of fact I could not. I don't know whether it was the rush or the climate
which I did not stand, the constant change of hot and cold, damp and dry,
winds and close in any case I got a cold and felt so dreadfully tired
that I went to a doctor who made all possible tests without finding any-
thing wrong. With a number of tonics and vitamins I kept myself awake
until we got back to Rio where after one day I was perfectly alright,
although the Brazilian climate too, is anything else but invigorating.
An interesting fact is that although the law in Argentine - and
nearly all South American States - does not allow foreign doctors, and
requires that they do their studies all over again including the
matric and on top of that must be naturalised - anybody may give
a prescription which is accepted without name or question by the
chemist. - By the way, a nose and throat specialist whom we met in
Buenos Aires made me an interesting proposition for an asthma
treatment which he said had success in about 80 percent of the cases
in Argentine and in France where he has studied and learned the
process - introduced I believe by Ahlfeldt - about 50 percent of success).
The treatment consists in touching a ganglion in the upper part of the
nose with some kind of liquid which reduces the oversensibility,
and after a needle with repeating this about a dozen times in an inter-
val of 2-3 days each, the asthma should be cured. It sounds phan-
tastic to us, but this Dr. Bonpet is university professor with a high reputation
and he would not have accepted payment, so he did not want to do it for the money!
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief von Lotte Zweig.
Rückseite des Briefes, durchscheinender Text der Vorderseite.

pages.transcription:
Have you ever heard about it? Had I been long enough in Buenos Aires,
I might have tried it as I had great confidence in him and as he
guaranteed that it could have no bad effects whatsoever. But please
dont misunderstand me in the sense that I need treatment - I am
quite alright and stand the heat just as well as any European summer.
Nevertheless we are looking forward to a bit of winter. One gets tired
of the heat and through the heat and one is slowly invaded by the Bra-
zilian indolence which is in sharp contrast with our European conscience
which still asks for activity, reliability, punctuality. I am also sorry to
say that nothing has come of my good intention to go down to swim every
morning at 7. I have not the energy to get up just in order to bathe.
Well, enough for to-day. The next letter
will probably be written somewhere on the way north.
Your letters which arrive after your departure will be
immediately forwarded to us. We could not let you know
before, we were ourselves undecided when to leave and
how to travel. Although we have in reality about enough of
travelling for a while, I am looking forward to a week of
sightseeing in the North. We are told that the heat will not
be worse than here and Bahia promises to be most
interesting. We will have all facilities and conveniences
- to be paid by attending receptions and banquets and
giving interviews.
With very best love
Lotte
pages.notes: Zweite Seite des Briefes.
Rückseite des Briefes, durchscheinender Text der Vorderseite.

pages.transcription:
12. January 1941 Dear Manfred and Hannah, we got today your
letter from the 18. Dec. and soon you will have news about Eva. We
are flying the 15 th to Bahia, Recife, Belem in the North of Brazil
for six days
and this part (nearly the half way) is paid to us, so that we have
only the other half on our own account; you see we manage things
all right and as I have nearly finished the book on Brazil, I can
always rely upon the people here and I hope, that if for Tristental
the Argentine visa should not work - the consul had not only one
cable to deliver a tourist visa to him but two - I can try to get it here
for him as a special favour. Now to Eva. We will stay about three to
four month in the States and of cause our first idea was to take her
here with us, but I am afraid that it is not possible as we will be often in
town till late at night and has to leave her alone. But I think we will
find someone, if she would like a change - all this has to be in-
vestigated {meanwhile} sure place[?]. Should we go back to Rio the question would arise
to take her with us. Here all is much easier and we could take a
flat or little house, the only difficulty is school. There are good English
or American colleges here, but it exists the obligation, that all schools
have to teach (mostly) in Portuguese and she had to learn a new language
still and a language which is not so important as French or Spanish.
But it is still much to early to make plans as we ourselves have not
yet decided - who can make decisions beforehand in such times?
In any case, please rely upon us, that we will do our best and not
only for yours sake but because we love both Eva and know how impor-
tant these years of development are. My sister-in-law wrote that she
did send Christmas presents to her and to the little boy, without to get
a single word of reply and also to us Salmons never answered and you
may imagine that we wrote to these stupid people in the most kindest way.
You understand, that we do not like the idea that Eva should be
educated by people who are lacking themselves of the faintest
notion of manners. But please do not worry about all this and
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief auf rosa Papier. Die Tinte ist violett. Die Zeile 'for six days' wurde handschriftlich eingefügt.
Rückseite des ersten Blattes, leer.

pages.transcription:
2)
remember always that she is safe and you have not to be exited[?]
about every alarm while she would be in school or out of the house
in England. I am more concerned about you, that you have too much
to do and not enough time for rest, let us hope that the worst is
over, here everybody is convinced of the British-American final success and
then all our pains and losses would be no more without sense - it
would be again a world to live within. When this beast Hitler should
be definitively overthrown, no price would be too high.
We are somewhat tired and glad to come out of the heat. The weather
is splendid, the town beautiful, but we have both the feeling, that a
little winter will do us good. Myself I feel, that I have to retire
somewhere to do quickly my work and not to see more people -
I believe we have been on this voyage six hundred to six thousand
and I do not know more, what language I am speaking and this
is a heavy strain. We hope to be the 23 or 24 at the Wyndham Hotel
42 West 58 Street but only for a week and you will have our
adress by cable (please cable always with reply) In any case letters
or communications will reach us c/o Viking Press 18 East 48 Street.
Love to Martha and all others and ever yours Stefan Zweig
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief auf rosa Papier. Die Tinte ist violett. 'everybody' wurde über 'all' eingefügt.
Rückseite des zweiten Blattes, leer.

pages.transcription:
Bahia, 16. I 1941

Dear Hannah and Manfred, we are now
here for three days and all what we
have seen is most wonderful; it is the most colour-
ful town I ever have met and today we assisted
the great popular festivity, the Lavagem do Bom
Fim - that means that a good part of the town,
most negro, come to wash the church in honour
of their saint and this washing which starts as
a religious ceremony and finishes in orgie of thousand
people who dance, cry, wash and become comple-
tely mad. I have never seen anything of religious
men-hysteria and all this in the brightest colours
and without any artificial tricks - there come
never strangers to see this and it would be in a
theatrical production or a film the greatest hit.
Tomorrow we are driving into the country, we
are guests of the government here and Lotte is again
photographed all day long, we send you only one
little photo of our arrival as the most are more
grotesk - myself with a little negro boy or
with the "intellectuals" of Bahia. You cannot
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief auf Briefpapier des Palace Hotel, Bahia. Die erste Zeile 'Adres: Newyork c/o Viking Press 18 East 48 Street' ist am oberen Rand notiert.
Rückseite des ersten Blattes, zeigt den durchscheinenden Text der Vorderseite (spiegelverkehrt).

pages.transcription:
imagine what it means to see this country which is not
yet spoiled by tourists and so enormously interesting.
-today I was in the huts of the poor people who
live here practically from nothing (the bananas
and mandiocas are growing round) and the children
go like in the paradise - her whole house with
ground did cost them six dollars and so they
are proprietor for ever. It is a good lesson to see
how simply one can live and comparatively happy
-a lesson for us all, who will loose everything and
are not enough happy now by the thought how to
live then. In two days - we go tomorrow over land
to the fazendas and tobacco-factories - we will be
at Pernambuco, in five days in Belem, then after
a day in English territory (Trinidad/on the way)
to your daughter and then it will be to Lotte to
write the long letter you expect so eagerly. I
hope you feel alright and will perhaps dance
over to Bath, Lotte stands the heat and all the
excursions extremely well, only when we have
to go up in the morning at 5 or 5:30 to catch
the plane, she is hard to awaken. Fischauer is
in Rio and told me, who did not believe if he
were our communist - in any case he seems to
have saved enough money and I am like always
his admirer, how he knows to manage all with
his lying technique. Kindest regards from the
6:30 in the morning, waiting for the little time to write.

pages.transcription:
in the plane to Miami 22nd Jan 41
Dear Hanna u Manfred, We sent you a
cable yesterday to thank you for the tickets
which were given to us in Belem, and we
hope to have a cable from you in Newyork as
your last letters will have to be forwarded
to us from Rio, We could not let you know
earlier because we decided rather sudd-
ly. It was very hot in Rio, we had only one
room in the hotel and one was losing all
energy for work. And as Stefan had to go to
Bahia anyhow, ~~and~~ we decided to
fly. Now we have been on the plane
with interruptions - for a week and we
shall be glad to get to Newyork to-
morrow morning. Stefan has written you
from Bahia; that was our first stop
from Rio - 6 1/2 hours by plane. He was
delighted with Bahia, and we were spared
official banquets etc. through the
energy of our companion - a young
journalist who accompanied us from
Rio to Belem a very nice medium-brown
Brazilian. Not so easy it was to escape
the constant company of the director
of the propaganda department in Bahia who
was delegated to show us round and

(Margin: Thursday morning i just arrived in Newyork)
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief auf einem Aerogramm-Formular. Die Randnotiz wurde links vertikal geschrieben.

pages.transcription:
who was a great talker - in Portuguese,
and we regretted that we ever admitted
to understand it, for we have still to
listen carefully in order to follow it
in conversation, and it was a mental
strain. With our companion we could
at least speak in Spanish which is
a little easier for us; and it would
had been our intention to see the
sights with him alone, but this was
not possible. The government of the
states of Bahia, Pernambuco and Para
wanted us to be their guest and their
representatives wanted not to lose a
moment of our stay. That and the fact
that we covered enormous distances
by plane was rather tiring and we
will be glad to settle down quietly,
but the journey itself was extremely
interesting, so interesting that I leave
it to Stefan to describe it, and I'll
keep to the more personal and prac-
tical part. I suppose you will have
a look on the map to follow our
journey and see what phantastic
distances we covered, about 2500
miles to Belem and at least that
much to Newyork. As to the time we

(Margin: & and to be photographed of course / on all places except the W.C.)
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief, Fortsetzung. Randnotiz links vertikal.

pages.transcription:
spent in the air, it is quite impressive
too: Rio-Bahia 6 1/2 hours, Bahia-Recife
5 hours, Recife-Belem 10(!) hours,
Belem-Trinidad 6 1/2, Trinidad-Miami 9 1/2,
Miami-Newyork 9 hours. The plane Belem-
Miami is a big clipper with huge arm-
chairs, hot food and comfort, tables
games and room between the seats. The
journey along the coast Rio-Belem
was by sea-plane, with many landings
in obscure little places with beautiful
names, interesting but rather uncomfortable
journey as the planes were small, narrow
and badly ventilated, whereas the clipper
flight is extremely comfortable but
uninteresting as it goes either above
cloud banks or over the ocean. This
night we will fly on to Newyork - no sleeper-
after spending the afternoon in Miami.
By now we have become early risers as
most trips start at 6 in the morning, which
means that you have to rise at 4.30
in order to arrive at the airport at
5.30. Now we will stay about a week
in Newyork, seeing Eva, looking for
a place to go to, seeing people about
business affairs and a few friends.
I suppose we will take a furnished
flat for about 3 months and keep a
household as we are tired of hotel food
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief, Fortsetzung.

pages.transcription:
and Stefan wants to retain his slimmer
looks which he has acquired through
perspiring in the heat and through
the uninteresting food in the
Rio-Hotel. We will try to see as
much as possible of Eva and as
soon as we have come to a conclusion
decide what is best for her. Had we
definite plans for more than the next
3 months we would have liked nothing
better than to have her with us. But
we have to see clearer about our own
position in the States and the general
situation before we can decide
when, for how long and if at all we
return to Rio. But in any case we
will be near Eva in the next months
and as often as possible with her, so
you need not worry any more. She will
not be lonely and you will get reports.
We shall of course write as soon as
we have seen her, investigate closely and
decide carefully and choose still more
carefully should it be preferable to
transfer her. - Although your letters to us
will be somewhat delayed for the next week
by being having to be forwarded from Rio,
we hope to have direct news through Eva.
Address until further notice
Viking Press, 18 East 48th Street
Newyork.
Love and kisses Lotte
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief, Ende.

pages.transcription:
AEROGRAMMA
VIA PANAIR
Dear Hannah & Manfred, I write from the
Plane, which has become since days our
normal way of living. For the first time I
must confess that I become a little tired and
no wonder; rising every day at 5.30 or even
4.30 and always surrounded by people when
you arrive and photographer and interviewer
while you are looking for your luggage. You
cannot imagine what travelling means today
and one pays all the beautiful things one sees
with a constant nervousness if all is in order
for the different frontier examinations. We
carry with us a whole bag of different papers,
our passports, our Brasilien permanence idea-
lity cards, which facilitates visas, our English
our Brasilien health certificate, our luggage
ticket, our luggage insurance, our air-tickets,
our American entry-papers, our fingerprints,
a dozen of photographs, and {more} our lecture
invitation-letters and I do not know what and
you have continually to fill out papers how
old you are and with what ship you arrived {32 years ago}
and at what date. And to know that if a single
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief auf einem Aerogramm-Formular. Die Tinte ist violett. Der Text ist gut lesbar.

pages.transcription:
of these papers goes lost while you show them
continually, you are held up and cannot go
forward or backward. We change now the
countries more than the shirts, yesterday we
had to live in the morning in Milreis, evening
with English coins and Trinidad
dollars (I never knew that they had other than
English money) and now I am perplexed by
the problem where to change my tropical clothing
against warm one, as all our luggage is
in the plane and we have no time to change
- I believe they will take me in Newyork
for a clown if I arrive at 15 below zero
in a tropical white and thin suit. By
this you can imagine, what distances we
hurry through - tonight we arrive after
8 hours plane in Florida, have to fight
for the refund of our tickets and to go
without sleeper sitting all night to Newyork
where we shall arrive at 6 in the morning
- the exact time we generally leave. I
hope to avoid that any newspaper will
know of our arrival, as we want badly
a few days of rest and not even days -
we are longing to have a few weeks or
month without hotel life and publicity
pages.notes: Fortsetzung des Briefes auf der Rückseite des Aerogramms.

pages.transcription:
But on the other hand it was a marvel that we
could do all this, as the greater part of the {Brasil}
voyage was paid to us and the other procured
by the kindness of our dear relatives; and it is
not to describe what we have seen all the way
long. Lotte is very courageous, He looked very
well in Rio and got even compliments; the
last days we are a little down, because we
had no sleep, constant talking and seeing
and seensighted (not only sightseeing). But I
am sure, a few days of rest will {give} her
a pep, as one says here; unfortunately we
will have to be busy a whole week in Newyork
before we can settle down for a while. What
after these weeks of rest? I cannot tell any
thing. We live in a time where it is impossible
to make arrangements beforehand, but we
are nearer now and you will always hear from
us.
We follow all the news with keenest interest,
and it seems that all the terrible sufferings
we all go through (and especially you)
will not be senseless. If this devil Hitler
is finally overthrown no loss, no price, no
suffering was too high and too long. I am
now very interested to see how the United
pages.notes: Fortsetzung des Briefes auf einem weiteren Blatt.

pages.transcription:
States feel - you know how depressed we
have been in July about her indifference, But
all this is now definitively over.
I hope that I shall hear about
Freudenthal and the few other friends. I
suppose that Manfred when he has finished
his Xray course will have a complete rest
and retire to Bath to complete rest. I do
not yet know if we can cable you from
Newyork as often as before and will try
to arrange it; I know that you are impa-
tient also to hear about your daughter
and it will be to Lotte to give you as
many particulars as possible. I myself
will have much to do in Newyork and
she has to go alone to La Rochelle the
first time.
Now while I write we are going
over Portorico and in a few moments
we will land there and enjoy a rest
of 20 minutes on the earth - this
stupid earth, which one loves without
to know why. Love to you all
StefanZweig
pages.notes: Schluss des Briefes.

pages.transcription:
AEROGRAMMA
VIA PANAIR

Dear Hannah and Manfred, we have yesterday
arrived and I suppose you are hungry for news
about your daughter; I hope Lotte will feed you
substantially as she was yesterday at La Rochelle
and we have Era today here in New York. She is looking
all right, somewhat grown up and a bit shy; you
will pardon me that I was a little severe with her
when she had to confess not to have written a
single line to her grandmother through half a year
(and what a year!!) I think one must fortify in
her the sentiment for responsability at this early
hour and especially as she is now under indiffe-
rent care. Physically she seems to have had
the best choice but I doubt if in the long run
the milicu[?] would be useful.
I had a letter from Edemann today. If
he finds something particulary good for me
there will be soon opportunity for I shall
have some cash {on my account at the Westminster Bank}
from the investments
have has to deliver and so I can dispose
of more money in England. Here we arrived
completely exhausted after the long voyage
- we started for the last part at Trinidad
pages.notes: Aerogramm, handschriftlich in violetter Tinte. Die Zeile 'on my account at the Westminster Bank' wurde über der Zeile eingefügt.

pages.transcription:
at 4.30 in the morning, arrived at 5 oclock
in Miami, had a view of the town and the
beach and went straight on with the night
clipper without sleepers at 9 and arrived at
6 in the morning (the sister airship crashed
in the same night.) We found, just coming
out of the tropical heat a nice snowstorm
and you may imagine how we are longing
to settle down for a few weeks of work and
rest. I found here offers from reviews and
newspapers and could write here as much
as I liked, but I have to finish my book.
(or books). By the way: I hear that a 'The
Tide of Fortune' has finally appeared in Eng
land - the first edition was completely
destroyed by fire at the bookbinder and
they had it to print again. I hope, they did
send the six authors copies to Bath - I have
here those of the American edition. Pardon me
if I write so little about what interests you
most - your Eva - but I leave this to Lotte.
Yesterday we had a family dinner at my
brother, tomorrow we are with Berta. Yours
Stefan
pages.notes: Fortsetzung des Briefes auf der Rückseite des Aerogramms.

pages.transcription:
AEROGRAMMA
VIA PANAIR

Saturday, 25.I.41.

First part
Dear Hanna & Manfred,
I find it somewhat difficult to give
you to-day already a definite opinion
about Eva's stay at Salmon's. I saw her
yesterday and to-day - shall meet Mrs. S.
on Monday in town - and can only say that
perhaps the surrounding atmosphere - in
cluding Mr. and Mrs. S - is somewhat dull
in comparison with all she saw and
heard and learned in your house and also
in Bath. They seem to be very kind with
Eva and she said she liked them both
- on the other hand ~~the~~ I suppose she
would have spoken differently of people
like for instance Raumanns. She just
finds them nice and likes it there
without being enthusiastic. But I
feel certain that this „liking“ is
real on her part, and so, even if we
should decide that it is better to
move her to another place you can
be quite reassured that no harm has
been done and that she has been quite
satisfied in friendly surroundings, even
though from an intellectual point of
view they were not ideal. - As to the
school Eva told me that the teacher
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief auf einem Aerogramm-Formular. Die Tinte ist gut lesbar.

pages.transcription:
had suggested that she should go already
to a high school instead of the one she is
in now - so that may give an easy
excuse for a change, if necessary.
In any case please don't worry
about this any more. We are near and
will look after her and only feel sorry
that owing to our own uncertainty we
cannot take her to live with us.
So these are our general first
impressions, and now you can turn
over to the other part in which I
just tell you about Eva. I thought
you might want first to know
our impression before you read what
we did together and how she lives.
Lotte
pages.notes: Rückseite des ersten Blattes. Handschriftlich.

pages.transcription:
AEROGRAMMA
VIA PANAIR

Read the other letter Newyork, 25.I.41
Dear Mummy. first
I was with Uncle Stefan and
Auntie Lotte today. It was very
nice. I hope you are well.
Love
and
kisses
Eva.

Dear Hanna & Manfred, I made Eva
begin the letter as a visual proof to you
that we have been together. I saw her yester-
day for an hour at New Rochelle - there was a
snowstorm and I had to leave earlier and
got out later than intended. Mrs. Salmon was
not at home, but I cannot blame her for it
for she rang me up inviting me to dinner
or to postpone my visit as she would be out.
But I wanted to see Eva, so I went out
and arranged to meet Mrs. S. for lunch on
Monday (I shall report on that as well, of
course). As to the surroundings: New Rochelle
is a suburb, very nicely situated in midst
of trees and woods, and the house looks out
on a little lake where there was skating.
Eva has got a pair of skates and begun to
learn already. As the skating started only
this week she cannot yet be an expert, but
she seemed to like it. - I stayed with her in
pages.notes: Zweites Blatt des Briefes. Enthält einen kurzen Abschnitt von Eva und den Beginn des Haupttextes von Lotte.

pages.transcription:
a lovely sitting-room, a huge window over-
looking the little lake, the room with modern
and tasteful furniture, a baby grand piano,
a huge Alsatian dog and the little boy
Peter - a nice-looking boy of 3 - crawling
about, too shy to speak. Eva herself was
a little bit shy too, in the beginning, and
I can in a way understand it; for me too,
it was a strange experience, coming to see
her as a visitor, where we had been living
a common life, so to speak. As I said, I
stayed about an hour, talking to the maid
which is nice, listening to a prelude of
Chopin for Eva did not want to play
me the Beethoven. She told me that the
teacher was much stricter than Miss
Luton, always picking out the difficult
parts for her to study specially - like
daddy. She likes the teacher but I
do not quite understand why this teacher
makes her play the Moonshine Sonata
and Chopin preludes if on the other
hand she takes it seriously. Eva said the
teacher had told her that the Moonshine
sonata was easy and that she could play
it. Well, I did not hear it, only the Chopin
prelude which she played quite well,
although rather too painstakingly. I also
pages.notes: Rückseite des zweiten Blattes. Handschriftlich.

pages.transcription:
saw her room which is very nice, has a writing
table and a terrace and all one wants. The
house itself seems not bigger than auntie
Ine's in Coverdale Road, but is in a good
neighbourhood and tastefully furnished as
far as I saw it. As to the little boy Eva
says that she does not play too much
with him because he bores her, which
seems quite normal in view of the difference
of age. She has a number of school friends
which she apparently sees quite a lot, but
she could not give any answer to my
motherly question (which I myself had always
hated to be asked) what their parents were
and which their father's profession. - In case
Eva has not given you a description of her
day, here it is: getting-up at 8 breakfast
at 8 1/2 (chocolate and roll) school at 9, lunch
in Salmon's house, school again and at
4 again at home. Then she reads,
afterwards practises, at 7 Mr. S. comes
home, Mrs S. is mostly at home, Eva says,
then they have dinner, afterwards Eva
does her homework and is in bed about
9. - Eva looks well and has grown some-
what, was wearing that check dress on
Friday and Saturday the red velvet dress
which now fits her perfectly. Saturday
Eva spent the day with us as fortunately
the piano lesson did not take place as
usually on Saturday mornings. She came
pages.notes: Drittes Blatt des Briefes. Handschriftlich.

pages.transcription:
to the hotel, later we had lunch together
(potato salad!), then I took her to a studio
tour through the Radio. Then we went
back to the hotel and stayed there
until it was time for her to go
back. There is a kind of taxi service
out to New Rochelle, which takes about
one hour and brings one from house to
house, running every hour and accomo-
dating 6 passengers. That is very convenient
as Eva does not need any company for the
way because she is fetched at home and
brought directly to her destination,
which before usually was Zweig's and
now is our hotel.
As to ourselves we feel already
rested and Stefan is longing to begin
work again. We hardly have seen any-
body except Huebsch and my brother-

we met in the street we have remained
so far anonymous and enjoy it. I hope
to hear soon from you c/o Viking Press
and expect also one or two letters for-

18 East 48th Street                                Newyork, 27.I.1941.

Dear Hanna & Manfred,
I have had a long talk with Mrs. Salmon today and we
have agreed - in all friendship - that it will be better for both parts if
we find another home for Eva. I find it hard to blame one or the other, it
is just that they are not suited to each other. Mrs. S. told me: "We thought
of taking in a child, but she is just a guest". Mr. S. who apparently tried
very hard in the beginning to gain her confidence, did not succeed, and when
he later tried teasing, apparently this did not turn out too well, either. I
must say that I had not a bad impression of Mrs. S. - quite apart from her not
answering letters and disliking visitors, a point which I did not even mention
when I saw that it was not only our, but also their idea that a separation
might be the best. Eva does not seem to know quite clearly what is wrong,
but I wrote you yesterday, she seemed bored, and she seems to have shown it.
They have not been able to establish a real contact with Eva which they defi-
nitely have tried, and they, too, were somewhat disappointed. If it was any-
one's mistake, it probably was mine, for when Rose Wohl told me that Salmon's
wanted to take a child, she said that they were no intellectuals, and at that
time where our own future was absolutely uncertain and the chances for our re-
turn to USA seemed not too good, I was only concerned in finding a home where
the people really wanted a child and where I felt sure that they would be kind
And that they have been kind to her, and that, if they did not really become
intimate friends, they lived well together and Eva was in no way unhappy,
there can be no doubt, and definitely no harm has been done. I am now trying
to find another home for her and we are thinking that perhaps a boardingschool
might be best for her as in this moment she seems to be in a period where she
does not know what to do with herself and needs stimulation (which I admit she
did not get in S.'s home) as well as some kind of discipline. I am afraid it
is no good that I tell you in detail how and where I try to get information
about a new place. But you may be sure that there is not the slightest need
in transferring her in a hurry and that we will do all our best to ensure that
no further change will be necessary. As to Mr. Haas - (I just now got your
letter of Jan 7th with the address) - I will do all I can to visit the childre
or at least to see him. I have no idea about the distance to Scardale, and at
the present moment the snowstorms make travelling aut to the country somewhat
of an adventure. I am sorry we cannot consult you before making a decision,
but you understand that this is not possible by letter and by cable we could
not give any details. In any case the matter will soon be settled and pro-
bably before you get this letter, Eva will be in new surroundings, this
time chosen deliberatly more with regard to the milieu than it was possible
a few months ago. - By the way, before I finish my report about Eva today,
I only want to say that a short time she sent a letter by boat. I understood
that Mr. Salmon had written you too, and apparently the letter became too
heavy. So do not worry if there should be a gap in the arrival of the
Eva's airmail letters.
We were glad to get your letters to-day and surprised
to hear that Manfred is already about to pass his examination. It is already
the final one? I have no doubt that you will pass it without difficulty, and
I hope that you will both spend a longer period in Bath after that. I have
the idea that I wrote to Raumans some time ago, but I am not quite sure and
will write them again. They are certainly good lodgers and I have no doubt
about Mrs. R.'s cooking. - Have you now settled down completely in Regency
Lodge and where did you put your furniture in Bath? I am glad that Marta can
remain with you and I am sure Smollett's are very content too. - We have
already cabled you that we got the tickets still in time and could use them,
and I hope you did not have too much trouble in arranging all that. We are
glad to have done with flying and sightseeing for a while, and that this time
our rooms look out on a big stone wall, is almost a welcome contrast after
all the beautiful things and views we have seen. We have acclimatised our-
selves very easily to the cold, but find it more difficult to get used to

the central heating. Stefan has not yet begun to work in earnest and I did
not begin working at all. We have rested these days, went to bed extremely
early and only saw very few friends. I went to see Rose Wohl yesterdaybecause
I wanted to get some information. Of course I got quite a different account
of the story about John, but I am inclined to believe it. The trouble was
that John arrived in America with the firm determination to dislike everything
as he had not wanted to come, and they said that for five months nothing had
interested him but the movies and nothing had been good enough for him. And
that they had tried to understand and discuss his way of behaving, seems to
have made the matter worse, for he despised them for it, and from what they
told me behaved as disagreeably as he could, and of course influenced Robin.
Since a fortnight he is with a friend of Carmel's, but they separated quite
peacefully and he comes to see them all the time. Whether he felt happier
there, they did not yet know. I saw Robin coming home from the pictures, and
he looked very well and seemed to feel quite at home. They have slightly
larger flat now, Robin has the one bedroom, Berner's the other and Rose sleeps
in the dining room. I have thought a moment of writing Carmel directly, but I
do not think she would very much appreciate if I just tell her what I had
heard. If you see her, tell her that I met Robin, that he looked well and
quite happy, and that I had gained the impression that Berner's as well as
Rose had done their best. Rose explained her not writing to Carmel by saying
that they were so troubled and did not want to report this while they still
hoped that John might settle down.
We are at the moment considering to go to Newhaven
where the Yale university is, about 1 1/2 hours from New York and good connections
by train. We are both looking forward impatiently to settle down for we are
tired of hotel rooms, restaurant food and above all of the little space
available for working purposes. But I suppose it will be at least another
week before we have settled everything here. I have not the slightest
idea what Newhaven is like, but as long as it is possible to rent a two- or
three room flat furnished for two or three months, I shall be satisfied.

I have told you very much in detail and with all sin-
cerity about Eva and Salmon's to explain the situation, and you may be abso-
lutely certain that there is nothing else behind it. It is nothing wrong
between them, there have been no incidents and no quarrels, it is only the
difference of milieu - he likes football and fun- which makes them not abso-
lutely suited to each other. There is nothing we have hidden from you and
nothing for you to worry about. And now we are near and we still have not
given up our guardianship and do not intend to do so. All we want you to
do is to keep well and fresh and to look after our house in Bath by spending
as much of your time there as you possibly can.

Fondest love and kisses,
kindest regards to all the friends,

Lotte.

27. I 1941 Dear H. a. Manfred, Lotte will write
you about Eva more in detail. Please do not
worry, we shall find the right thing. I personally
believe she should be somewhere, where there is
more discipline and also more continental atmos-
phere; perhaps because I am a writer that I attach
more importance to spontaneous writing {than others} and I was
not satisfied with Eva on this behalf - for instance
my sister in law did send her very nice Christmas
presents (also for the boy at Salinas) and she thanked
for it the 16th of January, three weeks later! There
must be someone who looks after her in all those
things of negligence which are every one trifling
but if they become a habit would affect her charac-
ter and be a big disadvantage in later life. I am
sorry we cannot take her with us when we are
going now to a little place {or town} because all is
too uncertain how long we shall stay there as it
will suit us there - I believe some boarding-school
would be the best and we will look round in the
next days to arrange all as well as we can
before we leave, which will be in any case not
before the first week-end in February. The weather
is here as bad as possible - what a contrast with
Rio! We hope you feel alright! Kindest regards
to all! Yours
StefanZweig

18 East 48th Street
Newyork.                                Newyork, 29th Jan. 1941.

Dear Hanna, dear Manfred,
I hope you did not expect a cable after our
meeting with Eva, but Stefan thought I should wait until I had some-
thing definite to tell. This also can only be a preliminary report
as nothing is decided yet and I am now waiting for neutral reports
and references of the different places in question. I have been at
Croton on the Hudson - three quarters of an hour by train from Newyork -
and seen Mrs. Schaeffer, the wife of the German poet Albrecht Schaeffer
who came here also as refugees and who has a large house and in addition
to her many children (three in school age, two grown up and one appa-
rently ill and not with them) about twelve to fifteen children in all
different ages. There is none exactly in Eva's age, but two girls of
ten and a few boys of twelve and thirteen. I had an excellent impression
of Mrs. Schaeffer, the first women who in her way of thinking and
speaking reminded me a little of you and with whom I could discuss
things as we would have done it. The house is already a little small
for them and they are planning to build one or two more rooms in March.
It is a little ~~prx~~ packed, therefore, and very plain, but I don't
think this would matter. The house itself is situated in a large
garden, has vegetable garden, orchard and fowls, and the children are
supposed to help a little with all that. They also have to make their
own beds, clean their shoes and help serving at table. There are also
different hours where instead of English they are supposed to speak
French or German. Personally I liked all these arrangements, and Mrs.
Sch.'s husband, the poet, does not hinder in any way as he lives across
the road in a tiny little garden house and does some poetry so pure
that it goes above our heads. As to religion, they have some christian
and a few Jewish children. They themselves are Christians but besides
a general "christian spirit" there is no religious service or influence
in the house. I am hesitant, however, about the choice of schools
should I decide to put her there. There are two, one very modern and
"progressive" ( a term which I have not yet been able to analyse pro-
perly except that it has something to do with awakening the creative
in the child and group work), the other the Croton public school. I
am expecting reports about these two from an Educational Advisory
Committee where I have been today. The problem is that most of the
children at Mrs. Sch.'s - 13 out of 15 - go the progressive school,
and that, if we do not like the idea of that school, it seems a little
doubtful whether she/feel happy to go to the other. - This is the one
possibility which would we are still examining from all points of
view. The other one is a boarding school of about forty girls, also
near Newyork which has been recommended to me by friends of my sister-
in-laws. I have met the proprietress here in Newyork to-day, a little
the Galician Jewish type but quite civilized and clever. I shall go
and see the school on Sunday and cannot form a judgment before. I shall
also try to get information about it through that committee. That would
be again anxxx a completely American surrounding, and I would have to
find out what the teaching is worth. - Number three is that I have
written to Einstein's and am expecting their answer. - Number 4 is
an offer of an immigrated doctor whose wife has two nearly grown-up
children and would like to have a younger one again in the house.

18 East 48th Street
Newyork.                                Newyork, 31st January 1941.

Dear Hanna and Manfred,

My wife has written you that we have finally
settled Eva, and I believe that the whole matter will be arranged to
your entire satisfaction. In the school she will have plenty of
company and of Mrs. Schaeffer, in whose home she is going to live,
we have an excellent impression.
Now the material side of the matter. Thanks
to the generosity of Mr. Salmon where she has been living until now
you have been up to now in the privileged position not to have had
to ask the Treasury for any permission of sending your child money
for nearly six months. Also now the expenses will be nearly com-
pletely covered through reduced fees and through relatives. It will
be only necessary for you to ask permission for the transfer of a
limited amount for smaller expenses, for books, dresses, shoes,
luncheon money, fares, stamps etc. as we would not like to ask our
relatives here also for those things; you know they have plenty of
other obligations. We have been informed that such trifling sums
for the extra expenses have been granted to the parents of British
children over here, and I would advise you to make an application
for such additional monthly contributions. I can assure you that
the school as well as her new home are run on very simple lines, but
nevertheless you know that there are always a number of small extras
to be paid. If you get permission for such a transfer, the money
should be sent directly to Eva's new home, Mrs. A. Schaeffer, Amity
Hall, Mount Airy Road, Croton-on-Hudson, New York.
We are alright here. We have had a good rest
after that exhausting journey, and I have now taken up my work again,
happy to be quietly in my room without any social obligations for the
time being.

Warmest regards

Stefan Zweig

Dear Hannah and Manfred, As I know you will be anxious about
your child I want to give you some details about her new guardians.
I know Albrecht Schaeffer since twenty years, he is from a very good
protestant family and an excellent poet - all his books have been
published at the Insel - and an upright caracter, our friends the Belau
or Fricental can give you full information. In the last years he did
more philosophe and abstract work, has retired into the country and
his wife, who is a very intelligent, active and motherly person, has always
managed his material life; you may rely upon her, she is not greedy
or business-like and the nation will be an excellent one. I like that
Eva should be in a niet atmosphere of English, American and also
some, but only some Jewish children, get accostumed to an simple
but in the same time intelligent way of life and remain friends of
America in a continental atmosphere. Schaeffers left by disgust and
sentiment of freedom without racial or political reasons, they are
upright people like Haas and Belau without the resentment and
exaltation of the Newyork-refugees. I am sure it will work well and
as I am very sceptical about the manner of pure American education
which is superficial and creates but an arrogant shallowness, I
am glad that she will be in a nation which combines strictness
and order with intelligence and culture. Furthermore we will be
near the next months and so you can be absolutely sure, please do
not worry; we have felt our responsability and closer after con-
sidering all the most various possibilities before (there was an ex-
cellent doctors faculty but it was in Newyork and there she would
have had no company and not the right opportunity of being in
the open air) it is better for the future, not to be educated as a
society-lady but accostumed to practical simple life as you have been
in your birthplace. - We ourselves are anxious to leave Newyork. I
get depressed in being the luxury-shops, the thoughtlessness of all this
people, the stupidity of the refugees and the lack of real compassion

[Randnotiz links:] I hope to go to Newhaven, a little town 112 from Newyork but which contains the
Vale University with the library, there we will live the next two months and work
and study; I had yesterday a long talk with [?]

Dear Hanna And Manfred,
Eva has just left after spending the day with us,
and she was as she has always been with us without any trace of shyness.
We told her that we were going to transfer her to another school and home,
and after making sure that it was not in Newyork itself - did she always
dislike the big towns like that? - she seemed to like the idea, although
she said she regretted a little having to leave that school and her school
friends. But I reassured her that if these were really good friends, they
could come and see her as New Rochelle and Croton are only about forty
minutes distance from each other. On the whole, I think, she likes the
change and I am confident that she will like it even better when she is
there. We told her that we have considered a change as that school there
was not the right thing for her and as she was rather lonely without
children in her age in the house. - But now you will want to know every-
thing about the new arrangement. I wrote you in my last letter about Mrs.
Schaeffer, the wife of the poet Albrecht Schaeffer (who lives in a little
summerhouse in the garden) who came here as refugees and have immigrated,
has taken in addition to her own children - three in school age and one
grown-up daughter who helps her - about a dozen or forteen other children
in various ages in her house and runs the whole as a large family, with
the help of two councillors and a married servant couple. I liked her very
much; that she is not Jewish and has six children, gives her a mixture
of detachment combined with motherly understanding and I have a
feeling that you would like her very much and that your ideas on the whole
are very much like hers. She said that except a few basic rules which she
strictly imposes - punctuality, writing home once a week, clean hands and
good table manners, no "funnies", no wireless except for special programs,
pictures only if there is something worth seeing and no chewing gum - the
children are free to do what they like. They have a few household duties,
make their own beds, help to serve at table, clean their own shoes, feed
the chicken, and that they are supposed to speak French one hour of the day,
the hour varying so that they get used to express themselves in different
circumstances, somehow brought me back our common life at Bath. At
first I was a little doubtful because there are no children exactly of
her age, but there are I believe two girls of ten and boys of 12 and 13,
and I think that will be alright.

Then I was for some time undecided about the school question, and I believe
I wrote you about it. But after making enquiries in various quarters and
being told that I should be glad if the "progressive" school would take her
as just this one has an excellent reputation, I decided for that one, the
more so as Mrs. Sch. from the beginning was more in favour of that one al-
though she said that the Croton public school was also very good and had a
very good reputation. - So we are going up there on Tuesday with Eva and
possibly Stefan, and if the interview with the headmistress is satisfactory,
I hope to have settled the matter so that you can be quite reassured. If
Mrs. Sch. tells me that they will probably keep her one or two days in the
school on trial to see whether she likes it, and should this not be the
case she can always go in the public school which, as I told you, is also
supposed to be very good. In that progressive school which is a private
school, we expect to get Eva a full scholarship. About the material side
Stefan has written to you. At Mrs. Sch.'s there is not very much to pay,
but it would of course be a relief for our relatives with their many
obligations if you would get permission to transfer a certain sum as a
contribution to your child's education. I was told that this can be done.
- Last week I went with all my doubts and problems to the Child's Study
Association (the address was given to me by Mrs. Haas) and I shall remain
in touch with them in any case, I had such an excellent impression of Mrs.
Cury with whom I discussed everything. She has lived in England, had a
school in Hamstead herself and has children who also, when they came over,
found the schools here so easy and so different. Somehow I have a feeling
that it is good to know someone in these committees who can advise and
might be useful in any little problems that may arise. - The Smollett
children I could not yet see, and please explain to Lotte that they live
about 20 miles out of Newyork, which takes some time if you have no car,
and as Mrs. Haas is busy with some charity work and wanted to make an
appointment days before, I could not arrange it this time as we had a lot
to do, I had many appointments about Eva and now we have not yet been to
Newhaven to look for a flat and will have to do it this week. - Please
inform also Mother that I shall probably not be able to write her a se-
parate letter this week. Next week we hope to be settled already and I
hope to find a flat which will also allow us to have Eva stay with us
for a little while when she has holidays again. Let me emphasise once
more that you should follow Stefan's advise that Manfred should take a
long rest in Bath after his exam in February. I think that he is quite
right that under no circumstances should you spend the beginning of spring
in London. We would feel so much happier if we know that you both are
taking a well-earned rest in Bath just in these next months after this
hard winter.

With best love and kisses

We have just been after months being ourselves
the healers and the others the listeners in Bruno Walters
concert in his box with a lot of ghosts from another life like
Mrs Stresemann and a singer which I heard first 42 years ago.
We had after that a nice talk with Walter and Erica Mann
your, Lotte

pages.transcription:
4.II.41
Dear Hanna u. Manfred,
I'll have to be a little shorter to-day as we have
to go out very soon. Fortunately I have written you almost everything so
that I need not add much. Our telegram to-day gave you Eva's address:
Amity Hall
Mount Airy Road
Croton-on-Hudson
New York.
We took her up there to-day - that is to say we went to New Rochelle and
Mr. Salmon took us over to Croton in his car, waited until I had been at
the school, discussed all the arrangements with Mrs. Schaeffer, and then
took us back to New York. I believe I wrote you all about Mrs. Schaeffer
in my last letter. The house, as Stefan writes, is beautifully situated
with large grounds, but it is very plainly furnished and run on very simple
lines. It is a little on the primitive side (but has good windows and
centralheating) but I do not think Eva will miss anything. The food is
plain and good - I had lunch there twice - and as to company there should
be several among fifteen children between 3 and 14 years of age. That she
will have to choose herself, I did not see more than one or two children,
as most of them were at school.
As to school, we decided for the Hessian Hill School,
a rather progressive private school, that means a lot of independent and
private work if I understood it right. I was a little hesitant at first,
as I am beginning to get oldfashioned, but it was recommended from various
sides as an excellent school with only very good staff. So Eva will go
there to-morrow and the day after as visitor and will get to know it. Mrs.
Sch. who has 13 of her 15 children in that school warned me that probably
it would take a week for her to adapt herself to that different way of
learnin and teaching. But she says that it has an excellent influence
on the children, and she is very sensible, normal and not at all verstiegen
in her views, and I trust her opinion. Also Stefan had a very good impression
of her, and he knows her husband since many years. - I'll phone Eva in a
few days to see how she feels in the new and completely different surroun-
dings - imagine the contrast between Salmon's house where she had all the
attention and could do what she wanted and had every wish granted and a nice
but very modest home with fifteen children. But I hope she will feel at
home there very quickly and like the change.
As to Salmon's I must say that they behaved very decently;
Mr. S. seems to have overdone his efforts to gain her love and confidence and
in some strange reaction she does not care very much for him although she
likes them both. But Mr. S. really felt sorry at her leaving and immediate-
ly arranged with Mrs. Sch. that Eva should spend the first free weekend -
they are allowed to go away for the weekend once a month,but can have visitors
every Saturday and Sunday and go out with them for the day - again at his
house.He is quite determined that the ~~xxxx~~ relationship shall not be at an
end, and maybe that they will understand each other better when they are not
always together. Of Mrs. Salmon too I had again not a bad impression. She
is much cooler and reserved than her husband, but as I myself am not too
effusive towards people I hardly know, I hm not the one to blame her for it.
On the whole I believe Eva will be more satisfied in her new surroundings in
spite of the fact that at S.'s she was spoilt and could do whatever she felt
like doing.
As to music lessons, the Hessian Hill School is supposed
to have very good teachers, and she can take her lessons there. There is a
piano at Schaeffer's although not a grand piano and I am afraid, even not a
very good one.
I hope you are well and follow our request and go to
Bath now for some months, I both of you. Kindest regards, best love Lotte

[Randnotiz links, vertikal geschrieben:]
Thanks for your letter of jan 13th which we received two days ago.

pages.transcription:
Dear Hannah and Manfred, I write to you as short and clear as possible
without to alter the facts; I suppose you want to know my sincere impression.
We took today Eva from Mr Salmons house who was so kind to bring us over
with the car to Croton. The Salmons house is charming and I must say frankly
it was not Salmons fault if all did not work as we hoped. He is a very nice
fellow, and has given Eva all possible care and love. His weakness is perhaps
that he wants a little too much ~~admires~~ {to be} admired, loved
and thanked. And it seems that Eva by a kind of unconscious opposition has
just this refuses to him, she treated him (I have observed it myself) in a bit
cold and ironic way just because he wanted effusion and tenderness. Mr
Salmon and I agreed upon several points, especially about the question of letters.
As myself he was disappointed (and suspected an indifference of the heart
or the imagination) that she has always ~~been~~ pushed and forced to write to
you and he called quite rightly her letters to you „masterpieces of lack of
information“ She is indeed clever and yet enough not only to write to you
her silly „It has been nice“ but to think over what she has to report over
her school, her daily life, to give details and to understand better in
what danger and plight you live. All this I said her most seriously also for
my part, as it was really unpardonable, that she thanked my sister in law, who
went in aid of the Christmas trouble to buy her presents, just four weeks after
and that she had not the thought herself to write a line to her grandmother
in six months. As to the piano-playing her ambition is much greater than
her eagerness to practice; she is, I believe, just in an age or a transition,
where one must beware her of certain „Wurschtigkeit“ of sentiment and care-
lessness. Therefore I am glad that she is now at Mrs Schaeffer, who by having
educated six of her own children {and will look after her in} a more continental way will be much
more efficient. The boarding house is beautifully situated but, what I do not
want to conceal from you, run on very modest conditions. Eva will not
find the commodities of Salmons, not be the centre of attention, but to have
to clean her boots, her room. But believe me, a real American boarding school
would have brought silliness {and} superficiality and as the future of us all
is very obscure, I am convinced that it is better if she gets accustomed to
modest surroundings. The school seems to be excellent and as to Alfred
Schaeffer I know him since years - he is upright and a completely immature
little men, for whom his very effective wife cares like for a child - she
pleases me very much and we have the best feeling, that Eva is in units of the other children will
have a good time. Mr Salmon will continue to look after her and we ourselves will as to far as possible
for not to come again to Croton. Thats all and please - more to both both as soon as possible
Please write to Salmons - they have really been very nice to her.
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief auf einem Blatt, beidseitig beschrieben. Der Text am linken Rand und am rechten Rand ist vertikal geschrieben. Die Tinte ist violett.
Rückseite des Dokuments, leer.

pages.transcription:
Newyork, 10. II. 41

Dear Hanna,
I am in a hurry, having to leave for
Newhaven in a few minutes where I am flat-
hunting. I want to tell you that I went to see
Eva yesterday in her new home and found her
very satisfied, and in my opinion already more at
home than she ever was at Salmon's. She likes the
new school, there are very nice children at Schaeffer's
as far as I saw them yesterday. I spent two hours
there and liked it very much and Eva was her old
self, gay, affectionate and lively. For the moment
there are no girls in her exact age at Amity Hall,
but just yesterday a girl of 14 arrived and more are
in prospect. What Eva is not yet quite used to,
she says, is the noise and being so much outdoors.
But the weather was particularly bad the last days
and as she is her father's daughter I can under-
stand that it will take her a little time to get
to like outdoor sports. But everything else she
likes very much.
I have to leave now, so only best love
and thanks for your letter N°2 to Newyork of Jan 22nd.
Yours, Lotte
Dear Hannah, before all, you must not worry about Eva. We have
the best impression of Mrs Schaeffer's house, especially when this horrid
cold weather will be over and the verandahs, the garden to be used
so that the children there will more dispersed. Now they are in the eve-
ning all together in one big hall and of all ages, but these days of
bitter frost will pass soon and she has already made many friends. Mrs Schaeffer
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief auf zwei Seiten (Vorderseite). Die letzten Zeilen sind am unteren Rand quer geschrieben.
Rückseite des ersten Blattes, leer.

pages.transcription:
so that you can give it to my lawyer Mr. Wilenor[?]. You cannot imagine
how through this travelling from Uruguay to Brazil and the States all my
correspondence is in disorder, I hear and have nothing and it will be diffi-
cult to keep order. We feel physically all right, but imagine how we hate
this continual packing, how boring it is to travel with all manuscripts and
notes and different drafts from hotel to hotel, never to have space and to
have at the same time a house at home, where I could work quickly - poor
Lotte does not know where to correct the different copies, the bed, the floor
all is always overflooded with typewritten paper. I would be glad could we
find at Newhaven, where the Yale University gives me all facilities a flat
for two or three month to finish my book!! But there are no factories
and all flats taken and I will not stay at Newyork, which is rather ex-
pensive and where I have no quiet moment. I asked here my friend at
the consulate, he tells me that there are now no possibilities of passage
and the clipper is taken for months; so we will probably return to Rio
in the summer. But who can make plans! Who can say "I will", "I intend"
- one must be satisfied to live and I want all my will-power to
continue working in midst of this turmoil.
About your friend Forschauer nothing will astonish
me. He came and told that he is citizen (that surely is not true / has
visit cards (for bluffing) as "Chairman of Associated Correspondents"
and perhaps he will catch some innocent people by this blunder. I be-
lieve he will soon leave Brazil as now visas for immigrants are rarely
available for all who are out of Europe; the quota became suddenly opened
as all those who has the numbers in Europe are unable to travel; all those
who are already in Cuba, Mexico or South America can get them easily
and if Eva would come to Cuba all would be easy. I spoke with
his daughter, he wish both to have him over and are both afraid of the
voyage in this moment. I hope you will go soon to Bath with Lartor[?],
I would prefer to know you there for a rest after the strenuous weeks.
And please, be sure, that Eva is in best care. To be traveller yesterday to see her
today she is in Newhaven - how wonderful must it be to sit quietly
a few weeks in the same place! Yours Stefan Zweig
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief auf der zweiten Seite des Bogens. Am linken Rand befindet sich ein vertikal geschriebener Zusatz.
Rückseite des zweiten Blattes, leer.

pages.transcription:
is excellent and very careful, but now she phoned me, that she wants like
to bring Eva (without any actual pain) to the dentist, because she has not
been looked over since more than half a year. You see by this little detail
that she thinks on everything and I believe that Eva by being mixed with
children of different age (till to 14 / different languages, religions and so on
will get beyond the school-instruction a good deal of life-experience. She
has an easy way to adapt herself and we hope that the school will accept
her without any fee. It seems to be a very interesting school and your
daughter has to do her first essays in art, she painted a view of Bath
and has to try modelling and they give lectures and play theatre - you
must understand that all is not very serious and mixes fun with in-
struction in a quite new way. As on the other hand she has continental
education at Mrs Schaeffer at home, she will have in my opinion very
great advantages and she will have to tell you a lot when we meet again.
Now I have to ask you a favour. I do not like very much to
worry you as I know that every little way and walk is no pleasure now.
When we left we forgot to take with us our birth-certificates and
our marriage certificate; we could manage to get the different visas by
protection without that, but in the long run - who could believe that
we could not return in December? - it would be better to have them. They
are in the library in the documents safe and you will easily find them
but it would be better before to send them to let make a simple photography
the birth-certificates (the other we have in two copies) and perhaps let
certify the copies by a notary (Ingram or other). We do not want them
for a special purpose, but we may want them; it was a great mistake
of ours not to have these documents with us, but who could think of all
this formalism which rules now everywhere!! It is a harry at all!
I wrote to Cassels to send the author-copy of my last
book to Bath and I hope he will do it. By the way I would ask you
to make regularly notes of all that came in during my absence
on literary income (not income from investments, this will be done
directly by the bank) as in April I have to have it ready for the person
